objectives: To investigate the risk perception of professionals regarding prefabricated buildings when adopting the EPC (Engineering-Procurement-Construction) delivery mode in China, to identify major risks, establish a comprehensive risk-assessment system, construct a grey-fuzzy evaluation method, and apply it to a real case project.
problem_statement: Existing research on prefabricated buildings in China has rarely linked risks specifically to the EPC delivery mode; professional understanding of EPC-related risk perception is insufficient despite many risks being identified in prior studies; and there are limited comprehensive assessment methods for prefabricated buildings using EPC.
methodology: Mixed-methods triangulated study: literature review to generate an initial list of 30 risk indicators; questionnaire survey (159 distributed, 137 valid responses) of AEC practitioners in China's Yangtze Delta region to refine/validate indicators via descriptive statistics (mean, SD, discrete value) and Cronbach's alpha reliability testing; development of a combined AHP-Entropy Weight Method (AHP-EWM) for indicator weighting; construction of a grey-fuzzy comprehensive evaluation model; application of the model to a real case study - a school project in Nanjing, China delivered under EPC with >40% prefabrication rate, using expert scoring from 12 managers/engineers in two groups (importance scoring and risk-level scoring).
key_background_studies: Jiang et al. [1,2] - SWOT analysis and interviews identifying barriers to prefabricated building adoption in China (policy, market, skill gaps)
Razkenari et al. [30] - SWOT framework analysis of offsite construction industry in the United States
Nadim and Goulding [31] - argued European reluctance to adopt assembly methods due to past unsuccessful experiences
Rahimian et al. [33] - examined offsite construction risks in Nigeria including negative perceptions and technical capacity gaps
Gan et al. [3,4] - identified stakeholder collaboration as a key risk in prefabricated building development
Xue et al. [6] - explored relationship between stakeholder cooperative management and cost performance in prefabricated buildings
Pal et al. [47] - investigated subcontractor relationships and their effect on EPC project performance (trust, cooperation)
Gao and Wang [48] - determined main risks faced by general contractors in EPC through case analysis across bidding, design, procurement, construction stages
Yang et al. [43] - path analysis showing interface management and partnering improve EPC project performance and risk management
Jin et al. [27] - argued EPC integrates upstream/downstream labor divisions into a complete construction chain
findings: The risk-assessment system finalized 7 first-level and 27 second-level risk indicators. Applying the AHP-EWM combined weighting and grey-fuzzy evaluation to the Nanjing case study yielded an overall risk evaluation value of 3.3203, indicating medium project risk. Construction risk (weight 0.4814) and design risk (weight 0.2298) were the dominant risk categories, followed by procurement (0.0885), management (0.0864), nature (0.0570), and policy (0.0251, least impactful, attributed to favorable regional policy in Jiangsu). Within construction risk, temporary support system instability was the largest sub-risk; within design risk, insufficiently in-depth design dominated; within procurement, quality defects of precast components dominated; within economic risk, developer credibility/payment ability dominated.

ideas.idea: EPC transfers most project risk from owner to general contractor, who becomes responsible for design, procurement and construction as an integrated whole.
ideas.quote: The EPC mode transfers most of the risks in the project from the owner to the general contractor

ideas.idea: The complexity of coordinating design, manufacture, transport and site assembly across many stakeholders is a core challenge of prefabricated construction that EPC is meant to solve.
ideas.quote: the supply chain involves multiple stages in prefabricated buildings, including design, production, transportation, and hoisting; any disruption that occurs at the upper part of the supply chain affects subsequent stages

ideas.idea: Under EPC, the general contractor takes a leading design role and comprehensively coordinates manufacture and assembly, avoiding split/fragmented construction common in prefabrication.
ideas.quote: The general contractor takes on the leading role in the design and comprehensively coordinates the manufacture and assembly as it pertains to the overall objective of the project [29], which can avoid the split construction of prefabricated buildings.

ideas.idea: Insufficiently detailed ('in-depth') design of precast components, requiring close coordination among disciplines, is a major source of design risk in prefabricated EPC projects.
ideas.quote: errors and omissions of precast components can only be avoided by close cooperation between various professionals and participants

ideas.idea: Design and procurement can and should overlap under EPC, since material/component requirements are determined during design, enabling three-way collaboration between designers, engineers and purchasers.
ideas.quote: design and procurement in EPC can intersect reasonably, since the materials required for the whole process of a construction project are also determined in the design stage.

ideas.idea: Quality defects in precast components (size deviation, insufficient strength, non-conforming specifications) and transport damage are dominant procurement-stage risks specific to prefabrication.
ideas.quote: the procurement risk focused on the quality defects and transportation damage of prefabricated buildings

ideas.idea: Temporary support systems for hoisted precast components are a critical, high-weight construction risk requiring careful design and anchoring rather than temporary fixes.
ideas.quote: Temporary supports, precast components, and completed structures need to be anchored with reserved bolts rather than temporary frills.

ideas.idea: Because EPC contracts are typically fixed-price and place nearly all responsibility on the contractor, economic risks such as developer payment delays and price fluctuations disproportionately burden the general contractor.
ideas.quote: Since the EPC contractor undertook almost all of the tasks with a fixed price, it was a great challenge for them to take all or most of the risks.

ideas.idea: Lack of standardized design techniques and unsound specifications for prefabricated buildings under EPC represent policy/regulatory risk that varies significantly by region due to uneven government incentive programs.
ideas.quote: policy had the least impact on the final determination of the risk level... Jiangsu has more beneficial policies, in terms of both technology and management, which provide a guarantee for the advancement of prefabricated buildings.

ideas.idea: EPC general contracting management goes beyond simple superposition of design, production, procurement and hoisting; it requires strategic, integrated supply-chain management capability.
ideas.quote: EPC general contracting management is not simply the superposition of design, production, procurement, and hoisting. It goes beyond the project to the level of business operation and development strategy.

objectives: To develop a comprehensive typology of the causes of disputes in construction projects through a systematic literature review, to identify significant causes, analyze their distribution across countries, and build a conceptual framework depicting the interrelationships (antecedent and descendant causes) among dispute causes, with particular focus on payment delays.
problem_statement: Despite extensive prior research on construction disputes, disputes continue to occur frequently and cause severe project impacts; existing studies offer fragmented, inconsistent classifications of dispute causes and lack a systematic, comprehensive framework that maps the interrelationships between causes (antecedent and descendant), leaving a gap in understanding root causes for proactive dispute avoidance.
methodology: A systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2021 flow diagram was conducted using Scopus and Web of Science databases. An initial 2,816 articles were identified via a search string on disputes/causes/avoidance in construction; after removing duplicates, screening titles/abstracts/keywords, and full-text screening, 43 journal articles (2013–2023) were selected for detailed review. Causes were extracted, grouped by frequency and similarity into 136 causes and 12 primary dispute categories, informed by contract theory, systems theory, and behavioral economic theory. A conceptual framework was then developed using process modeling technique to depict antecedent and descendant relationships, focusing in depth on payment delays by clients.
key_background_studies: Wang et al. (2023b) - classified dispute causes into delay-related, communication, contractual, site condition and design problems; used as a comparative classification
Alrasheed et al. (2023) - Kuwaiti court case analysis proposing four dispute classifications (abnormal conditions, financial, project delays, project management) and quantifying claim values by cause
Titus et al. (2023) - Nigerian study linking contract incompleteness and opportunism to dispute frequency
El-Sayegh et al. (2020) - UAE study identifying owner/designer/contractor/contractual causes including poorly drafted contracts, bidding to lowest price, and unrealistic timeframes
Francis et al. (2022) - Sri Lankan study identifying payment delay as most frequent cause and detailing client- and consultant-driven payment delay mechanisms
Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2021) - US modular construction study showing scope of work changes and bid-related issues leading to disputes
Cheung and Pang (2012) - theoretical work defining contract incompleteness and opportunism as sources of dispute
Rahnamayiezekavat et al. (2022) - Australian (NSW) study ranking contract incompleteness and quality disputes among most frequent
Mahamid (2016) - classification of dispute causes into direct and indirect categories
Tanriverdi et al. (2021) - causal model of 11 factors contributing to scope changes and variations
Senaratne and Farhan (2022) - identified cost-related payment claims as most common dispute source
Hansen and Nindartin (2022) - Indonesian case study on contract change order disputes classified by owner/consultant/contractor
findings: The review identified 136 distinct causes of construction disputes grouped into 12 primary categories (payment/financial, delay, design/scope, contract, bidding, project management, client administration, quality, risk, claim/dispute management, behavioral/professional, and external factors). Payment delays by the client emerged as the most significant and frequently cited cause (28/43 studies), followed by scope of work changes and contractual ambiguities. Disputes occur in both developed and developing countries, though the dominant causes vary by context (e.g., contract ambiguity in Middle East, payment delays in multiple regions). A conceptual framework was developed showing payment delay's antecedent causes (e.g., contractor progress delay, budget overruns, funding issues, poor quality work) and descendant causes (e.g., cash-flow difficulties, bankruptcy, work suspension, further delays), with some causes acting as both. The study concludes that understanding these interrelated causes enables proactive dispute avoidance and provides a roadmap applicable to other critical dispute causes.

ideas.idea: Scope changes and design alterations are common in modern/modular construction projects, leading to disputes when project requirements are not clearly incorporated into design.
ideas.quote: Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2021) indicated that many changes in the scope of work are witnessed in modular construction in the United States. These lead to excessive design changes and thus delays in completing drawings and plans.

ideas.idea: Poorly drafted or ambiguous contracts, especially lump-sum agreements requiring finalized drawings before contractor selection, are a major source of disputes.
ideas.quote: El-Sayegh et al. (2020) explained that a poorly drafted contract causes disputes between the parties, as the project is based on an inadequate agreement, leading to miscommunication between the parties. This is especially true for lump sum contracts, where owners and contractors settle on a fixed price.

ideas.idea: Contract incompleteness—ambiguity, deficiency, inconsistency, and defectiveness in contract documents—is a primary driver of disputes, often neglected at project outset.
ideas.quote: Rahnamayiezekavat et al. (2022) pointed out that contract incompleteness is the most frequent factor contributing to disputes, usually neglected in the early stage of projects.

ideas.idea: Unfair risk allocation, where owners transfer risk onto contractors, is a recurring contractual cause of disputes.
ideas.quote: D-03 Unfair risk allocation, owner transfer risk to contractor 14

ideas.idea: Payment delays by the client are the single most critical and frequent trigger of construction disputes, with cascading effects on contractor cash flow, quality, and project viability.
ideas.quote: Payment delays by client were quoted by the majority of studies (28 out of 43). ... Due to these circumstances, the contractor's cash-flow gets affected and the contractor financially suffers which in return effect the overall quality of the project.

ideas.idea: Variations and scope changes, often client-initiated, directly impact costs and are a leading category of dispute, closely tied to project delivery method and design completeness.
ideas.quote: Senaratne and Farhan (2022) stated that variation refers to an alteration of the scope of work, thereby impacting the associated costs. Variations are very common among construction projects.

ideas.idea: Bidding-stage practices, such as selecting contractors by lowest bid rather than performance or quality, generate downstream contractual disputes.
ideas.quote: Elhag et al. (2020) indicated found that UAE clients typically prioritize the lowest bids over performance, quality, or value when choosing contractors, leading to increased project issues including delays, claims, and disputes.

ideas.idea: Extension of time (EOT) claims that are rejected or reduced by consultants frequently escalate into disputes, reflecting contractual claim-handling weaknesses.
ideas.quote: In some cases, though the extension of time (EOT) claims are submitted as per the timeframe, the consultant failed to approve it on time. All the EOT claims became disputed at the end (Francis et al. 2022).

ideas.idea: Differing site conditions and force majeure events represent risk-allocation issues embedded in contracts that generate disputes when unforeseen conditions arise.
ideas.quote: Differing site condition refers to the situation when the contractor faces a site condition that significantly deviate from either the typical conditions in the project area or those explicitly outlined in the contract (Ahmed and El-adaway 2023).

ideas.idea: A framework linking antecedent and descendant causes (e.g., payment delay causing cash-flow problems, which in turn causes progress delay and poor quality) illustrates how contractual failures propagate through the project delivery chain.
ideas.quote: Payment delays lead to severe impacts such as cashflow problems, bankruptcy of contractor, suspension of work, reduced progress of work (Peters et al. 2019), and poor quality of work (Francis et al. 2016).

objectives: To present a fundamental understanding of modular and prefabricated construction systems and to suggest an appropriate construction procurement method based on project type in order to achieve sustainable modular construction, using a hypothetical 20-story office building as a case for analysis.
problem_statement: Modular/prefabricated construction offers benefits (speed, cost, quality, safety, sustainability) but design and administrative coordination between factory and on-site activities may be neglected if an inappropriate procurement method is chosen, particularly given the complexity of precast concrete design and construction.
methodology: A literature-based conceptual study that devises a hypothetical construction project (a twenty-story urban office building) and evaluates modular design options (precast concrete structure, architectural cladding, service modules) against findings from three key prior sources (Torre 1994, Gibb 1999, Schoenborn 2012) plus an industry brochure, to derive procurement and delivery method recommendations.
key_background_studies: Torre, M.L. de la (1994) - thesis on modular construction practices, providing advantages/disadvantages and industry survey, central for cost, schedule, and management implications discussion

Gibb, A.G.F. (1999) - textbook 'Off-site fabrication', providing case studies (Embankment Place, Scottish Widows, Crown House Engineering) and procurement/design implications for off-site construction

Schoenborn, J.M. (2012) - thesis identifying constraints and barriers to design innovation in modular construction via industry interviews, offering modern perspective on procurement, BIM use, and life cycle costs
Precast/Pre-stressed Concrete Institute brochure - industry publication promoting total precast concrete structures with cost/time comparisons for office buildings
findings: The study concludes that for a hypothetical twenty-story urban office building, total precast concrete construction is the most effective structural and cladding solution, offering time and cost savings, quality control, and safety benefits, but requiring early involvement of manufacturers and specialty contractors. Traditional design-bid-build delivery is unsuitable due to the need for early manufacturer/contractor involvement; design-negotiate-build is an improvement, but integrated project delivery is identified as the best method to coordinate design, fabrication, and installation and maximize time/cost savings. Service modules (electrical, mechanical, plumbing, fire protection) can further reduce cost and schedule if coordinated with the precast structural sequence and supported by early, complete communication among all parties.

ideas.idea: Selecting an appropriate procurement method is critical to prevent design and coordination shortcomings from undermining modular construction benefits.
ideas.quote: some other concerns such as design considerations and coordination of factory and on-site activities, may be easily undermined if an appropriate procurement method is not selected

ideas.idea: Precast concrete construction demands highly skilled labor and more complex design than conventional methods, increasing administrative burden.
ideas.quote: precast members require highly skilled workers, more complex techniques, and a more complex design

ideas.idea: Because designers focus on perfecting modular design, administrative tasks like procurement and scheduling should be delegated to specialized construction management professionals.
ideas.quote: Because the design firm needs to concentrate on perfecting the modular design, the intensive administrative work should be delegated to a construction management firm.

ideas.idea: Design-bid-build delivery is unsuitable for precast/modular projects because it prevents early involvement of manufacturers and installation contractors.
ideas.quote: A design-bid-build process is undesirable because early involvement with the precast manufacturer and the installation contractor is necessary.

ideas.idea: Design-negotiate-build offers improvement over design-bid-build by allowing selection of experienced general contractors familiar with precast processes.
ideas.quote: The design-negotiate-build method is a slight improvement because only competent and experienced general contractors can be selected, and the chosen general contractor likely will have previous experience with the other parties.

ideas.idea: Integrated project delivery is identified as the best method for total precast concrete projects because it allows designers and contractors to be selected before the final design concept is set, enabling parallel processes.
ideas.quote: The best solution for a total precast concrete construction project is to implement integrated project delivery. Under this method, the designers and contractors are determined before the final concept of the project is realized.

ideas.idea: Owners can separate contracts for precast supply/installation from the general contractor to mitigate coordination risk between parties unfamiliar with each other.
ideas.quote: One way for the owner to eliminate the potential for problems between companies is to form separate contracts with a supplier and specialty contractor to perform the precast concrete work.

ideas.idea: Overlap of design and procurement phases is highly desirable in modular construction, disadvantaging traditional delivery methods that exclude contractor input during design.
ideas.quote: An important point raised by Torre is that an overlap of design and procurement activities is highly desirable in modular construction. This may put traditionally delivered projects at a disadvantage because the contractor cannot be involved in the design phase.

ideas.idea: Modular/prefabricated construction increases certain construction management responsibilities such as planning, scheduling, and coordination across fabrication, transportation and installation.
ideas.quote: Another problem with prefabrication is an increase in some construction management responsibilities. Planning and scheduling will be more complex due to the extensive amount of fabrication, transportation, and intensive erection procedures.

ideas.idea: Trustworthy procurement of modular components is difficult because specialty suppliers and subcontractors must be engaged very early in the project.
ideas.quote: Trustworthy procurement of modular components is much more difficult to achieve because specialty suppliers and subcontractors must be heavily involved early in the project.

ideas.idea: Strategic partnering, two-stage tendering, and nominated suppliers are procurement strategies that facilitate faster prefabricated project delivery by improving planning and procurement.
ideas.quote: All three of these concepts facilitate faster project delivery using off-site fabrication because they improve planning and procurement.

ideas.idea: Complex modular projects involving multiple trades require increased coordination when no single contractor can perform all the work.
ideas.quote: modules that encompass materials from different trades require increased coordination between subcontractors if there is not one contractor capable of performing all the work

ideas.idea: Service modules should only be used where the owner is confident of contractor competence, and early, complete communication among all parties is essential to realize benefits.
ideas.quote: The advantages of using multiple modular construction methods is contingent upon early and complete communication between all contractors and suppliers involved.

ideas.idea: An earlier relationship with manufacturers simplifies coordination, cost estimation, and contract administration, especially for owners and architects with prior experience with the same contractor.
ideas.quote: If the owner or architect has worked on projects with a specific contractor or manufacturer, contract administration and project management become easier to tasks.

objectives: To develop a dynamic compensation mechanism and associated optimisation models that enable general contractors and factories in off-site construction (OSC) to achieve just-in-time (JIT) component delivery, reducing component delivery waste caused by production or assembly schedule deviations.
problem_statement: The fragmented OSC supply chain, combined with the engineer-to-order nature of prefabricated components and inevitable schedule deviations, causes component delivery waste (excess inventory, double handling, overtime). Existing static compensation mechanisms place all responsibility on factories to manage demand fluctuation and fail to motivate general contractors to control schedule deviations, so JIT delivery is not achieved in practice.
methodology: Conceptual/quantitative optimisation research: literature review to identify gaps; design of a dynamic compensation mechanism (an 'inverse Kanban' table of surcharges/incentives released by factories for delivery date changes); formulation of two mathematical optimisation models (Scenario 1: minimise general contractor's total cost when assembly is delayed; Scenario 2: maximise general contractor's incentive revenue by trading schedule flexibility) with cost/revenue objective functions and precedence/date-change constraints; models solved using a Genetic Algorithm (MATLAB R2020a GA solver); numerical example data developed via consultation with industry experts; sensitivity analyses on on-site inventory capacity and surcharge/incentive levels.
key_background_studies: Ohno (1988/22) - originator of the Toyota Production System and JIT concept, identifying inventory as the most significant waste, underpinning the paper's waste framework.
Koskela (1992/35) - foundational lean construction theorist defining waste as non-value-adding activity, basis for applying lean philosophy to OSC.
Pheng and Chuan (1997/47, 78) - studied JIT feasibility in construction and reported general contractors' willingness to pay for flexible/reliable delivery, informing the compensation concept.
Khalfan et al. (2008/79) - reported a supplier-Kanban JIT system in UK public procurement, providing a precedent for Kanban-based coordination between client/supplier.
Luo et al. (2019/7) - documented poor communication/coordination in Hong Kong OSC causing inventory and double-handling waste, motivating the waste definition.
Viana et al. (2017/46) - found many components sit in on-site warehouses over ten days before assembly, evidencing the inventory waste problem.
Gosling et al. (2015/58) and Gosling and Naim (2009/56) - characterised uncertainty and information management challenges in engineer-to-order (ETO) production, framing OSC as ETO.
Im et al. and Low and Wu; Chen et al. (65,66,67) - prior JIT delivery systems for rebar and ready-mix concrete, showing JIT application in construction but for non-ETO, redirectable products.

National and AIA California Council (2007/70) and related IPD literature (71-77) - integrated project delivery and incentive-pool mechanisms, contrasted with the paper's operational-level, quantitative compensation approach.
Ju et al. (2019/72) - proposed redistributing responsibilities between upstream/downstream to reduce conflict, informing the dynamic surcharge/incentive design.
findings: The proposed dynamic compensation mechanism, implemented via an inverse Kanban and solved with GA-based optimisation, substantially reduces component delivery waste. In Scenario 1, optimised delivery delay reduced total cost from over $1 million to about $21,560 (~98% savings) compared with delivering as originally scheduled when assembly was delayed. Sensitivity analysis showed that on-site inventory capacity and surcharge/incentive levels significantly affect optimisation performance when inventory capacity is low, but effects diminish as capacity increases. In Scenario 2, the model enabled general contractors to trade schedule flexibility for incentives, yielding a maximum revenue of $1,800 in the example, though feasibility depended on delay tolerance of specific activities (some tolerance levels rendered the model unsolvable). Overall, the dynamic mechanism outperforms static compensation approaches by correctly reflecting real-time costs and incentivising general contractors to manage schedule deviations, benefiting both general contractors and factories.

ideas.idea: Off-site construction creates a fragmented, difficult-to-manage supply chain compared with traditional in-situ construction, contributing to coordination and delivery problems.
ideas.quote: The fragmentation of prefabrication and assembly, however, makes the supply chain difficult to manage.

ideas.idea: Poor collaboration, mistrust, and inadequate information sharing between general contractors and subcontractors/factories are recurring risks affecting OSC performance.
ideas.quote: The general contractors and the subcontractors usually have a mistrustful and conflicting relationship [8].

ideas.idea: Schedule deviations (delays or accelerations) in assembly or production are inevitable and create component delivery waste for either the general contractor or the factory.
ideas.quote: Component delivery waste in OSC is defined as time, inventory, and cost waste in component delivery processes when factories and general contractors individually deal with schedule deviations.

ideas.idea: Existing compensation/incentive mechanisms in construction literature are static and place the burden of managing demand fluctuation entirely on factories, without incentivising general contractors to control their own schedule changes.
ideas.quote: The static compensation systems reported in existing literature require factories to manage demand fluctuations but fail to encourage general contractors to control schedule deviations.

ideas.idea: A dynamic, quantitative compensation mechanism—surcharges for unfavourable date changes and incentives for favourable ones—can better allocate responsibility and encourage coordination between general contractors and factories.
ideas.quote: a factory shares possible changes for each component's delivery date to its clients on an inverse Kanban system... unfavourable changes for the factory schedule are allocated with surcharges... schedule changes that are beneficial for the factory are assigned as incentives.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) and multiparty incentive pools are strategic, project-level win-win mechanisms, but are not well suited to the operational-level, quantifiable cost of individual component delivery date changes.
ideas.quote: Component delivery, however, is an operational-level activity. The cost of a component delivery date change is quantifiable, and solutions would not naturally produce tactical win-win outcomes.

ideas.idea: General contractors often possess float/schedule flexibility that could be used as a bargaining resource to accommodate factory delivery changes, but this flexibility is rarely leveraged contractually.
ideas.quote: Even if the general contractor does not delay the assembly schedule as a response to uncertainties, float time can allow for an adjustment to the assembly schedule, thereby enabling the factory to change the component delivery date. However, little literature focuses on accepting suppliers' delivery delays.

ideas.idea: Because factories and general contractors are independent for-profit entities, JIT delivery cannot be achieved naturally without financial incentives or compensation arrangements.
ideas.quote: Because factories and general contractors are independent for-profit organizations, just-in-time delivery cannot be achieved naturally.

ideas.idea: Explicit, transparent information-sharing platforms (akin to Kanban systems) between contractor and factory are necessary enablers of coordinated, dynamic decision-making on delivery schedules.
ideas.quote: An information system holds shared information to facilitate coordination between the general contractor and the factory.

ideas.idea: Contractual/operational frameworks should allow either party (contractor or factory) to initiate and be compensated for schedule changes, reflecting a shared-risk, shared-reward approach rather than one-sided liability.
ideas.quote: The models can help both parties to reduce component delivery waste when either side has the motivation to change the original component delivery schedules.

objectives: To develop an adaptive smart contract mechanism that encodes construction constraints and their interactive relationships as blockchain-based management consensus, in order to mediate production bottlenecks in a prefabricated (modular) construction project and enable fair, automated reward/penalty payments among project participants.
problem_statement: Smart contracts show promise for streamlining construction management by automating consensus and payments, but they are not inherently 'intelligent' enough to handle dynamic, uncertain construction environments with multiple interacting constraints; existing research lacks methods to convert intangible process-level constraints into tangible, quantifiable smart contract consensus, especially for interrelated constraints affecting schedule and cost in prefabricated/modular construction.
methodology: Case study data collection from a high-rise residential modular construction project in Singapore involving 120 Prefabricated Bathroom Unit (PBU) installations (three types, three participants: fabricator, crane/operator, installation workers). Four constraints (external conditions/weather, material availability, equipment availability, labor availability) were identified with three variability levels each, generating 81 scenarios via a discrete-event simulation model built from historical productivity and precipitation data. Shapley value game-theoretic calculations were applied to the simulation outputs to determine fair reward/penalty payment rules for each participant under each scenario. These scenarios and payment rules were then encoded into smart contracts written in Solidity, deployed and tested on a private Ethereum blockchain (Ganache/Remix-Ethereum/MetaMask) to validate automated execution.
key_background_studies: Koskela (1999) - identified seven types of constraints (materials, equipment, labor, prerequisite work, design/methods, space, weather) that must be removed during construction planning, forming the theoretical basis for constraint categorization in this study.
Koskela (2000) - developed the Transformation-Flow-Value (TFV) production theory underlying flow-based construction management and waste reduction.
Hamledari & Fischer (2021a) - showed smart contracts improve information-sharing accuracy but depend heavily on human-designed consensus, highlighting risk of poorly designed contracts.
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - argued complicated construction environments create uncertainties that challenge smart contract execution, emphasizing need for flexibility.
Lu et al. (2021) - proposed turning construction resources into 'smart construction objects' with awareness/autonomy to enable blockchain-based checks on production.
Wu et al. (2021) - proposed formal ontology to represent constraints in construction quality regulations for auto-generating smart contracts.
X. Li et al. (2022) - highlighted challenges in developing adaptive smart contracts handling constraints, risks, and disturbances without redundancy.
Chen, Liu, Zhang, et al. (2023) - conducted simulation of prerequisite work readiness as a constraint for smart contract-enforced reliable workflow, providing methodological basis for this study.
Hamzeh et al. (2015, 2016) - identified that constraint removal during make-ready impacts lookahead planning and project duration.
Liu et al. (2011) - demonstrated positive relationship between workflow reliability and constraint removal via case study.
Szabo (1994) - coined the term 'smart contract' as a computerized transaction protocol executing contract terms automatically.
findings: The simulation across 108 scenarios (with/without weather) showed that without weather considerations, PBU delivery reliability was the dominant contributor to project outcomes, but under adverse weather conditions (especially wet weather), installation worker availability became the dominant bottleneck, as installation capacity failed to keep pace with PBU delivery and crane lifting capacity. Project duration increased significantly with worsening weather (up to 23.62% increase from dry to wet). The Shapley value method successfully quantified fair marginal contributions/penalties for each constraint-responsible party, and these were encoded into smart contracts that were validated on a private Ethereum blockchain, correctly triggering payments based on detected constraint reliability levels. The study concludes that ensuring sufficient installation labor is critical during adverse weather, and that smart contracts can proactively manage make-ready processes rather than reactively resolving bottlenecks.

ideas.idea: Reliable construction workflow depends on timely identification and removal of constraints before tasks are released into production (the 'make-ready' process).
ideas.quote: Enabling a reliable construction workflow requires timely identification and removal of constraints under dynamic construction scenarios (Javanmardi et al., 2020).

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate payment and coordination functions in construction but their effectiveness depends on how well they encode real-world constraints and uncertainties.
ideas.quote: The blockchain-enabled smart contract can streamline the work process by predefining “intelligent” consensus to facilitate central managers’ jobs.

ideas.idea: Poorly designed smart contract consensus can cause irreversible financial loss, underscoring the contractual risk of automating payment terms without adequate flexibility.
ideas.quote: Poorly designed smart contracts may lead to irreversible financial loss (Hamledari & Fischer, 2021a).

ideas.idea: Prefabrication introduces specific coordination constraints among fabricator, crane/logistics, and on-site installation labor that must be contractually or operationally managed to avoid production bottlenecks.
ideas.quote: The major constraints included uncertain and out-of-sequence PBU arrival due to the fabricator's preference for producing PBUs in a large batch, crane unavailability due to fully scheduled lifting activities, and a minimal number of workers assigned for installation to maximize profitability.

ideas.idea: External conditions such as weather can significantly affect on-site installation productivity in modular/prefabricated projects, shifting the location of the production bottleneck from off-site fabrication to on-site installation labor.
ideas.quote: These results suggest that severe weather (increased precipitation intensity) can increase project duration and crane idle time, while putting more pressure on installation workers.

ideas.idea: A fair, quantitative method (Shapley value) can be used to allocate reward or penalty payments among project participants (fabricator, crane, workers) based on their marginal contribution to project outcomes under different constraint scenarios, informing potential contractual payment structures.
ideas.quote: An equitable payment method based on the Shapley value algorithm was established to incentivize reliable constraint removal.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts encoding constraint-based payment rules can decentralize construction management decisions that traditionally required a central project manager, effectively automating aspects of contract administration.
ideas.quote: Decentralizing construction management requires smart contracts to be “intelligent” enough to function similarly to centralized project managers.

ideas.idea: The study's four-constraint model is a simplification of Koskela's seven constraint types, indicating that comprehensive contractual/managerial frameworks would need to address a broader set of constraints relevant to MMC/prefabrication projects.
ideas.quote: this research only considered the four major constraints that impacted the projects in smart contracts, whereas Koskela (1999) suggested that at least seven types of constraints should be removed during construction planning.

objectives: To provide a comprehensive, up-to-date mixed (scientometric and systematic) review of 172 journal articles on construction cash flow, identifying key contributing scholars, keyword clusters, research categories, methods, and gaps; and to develop a blockchain-based smart contract framework for automating payments in modular integrated construction (MiC) projects to address identified gaps.
problem_statement: Existing literature reviews on construction financial health lack a dedicated, comprehensive review of cash flow as the central topic, rarely apply quantitative scientometric methods to minimize subjectivity, and largely fail to analyze methods used to assess financial attributes of construction projects (aside from BIM/AI-focused reviews). There is also a lack of research on cash flow analysis for offsite/modular construction and on digitalized, automated payment systems for such fragmented supply chains.
methodology: A mixed review methodology combining scientometric (quantitative) and systematic (qualitative) review approaches. Articles were retrieved from Scopus using cash-flow and construction/building/modular keyword strings, yielding 1575 documents; inclusion/exclusion criteria (journal articles, Engineering subject area, English language) reduced this to 366; PRISMA screening and full-text evaluation reduced to 141, and backward/forward snowballing added 31 more, totaling 172 included articles. VOSviewer software was used for scientometric analysis (co-authorship networks, keyword co-occurrence clustering). A two-dimensional systematic classification (research topics vs. methods) was then applied to the 172 articles to identify themes, methods, and gaps, followed by development of a conceptual blockchain/smart-contract payment framework for MiC projects.
key_background_studies: Shan et al. [11] - reviewed construction financing practices in UK, US, Singapore, Australia
Vigneault et al. [12] - systematic review of BIM solutions for construction cost management
Gundes et al. [4] - bibliometric analysis of 259 articles on construction project finance
Durdyev [13] - bibliometric analysis of causes of construction financial distress
Bhadeshiya and Pitroda [14] - reviewed factors affecting construction financing, highlighting weak cash flow control
Afzal et al. [15] - reviewed AI methods used in construction cost assessment (2008-2018)
Ismail et al. [16] - systematic review of 152 articles on cost overrun issues
Elazouni and Gab-Allah [46] - initiated 'Finance-based Scheduling' integrating scheduling with cash flow
Elghaish et al. [56] - integrated 4D/5D BIM models linking cost and schedule for cash flow
Elghaish et al. [86] - proof-of-concept blockchain/smart contract payment automation across project life cycle
Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez [91] - smart contract for progress payment security and dispute reduction
Sigalov et al. [94] - combined BIM with smart contracts for automated progress payments
Sonmez et al. [87] - investigated BIM and decentralized blockchain for payment administration
Kaka and Price [97] - developed S-curve profiles for different construction project types
Ali and Elazouni [99] - integrated LOB/CPM techniques for cash flow in repetitive non-serial projects
Ikediashi and Okolie [61] - assessed 31 factors impacting cash flow in Nigerian construction industry
Zayed and Liu [42] - identified 43 factors impacting cash flow in USA and China construction firms
Le et al. [62] - grouped cash flow factors into six categories including financial risk and macro environment
findings: Cash flow research attention has grown substantially over the last two decades, peaking in 2020. Kaka A.P. and Elazouni A. are among the most productive and cited researchers. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified five clusters: financial risk/uncertainty, scheduling/optimization, cost/budget control, technology/digitalization (including blockchain), and contractor-client relationships. Systematic review classified the 172 articles into five categories: cash flow factors, cash flow-based schedule (most frequent, 60 articles), cash flow-based capital structure, cash flow-based project type, and cash flow and digitalization/blockchain. Optimization techniques are predominant across categories. Significant gaps exist regarding offsite/modular construction cash flow, procurement approach effects on cash flow, and fully automated payment systems. A conceptual blockchain-based smart contract framework was proposed for MiC projects with three stages (preparation, initialization, execution) to automate, secure, and expedite progress payments without third-party intermediaries.

ideas.idea: Modular/offsite construction (MiC) projects have complex, fragmented supply chains that traditional cash flow and payment systems are poorly suited to manage.
ideas.quote: Conventional cash flow systems are argued to be incompatible with the fragmented and complex nature of modular construction projects [113,114].

ideas.idea: MiC projects face financial barriers due to high initial capital costs, particularly in early project phases, which can threaten the financial stability of clients and contractors.
ideas.quote: the literature lacks studies on cash flow analysis in OSC. Despite the benefits of OSC, including waste reduction, cost/schedule savings, and minimum labor requirement, it faces financial barriers. The OSC projects are argued to be more expensive due to their high initial capital cost requirement, particularly in the earlier phase of the project

ideas.idea: Blockchain and smart contract technology can automate and secure progress payments among project stakeholders, reducing reliance on third parties like lawyers or banks.
ideas.quote: Through the association between blockchain technology and smart contracts, an endorsement policy, compliant with the contract's terms, is enforced for all participants without the need for the involvement of third parties, reducing the chances of potential conflicts and enhancing the project's financial health

ideas.idea: Payment delays by clients are consistently identified as the most significant factor negatively affecting contractors' cash flow, which is especially problematic in the complex supply chains of MiC.
ideas.quote: payment delays by clients was the most frequent and highest-ranked factor that could affect contractors' cash flow [61,62,64,115–117].

ideas.idea: A proposed three-stage conceptual framework (preparation, initialization, execution) uses blockchain-based smart contracts to automate progress payments in MiC, including billing plans, task verification, and confirmation-triggered fund transfer.
ideas.quote: Figure 12 comprises three stages to adopt smart contracts in MiC: the preparation stage, the initialization stage, and the execution stage... Upon confirmation, the smart contract immediately transfers the progress payments to the non-owner stakeholders according to the contractual terms

ideas.idea: Existing BIM-blockchain payment systems remain only partially automated, still requiring manual updates of schedule and cost data, and generally address only a single project delivery system without considering disputes.
ideas.quote: the developed payment systems by the association between BIM and blockchain technologies were partially automated, where the user needs to update the schedule and cost data manually on the system; (3) the developed systems did not consider the possible disputes among participants when developing the smart contracts.

ideas.idea: There is an unexplored relationship between project procurement approaches (contractual relationships among participants) and cash flow, which is particularly ambiguous and different in OSC/MiC projects compared to conventional construction.
ideas.quote: There is an absence found in the literature on the association between project procurement approaches and cash flow analysis... In some types of projects, such as OSC projects, appropriate procurement systems are ambiguous and differ from conventional construction projects due to the vast difference in processes and, therefore, affect their construction cash flow

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can encode agreed billing plans, partial payment options, and contractual terms directly onto a blockchain platform tied to stakeholders' digital identities.
ideas.quote: the non-owner project stakeholders specify their billing plan and link it with the billing units. The agreed conditions, billing plans, and partial payment options are then coded into a computerized protocol (smart contract).

objectives: To investigate the application of just-in-time (JIT) principles in off-site construction (OSC) and to propose a conceptual model that enables dynamic, coordinated delivery scheduling between manufacturers and contractors to reduce time and inventory waste caused by delivery-schedule deviations.
problem_statement: When delivery of prefabricated components deviates from the assembly schedule due to unexpected events, contractors and manufacturers tend to rigidly comply with existing contract terms rather than coordinate, resulting in non-optimal, wasteful outcomes (excess inventory, overproduction, overburden). Existing JIT and incentive solutions in OSC are static and do not reflect real-time costs, and contracts effectively force parties into suboptimal behaviour instead of facilitating coordination.
methodology: A conceptual/theoretical paper: the authors review literature on lean production, lean construction (TFV theory), Toyota Production System/JIT, pull systems and Kanban, and existing information-technology and incentive-based solutions in off-site construction. Based on this review, they develop a conceptual model comprising an information-sharing platform, a dynamic resource management system for manufacturers, and an optimisation system for contractors, illustrated schematically (no empirical data collection or case study; validation is left to future research).
key_background_studies: Ohno (1988) – foundational definition of just-in-time and waste (muda, overproduction) within the Toyota Production System, framing the paper's theoretical basis.

Koskela (2000) – Transformation-Flow-Value (TFV) theory of lean construction, used to frame waste as non-value-adding transformation/flow/value activities and to note that waste stems from prior tasks/change orders.

Pheng and Chuan (2001) – survey evidence on contractors' willingness to pay for flexible delivery and manufacturers pushing components onto contractors, central to the incentive/compensation discussion.
Wu and Low (2012, 2014) – case studies showing manufacturers suffer high inventory and identifying large inventory as key non-value-adding activity in OSC.
Khalfan et al. (2008) – example of supplier Kanban and quality-price selection mechanism achieving JIT delivery in a UK public project, used as an example of incentive-based coordination.
Jeong et al. (2011) – linear-programming-based optimisation models for manufactured housing production planning, cited as IT-enabled JIT approach.
Hsu et al. (2018) – supply-chain coordination research integrating manufacturing, transportation and assembly, highlighting limits of intra-organisational optimisation.
Vrijhoef and Koskela (2000) – argument that waste commonly originates from the last stage of the supply chain, supporting the paper's conclusion about encouraging contractors to manage variations.
findings: The paper concludes that rigid contractual compliance during schedule deviations produces waste (excess inventory, overproduction, overburden) for both contractors and manufacturers in OSC. It proposes a conceptual model in which manufacturers issue dynamic surcharges or incentives for delivery changes via a shared information platform, and contractors use an optimisation system to decide whether to accept delayed/advanced delivery based on real-time cost data, enabling both parties to reschedule toward a new optimum. This dynamic, real-time compensation approach is argued to be superior to existing static incentive/compensation mechanisms because it reflects actual resource costs at the time of change, reduces manufacturers' risk, and motivates contractors to provide earlier notice of changes. The model does not eliminate contracts; contracts remain binding as a fallback if coordination fails. The authors note the model is conceptual and requires future empirical validation via case study.

ideas.idea: Contractual rigidity discourages coordination between contractors and manufacturers when delivery schedules deviate, producing waste instead of optimal outcomes.
ideas.quote: contractors and manufacturers tend to comply with contracts instead of seeking coordination to achieve just-in-time, which results in non-optimal solutions.

ideas.idea: The contract, originally meant to pull components efficiently from manufacturers, instead becomes a rigid push mechanism forcing adherence despite changing conditions.
ideas.quote: The contract originally is a method to pull components from factories; however, it turns into a push to force both sides to stick to the contracts when variations occur.

ideas.idea: Existing incentive/compensation mechanisms for flexible delivery in construction are static and fail to reflect the real, time-varying cost of schedule changes.
ideas.quote: Some static incentive solutions in the extant literature cannot perfectly reflect the actual cost caused by the change of delivery dates.

ideas.idea: A dynamic, real-time compensation/surcharge mechanism shared via an information platform can better align contractor and manufacturer interests than fixed contractual payments.
ideas.quote: Unlike static compensation such as additional payment according to contracts' prices and non-lowest tender, the surcharges defined in this research is determined by the real-time cost of the resource consumed at that moment, which can significantly eliminate manufacturers' risk.

ideas.idea: Even with the proposed coordination model, the underlying contract remains legally binding as a fallback if the parties cannot reach a mutually beneficial (win-win) rescheduling agreement.
ideas.quote: However, contracts are still binding if both sides fail to reach win-win.

ideas.idea: Contractors should bear greater responsibility for enabling just-in-time implementation in off-site construction, including willingness to pay for delivery flexibility.
ideas.quote: contractors should take more responsibility to implement just-in-time production in OSC (Pheng and Chuan 2001).

ideas.idea: The division between off-site manufacturing and on-site assembly creates an interface risk where poor management of delivery coordination can erode or negate the productivity benefits of off-site construction.
ideas.quote: The advantage of off-site construction will be eroded, even cancelled out by increased cost and time if the delivery interface between contractors and manufacturers is not properly managed.

ideas.idea: Because prefabricated components are typically engineer-to-order, they cannot be redirected to other customers if schedules change, making contractual and delivery flexibility especially important.
ideas.quote: The most components in the OSC are produced as engineer-to-order (ETO), which means if the construction schedule deviates, the customised components cannot be redirected to other customers as are raw materials (Bortolini et al. 2019).

objectives: To harmonize and critically analyze the fragmented literature on Modular integrated Construction (MiC) through a three-stage process (bibliometric search, quantitative scientometric analysis, and qualitative thematic analysis) in order to identify research trends, characteristics, benefits, challenges, knowledge gaps and future research directions.
problem_statement: Although MiC research has grown rapidly, existing reviews either treat MiC collectively with other off-site construction methods without differentiating its unique themes, or focus narrowly on specific aspects (e.g., sustainability, critical success factors, barriers), failing to comprehensively map the knowledge areas, current gaps, and future directions specific to MiC, including contractual and project delivery issues.
methodology: A multi-stage critical literature review combining: (1) bibliometric search using Scopus with iteratively refined keyword strings, yielding 237-238 documents; (2) quantitative scientometric analysis using VOSviewer and Gephi to examine countries, sources, co-authors, top cited articles, and keyword co-occurrence; and (3) qualitative thematic analysis of 107 screened articles categorized into six main themes and nine subcategories (sustainability, construction operations, building design, management aspects, information technology management, and others).
key_background_studies: Gibb and Isack (2003) - top cited article examining client perceptions of pre-assembly and early supplier involvement
Richard (2005) - conceptual paper on levels of construction manufacturing and industrialized building systems
Kamali and Hewage (2016) - critical review of life cycle sustainability performance of modular buildings, highly influential in normalized citations
Wuni and Shen (2019, 2020a, 2020b, 2020c) - series of studies on critical success factors, barriers, stakeholder management benchmarks in MiC/PPVC projects
Jin et al. (2018) - review of off-site construction (OSC) methods that grouped MiC with prefabrication and hybrid construction without differentiating MiC-specific themes
O'Connor et al. (2014) - identification of critical success factors and enablers for industrial modularization
Molavi and Barral (2016) and Dakhli et al. (2015) - studies addressing project delivery methods (CM, DB, DBB) for MiC projects
Wuni et al. (2019) - literature review identifying critical risk factors affecting MiC projects
Li et al. (2013) - risk identification and fuzzy AHP assessment of cost/time impacts in MiC
Song et al. (2005) - identification of factors affecting adoption of modularization in industrial plants, widely cited reference in decision-making studies
findings: Quantitative analysis showed ~50% of MiC literature originates from USA, Canada, Australia, and UK, with USA leading; top journals include Automation in Construction and Journal of Cleaner Production; keyword mapping revealed seven clusters linking MiC to simulation, sustainability, scheduling, structural design, and BIM, but lacking terms like risk, supply chain, contractual relationship, and disputes. Qualitative analysis of 107 articles showed building design and management aspects dominate research (~50% combined), followed by construction operations, information technology management, and sustainability. Key gaps identified include lack of quantitative/cost analysis for MiC innovations, absence of studies on optimal project delivery methods, and a complete absence of literature addressing contractual relationships, risk allocation, dispute resolution, and suitability of standard contract forms (FIDIC, NEC) for MiC projects. The study proposes future research directions including modeling stakeholder relationships in design, examining contractual relationships among participants, cost comparisons, and educational integration of MiC.

ideas.idea: The project delivery method significantly affects contractor involvement, coordination, and design liability sharing in MiC projects, yet has been addressed by only two studies.
ideas.quote: This point is highly affected by the project delivery method which has only been discussed two studies (Dakhli et al., 2015; Molavi and Barral, 2016).

ideas.idea: No existing literature has examined the contractual relationships between project participants in MiC projects, leaving critical questions about payment terms, variations, and risk unanswered.
ideas.quote: Therefore, a potential knowledge gap is identified as none of the consulted literature has addressed the contractual relationship between various project participants in MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Key contractual questions remain unresolved in MiC, including advance payment adjustments, early design freeze implications, variation order procedures, and transportation insurance responsibilities.
ideas.quote: For instance, will the advance payment for the contractor be adjusted due to the increased initial amount of money required for materials? How will the employers deal with the issue of early fixed design? How can the variation order procedures be adjusted to suit this new construction method? How the contractor's care for the works will be addressed during the transportation of modules? Will there be an additional insurance policy for modules transportation in the contract?

ideas.idea: Disputes between stakeholders in MiC projects have not been studied despite the likelihood that not all projects were completed without conflict, representing a gap for lessons-learned research.
ideas.quote: the literature has not covered cases of disputes between project stakeholders, even though it is hardly believable that all MiC projects around the world were completed without conflicts.

ideas.idea: Although risks in MiC have been studied, no research has examined how risks should be allocated contractually, which is expected within standard contract conditions.
ideas.quote: Nevertheless, no risk allocation to has been clearly discussed, which is expected to be included in the contract conditions.

ideas.idea: Standard forms of contract such as FIDIC and NEC are based on risk sharing, but their suitability for application to MiC projects has not yet been assessed in the literature.
ideas.quote: Standard forms of contract (FIDIC, NEC, etc.) are formed based on risk sharing. However, the literature is yet to assess the suitability of applying these forms in MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Early contractor/supplier involvement in the design stage is recognized as beneficial for coordination and communication in MiC delivery.
ideas.quote: Starting with the methods of delivering MiC projects, the owner should take advantage of his superior position and partner with suppliers or contractors to enhance coordination, communication, and planning.

ideas.idea: Construction management or design-build delivery methods are recommended over traditional methods due to the complexity of MiC projects.
ideas.quote: Furthermore, construction management (CM) or design-build (DB) project delivery method was recommended due to complexity of the project (Molavi and Barral, 2016).

ideas.idea: Cost comparisons between design-build and design-bid-build delivery methods showed DB to be more effective because it allows contractor involvement during design.
ideas.quote: Through two case study projects (DB and design bid build- DBB), cost comparison ranked DB as more effective as it allowed the involvement of the contractor in design stage (Dakhli et al., 2015).

ideas.idea: The absence of keywords such as risk, supply chain, contractual relationship, and disputes in the keyword co-occurrence analysis signals an underexplored area in MiC research relevant to contracts.
ideas.quote: the keywords identified lacked important and critical keywords, such as supply chain, risk, contractual relationship, and disputes.

ideas.idea: Lack of codes and standards for MiC is identified as a challenge that indirectly affects contractual certainty and risk allocation.
ideas.quote: lack of codes and standards (Rahim and Qureshi, 2018).

ideas.idea: Critical success factors for MiC projects emphasize early stakeholder engagement, robust design specifications, and effective communication among project participants during concept, planning and design stages, which have implications for contractual coordination.
ideas.quote: It was concluded that the most influential factors included robust design specifications, accurate drawings and early design freeze, good working collaboration, effective communication, and information sharing among project participants.

objectives: To critically review published research on the use of natural language processing (NLP) techniques to address legal issues in construction (contracts, regulatory codes, and legal cases), analyzing achievements and limitations of existing frameworks, and to propose a roadmap of future research areas to expand NLP adoption for legal text processing in construction.
problem_statement: Legal issues such as disputes, claims and litigation are common in construction due to ambiguous, incomplete or biased contractual language and error-prone manual compliance checking against codes/regulations. Although NLP has been applied in various construction legal contexts, the body of knowledge lacks a holistic synthesis of these NLP frameworks and their limitations, leaving gaps regarding future research needs.
methodology: A state-of-the-art literature review following a modified four-step method (Arksey and O'Malley 2005): (1) defining research questions and scope, (2) keyword-based search across databases (Google Scholar, ASCE Library, Engineering Village, Web of Science, Scopus, etc.) using terms such as 'construction', 'legal issues', 'disputes', 'litigation', 'claims', 'contracts', 'laws', 'codes', 'natural language processing', (3) screening 45 initially collected articles by abstract/conclusion review down to 28 relevant articles (19 journal, 9 conference), and (4) in-depth critical review and thematic categorization of the studies into three categories: contracts, regulatory codes/standards, and legal cases.
key_background_studies: Curtotti and McCreath (2011) - used corpus profiling to identify distinctive linguistic features of contract language versus general English, informing ambiguity detection.
Serag et al. (2010) - used ontology and logical reasoning to detect risk-prone/conflicting clauses, though unevaluated.
Lee et al. (2019) - developed rule-based NLP to detect poisonous FIDIC clauses biased toward owners, achieving 81.8% F-score.
Lee et al. (2020) - extended rule-based NLP to predict contractor-friendly FIDIC clauses (80% F-score).
Chakrabarti et al. (2019) - developed ML-based 'risk-o-meter' outperforming rule-based methods for risk clause detection (92% accuracy, 86% F-score).
Caldas et al. (2002) and Caldas and Soibelman (2003) - developed ML text classification models for structuring contract documents into categories/CSI Master Format items.
Hassan and Le (2020, 2021) and Hassan et al. (2020) - developed ML/deep learning models for contractual requirement recognition and subcontract scope extraction from design-build contracts.
Al Qady and Kandil (2010) - used shallow parsing to extract active/passive concepts and relations from contract clauses.

Zhang and El-Gohary (2016a, 2016b, 2017) and Zhang (2011, 2012b, 2017) - developed rule-based information extraction and compliance-checking frameworks converting regulatory provisions into machine-readable logic rules, including BIM/IFC schema extension.
Salama and El-Gohary (2013) and Zhou and El-Gohary (2016a, 2016b) - developed ML classification models for regulatory provisions and environmental compliance checking.
Jallan et al. (2019) - used LDA topic modeling to analyze historical construction defect litigation cases, identifying 14 topics.
Fan and Li (2013) and Zou et al. (2017) - developed semantic similarity-based case retrieval systems for legal case libraries.
Cavar et al. (2018) - developed deep linguistic NLP knowledge graphs to compare and contrast legal cases.
findings: The review found that NLP research addressing construction legal issues is still nascent but growing rapidly, especially since 2016. Existing studies fall into three thematic areas—contract review, regulatory compliance checking, and legal case analysis—with contracts (13 studies) and codes/standards (11 studies) receiving most attention, while legal case analysis remains underexplored. Machine learning-based approaches (especially SVM) generally outperform rule-based methods for large datasets, but rule-based methods remain competitive when data is scarce. Most models are proof-of-concept, tested on limited or researcher-labeled datasets, lack real-world validation, and insufficiently integrate domain knowledge (ontologies, taxonomies). Key future research needs include: contract drafting assistance, automated detection of dispute-prone or owner-obligation clauses, contract language simplification, tracing impacts of contractual requirement changes, enabling compliance checking earlier in design, extending NLP to construction-phase safety violations, and predicting litigation outcomes.

ideas.idea: Ambiguous or vague contractual language and lack of clarity about roles/obligations is a major cause of construction disputes.
ideas.quote: One of the most common source of legal disputes associated with contract draftin issue is the lack of clarity in contracts resulting in poor understanding among the contracting parties regarding their roles and obligations provided in contracts

ideas.idea: Contracts sometimes contain biased or 'poisonous' clauses deliberately inserted by owners to shift risk onto contractors, which can be detected via NLP.
ideas.quote: These biased clauses are often added in construction contracts by the owner to shift the maximum risks to contractors and other parties

ideas.idea: Incomplete contractual requirements, especially in subcontracts, often lead to disagreements and disputes among parties.
ideas.quote: incomplete project requirements in a subcontract often lead to disagreements among the contracting parties (Sun and Meng 2009).

ideas.idea: NLP-based classification models can automatically extract and structure subcontractor scope from complex design-build contracts to reduce missing information disputes.
ideas.quote: Such classification models for separating DB requirements into different categories, namely, design, construction, and O&M, can assist the general contractors in extracting the precise scope of a subcontractor from a lengthy and complex DB contract.

ideas.idea: Most existing NLP contract-review research has focused on contractor obligations, leaving owner obligations under-examined despite their significance for disputes.
ideas.quote: most previous studies on contract administration were orientated towards contractor obligations... However, owners also have several obligations in a project, such as making payments, providing site information, assistance with permits, work inspection, and reviewing and approving submittals.

ideas.idea: Standard form contracts (e.g., AIA, FIDIC, ConsensusDOCS) differ in how they define owner obligations, and NLP could be used to compare these differences across standard forms.
ideas.quote: researchers are encouraged to leverage NLP to examine highlight the similarities and differences in the owner’s obligation clauses between the standard forms. Each type of contract defines different obligations for the owner.

ideas.idea: Contracts often contain contradictory clauses within the same document, an issue that merits further NLP-based detection research.
ideas.quote: the inclusion of contradictive clauses in a single contract is a common issue found in construction project contracts necessitating further effort from the academic community

ideas.idea: Legal/contractual language is difficult for engineers to comprehend since it is not their native professional language, motivating text simplification research.
ideas.quote: reading contracts is a key task performed by engineers. However, legal language is typically not a native language of engineers, causing much difficulty for many engineers when reading legal text

ideas.idea: Tracing how a change to one contractual requirement impacts other requirements is essential for maintaining consistency but remains unexplored in construction.
ideas.quote: Assessing the impact of the changes made for a specific requirement on other requirements in the contract is essential to maintain the consistency and correctness of requirements

ideas.idea: Automated compliance checking research has focused on late-stage design verification using BIM, but selecting applicable code provisions earlier in conceptual design remains a challenge, especially for less experienced engineers.
ideas.quote: The selection of correct provisions from standards and codes is critical to control environmental risks involved in a project... the standards and codes are often complex documents including a large set of requirements which makes the selection of applicable requirements a challenging task especially for young engineers having limited knowledge and experience

ideas.idea: Predicting litigation/court outcomes from historical case data could help contracting parties evaluate claim worth before costly litigation, an area still overlooked in construction NLP research.
ideas.quote: There is a need to develop models for predicting the court outcome for a certain construction claim... Anticipating the likelihood of success would help the contractor and the owner avoids a costly litigation process.

objectives: To explore how specialist construction consultancy firms operating in a fragmented industry can develop their own product platforms, and to describe how the platform development process addresses vertical, horizontal and longitudinal fragmentation in construction delivery.
problem_statement: While existing literature explains how product-based manufacturers or housebuilders develop and deploy product platforms independently of project delivery, little is known about how specialist consultancy firms (architects, engineers, contractors) operating in a fragmented, project-based, competitive construction sector can transform their role and value delivery approach to develop product platforms of their own.
methodology: An explanatory single case study of a UK-based top-twenty construction consultancy firm (ABC) and its architectural joint-venture partner (DEF). Data comprised 15 semi-structured interviews with platform leadership/delivery teams (Aug 2019–Dec 2020), plus three interviews with industry experts and four informal conversations, supplemented by document review, site visits, and discussions with an industrial steering committee. Data were analysed incident-by-incident using constant comparison, with diagrammatic memo-writing and validation via a feedback session with ABC's Senior VP.
key_background_studies: Nam and Tatum (1992) - describe four strategies (acquisition, non-contractual alignment, contracts, information integration) to overcome vertical fragmentation between project phases
Sheffer and Levitt (2010) - framework for vertical, horizontal and longitudinal fragmentation dimensions in construction, adapted for this study's Figure 1
Robertson and Ulrich (1998) - foundational product platform theory describing benefits of platforms for efficiency and heterogeneity
Lessing (2006) - distinguishes technical and process platforms, and argues platform development should occur independently of specific projects
Jansson et al. (2014) - describe 'platform support methods' coordinating new components with existing platform elements
Simpson et al. (2001) - top-down vs bottom-up platform development approaches
Johannesson et al. (2017) - detailed exploration of platform preparation vs execution phases, top-down modelling stages
Barlow et al. (2003) and Winch (2003)/Wikner & Rudberg (2005) - distinguish engineering-to-order design/engineering phase from physical product delivery
Gosling et al. (2017) - detailed linear/sequential ETO design/engineering delivery phase description
Veenstra et al. (2006) - early bottom-up platform development case study for a housebuilder
Maxwell and Aitchison (2017) and Lidelöw et al. (2015) - distinguish platform core from novelty/service layer, open vs closed platforms
Fellows and Liu (2012) and Alashwal and Fong (2015) - discuss horizontal and vertical fragmentation causes in construction
findings: ABC and DEF developed two linked platforms—a digital product-development 'warehouse' of coordinated, information-rich components, and a process platform governing assembly—through an iterative approach combining platform development with live project delivery, rather than the purely top-down or bottom-up modes described in prior literature. Vertical and horizontal consolidation of engineering, manufacturing and assembly capabilities within the design/engineering phase enabled early, complete specification of both product and process, allowing coordination between engineering and manufacturing to be managed through fully specified contracts rather than vertical integration by acquisition. Longitudinal fragmentation was mitigated by retaining the same teams and reusing the digital warehouse across projects. The case demonstrates 'in-phase fragmentation' within the design/engineering phase itself, and shows how consolidating decision-making brings construction delivery closer to the linear, sequential models found in manufacturing, reducing decision deferral, on-site problem solving and associated inefficiencies, while enabling ABC to offer warranties and reduced delivery cost/time. Institutional procurement practices and planning requirements remain barriers to platform-based delivery.

ideas.idea: Vertical fragmentation across project phases (design, manufacture, assembly, operation) is traditionally addressed via acquisition, trust-based coordination, or incomplete contracts, each carrying distinct risks.
ideas.quote: under vertical integration by acquisition (Williamson 1971, Fergusson 1993) firms augment their end-to-end capabilities by acquiring other firms or assets... However, such asset specific investments introduce risks of asset redundancy

ideas.idea: Historical reliance on contracts struck under incomplete designs as a coordinating mechanism between phases leads to costly litigation.
ideas.quote: the historical reliance on contracts as vertical coordinating mechanisms between phases, struck almost entirely under incomplete designs, can lead to costly litigation (Li et al. 2012).

ideas.idea: Full specification of components and processes before procurement allows vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing to be managed by a fully specified contract rather than through ownership/acquisition.
ideas.quote: vertical coordination between the design and manufacturing phases can be achieved by a fully specified contract, rather than through acquisition, and assembly platforms can also be pre-defined.

ideas.idea: Traditional procurement uses 'or equal approved' specifications to defer decisions and preserve competitive tension, but this introduces inefficiency and compromises spatial efficiency.
ideas.quote: early specifiers caveat their outline product specification with "or equal approved". This provides the ultimate product specifier with flexibility in procurement... It introduces inefficiencies into the engineering process

ideas.idea: Decision deferral in traditional procurement protects clients through competitive tendering at each stage but creates incentives for suppliers to reduce quality to capture value.
ideas.quote: Decision deferral does protect clients, ensuring value at each client procurement stage through competitive tendering... However, it also creates incentives in the procurement process for suppliers to reduce quality
