ideas.idea: With full specification and unified platform control, ABC was able to provide a warranty on the delivered building, underwritten by an offsite assurance scheme, replacing the fragmented liability typical of subcontracted delivery.
ideas.quote: enabled ABC to provide a warranty on the delivered building, underwritten by an offsite assurance scheme.

ideas.idea: Sub-contracting of detailed design and delivery to specialist sub-contractors introduces cumulative margin costs and loss of value ('margins on margins'), which platform-based full specification eliminates.
ideas.quote: reducing designed-in inefficiency and the loss of value associated with the sub-contracting of the design phase, that is, no more "margins on margins" (interview 6).

ideas.idea: Institutionalized procurement practices requiring multiple competitive quotes create challenges for platform-based delivery, sometimes forcing redesign to allow other bidders to tender, despite negative cost/schedule impacts.
ideas.quote: ABC have previously been asked to re-design buildings to ensure that other bidders can submit tenders for their schemes, despite the negative impacts on delivery cost and schedule certainty.

ideas.idea: Deferred design decisions in traditional construction extend into the assembly/site phase (e.g., cutting to size), blurring responsibilities between design, finishing and assembly, unlike manufacturing's clearly sequenced phases.
ideas.quote: the design/engineering phase continues until the point of site-assembly (interview 15), overlapping with the assembly phase.

ideas.idea: Vertical integration by acquiring manufacturing facilities exposes firms to risk of asset redundancy under intermittent demand, motivating alternative contractual coordination strategies.
ideas.quote: Such acquisition-based approaches... However, such asset specific investments introduce risks of asset redundancy in the face of intermittent demand (Costantino et al. 2011).

objectives: To identify the causes of disputes and conflicts in modular construction projects by (1) examining actual U.S. case studies related to modular construction disputes, (2) highlighting the key causes leading to disputes among project stakeholders, and (3) studying dispute causation mechanisms and leading indicators using aggregated analysis.
problem_statement: While modular construction is promoted as a strategy to improve construction performance, it still faces contractual problems and disputes that limit realization of its benefits; there is a need to understand the causal factors of disputes and conflicts specific to modular construction projects so that contract administration practices can be improved.
methodology: The authors adopted a list of 28 common causes of disputes from prior literature (Cakmak and Cakmak) and collected 15 publicly available case studies of disputes in modular (residential and nonresidential) construction projects via Google Scholar, covering design-build, construction management, design-bid-build, and purchase agreements. They built a reference matrix documenting occurrence of each cause per case, converted it into an adjacency (co-occurrence) matrix, and used Social Network Analysis (SNA) via SocNetV software to compute network density, weighted degree centrality, and eigenvector centrality for each causal factor, identifying the most central causes of disputes.
key_background_studies: Cakmak and Cakmak [18] - provided the list of 28 common causes of disputes in construction used as the basis for analysis
O'Connor et al. [8] - showed higher modularization levels achieved when contractual/technical requirements favor it
Nadim and Goulding [9] - emphasized need for new processes and contractual models for offsite construction
Haas et al. [11] - provided definition of modular construction
Aljassmi et al. [21] - used SNA to analyze root causes of construction defects, informing methodology
Eteifa and El-adaway [22] - used SNA to model root causes of construction fatalities, informing methodology and SNA measure definitions
O'Connor et al. [28] - identified avoiding disconnects in contractual transitions between design phases as critical success factor for modular projects
findings: The dispute causation network for modular construction projects is highly interconnected (network density = 0.721), indicating disputes typically arise from multiple co-occurring causes rather than a single factor. The top three central causes of disputes, consistent across both weighted degree centrality and eigenvector centrality, are: (1) delays in work progress, (2) lack of team spirit, and (3) lack of communication. Unrealistic owner expectations (C5) showed no co-occurrence with other causes. The study concludes that lack of contractual terms promoting efficient communication and collaboration is a primary contractual risk in modular construction projects.

ideas.idea: Contractual and technical requirements significantly influence the level of modularization achievable on a project.
ideas.quote: O’Connor et al. [8] highlighted that higher levels of modularization can be achieved if the contractual and technical requirements favor the adoption of such a method.

ideas.idea: Offsite construction implementation requires new contractual models rather than reliance on traditional agreements.
ideas.quote: Nadim and Goulding [9] emphasized on the need for new processes and contractual models for the implementation of offsite construction methods.

ideas.idea: Contractual problems and disputes are a recognized risk specifically tied to the integration of offsite/modular construction methods.
ideas.quote: one of the risks associated with the integration of offsite construction methods are related to contractual problems and disputes [10].

ideas.idea: The fragmented nature of contractual agreements is identified as a barrier slowing modular construction adoption.
ideas.quote: Some of these challenges include the need for high initial capital cost [6], lack of clear codes and standards [8], increased design and engineering lead-in time [16], and the fragmented nature of contractual agreements [17].

ideas.idea: Delays in work progress are a leading cause of disputes in modular projects, driven by issues like site accessibility, worker unfamiliarity with modular methods, and poor offsite-onsite coordination.
ideas.quote: Some of the main reasons of delays were related to site accessibility issues, the unfamiliarity of workers with modular construction, and lack of coordination between offsite and onsite activities.

ideas.idea: Successful modular construction requires early and sustained collaboration among owner, architect, and contractor, and disconnects during contractual transitions between design phases undermine this.
ideas.quote: a critical success factor to modular construction projects is to avoid disconnects in any contractual transition between assessment, selection, Basic Design, or Detailed Design phases.

ideas.idea: Exclusion of the contractor from the design process leads to conflicts, design changes, and delays, illustrating the risk of inadequate collaborative contracting structures.
ideas.quote: the contractor has not been involved in the design process of the project leading to many conflicts and changes to the design and thus delay in the project.

ideas.idea: Lack of communication, including slow submittal/RFI turnaround, is a central and highly interconnected cause of disputes, suggesting contracts should embed communication protocols.
ideas.quote: the turn around time frame for the approval and review process of submittals and requests for information was considered high leading to accumulation of delays in the project.

ideas.idea: The absence of contractual terms that promote efficient communication and collaboration is identified as a primary contractual risk specific to modular construction.
ideas.quote: the lack of contractual terms promoting efficient communication and collaboration in the project is considered as one of the primary contractual risks in modular construction projects.

ideas.idea: Disputes in modular projects arise from the co-occurrence of multiple interconnected causes rather than isolated factors, implying contracts need to address clusters of risk together.
ideas.quote: The analysis of the dispute causation network shows that disputes and conflicts require the co-occurrence of more than a single causal factor.

objectives: To develop and test an automated text-mining classification tool that categorizes construction project correspondences as relevant or irrelevant to a claim, using four different machine learning classifiers optimized and validated across two separate construction projects.
problem_statement: Claim preparation on construction projects requires classifying large volumes of documentation, a task currently performed manually by contract administrators, which is time-consuming, costly, and prone to human error; no prior research has developed an automated tool for classifying correspondences specifically for claims use.
methodology: A four-phase methodology: (1) data preparation and preprocessing of a labeled dataset of 213 documents from Project No. 1, manually labeled by an experienced contract administrator, with text extraction (including OCR for scanned documents), cleaning, tokenization, stop-word removal, and stemming; (2) training four classifiers (KNN, Naïve Bayes, SVM, random forest) using 10-fold cross-validation, optimizing parameters (k value, term occurrence vs TF-IDF, n-grams) based on accuracy, recall, and precision; (3) testing the optimized classifiers on an independent dataset of 205 documents from a second construction project (Project No. 2) to assess cross-project applicability; (4) conclusions and recommendations.
key_background_studies: Al Qady and Kandil (document disclosure model considering actors and events generating documents, inspiring classification approaches)
Abdul-Malak and Abdulhai (categorization of claim/dispute documents into contract documents, project activity documents, and contemporary records)
Caldas et al. (automated classification of electronic construction records)
Ur-Rahman and Harding (text mining technique using Key Term Phrasal Knowledge sequences to classify post-project texts)
Alsubaey et al. (argument for the vital role of text mining in construction document management)
findings: Random forest achieved the highest recall (93%) with average accuracy (65%) on the testing dataset, while SVM achieved lower recall (80%) but higher accuracy (79%) and precision; Naïve Bayes had the highest recall (96%) but low accuracy (59%) and precision. TF-IDF vector creation outperformed term occurrence in recall across classifiers. Optimal n-gram levels varied by classifier. The study concludes that classifier selection should depend on user priorities regarding recall versus accuracy/precision, with random forest or SVM being recommended depending on the emphasis needed.

ideas.idea: Claims are an inevitable and important contractual mechanism for managing unexpected events, and effective claim management helps prevent escalation into disputes.
ideas.quote: Claims are important contractual tools for dealing with unexpected events on projects and, if managed properly, aid in preventing the escalation of issues and the avoidance of disputes

ideas.idea: Documentation is fundamental to substantiating and arguing claims, requiring large volumes of information to be classified and analyzed.
ideas.quote: documentation has been recognized to be a fundamental issue in submitting claims and arguing on the correctness of claims

ideas.idea: The conventional manual documentation and classification system used for claims is inefficient and needs improvement.
ideas.quote: the conventional documentation system that is currently utilized is inefficient—mainly due to problems with input information and documents—and must be enhanced to ensure appropriate claim management

ideas.idea: Manual classification of correspondence relevance to claims by contract administrators is costly, time-consuming, and error-prone, motivating automation.
ideas.quote: Not only does this method consume substantial time, effort, and cost but it is also prone to human error.

ideas.idea: Claim documents can be systematically categorized into contract documents, project activity documents, and contemporary records to support tracking and resolution.
ideas.quote: Abdul-Malak and Abdulhai [16] divided the documents presented in support of the claim/dispute tracking and resolution process into three groups, namely: (1) contract documents, (2) project activity documents, and (3) contemporary records.

ideas.idea: Text mining and automated classification tools can significantly improve construction information management, including for claims, by uncovering hidden patterns in large text datasets.
ideas.quote: there is a need for automated classification methods that are efficient in structuring project data and discovering hidden patterns in the data

ideas.idea: Model performance and appropriate classifier selection for claim-document classification depends on project-specific needs, balancing recall (capturing all relevant claim documents) against accuracy and precision (avoiding false positives).
ideas.quote: while the choice of the classifier will depend on the user's needs for the specific project and model, it is recommended to consider all criteria, with recall having the highest weight.

objectives: To investigate building code compliance and quality assurance practices for off-site construction/prefabrication across six countries (Sweden, Switzerland, UK, China, Singapore, Australia) and identify approaches that overcome compliance challenges.
problem_statement: Performance-based building regulations often lack a 'safe space' for innovative construction techniques not prescribed in codes, creating compliance and quality assurance challenges for off-site construction adoption, with unclear allocation of risks and liabilities across the supply chain.
methodology: A cross-country case study approach using questionnaire surveys distributed to manufacturers, builders/contractors, and building inspectors in six countries (Sweden, Switzerland, UK, China, Singapore, Australia) from February to August 2019. 374 stakeholders were surveyed with 122 responses (33% response rate). Data was analyzed using descriptive statistics followed by comparative cross-country analysis.
key_background_studies: Smith (2010) - argued difficulty advocating prefabrication without an enabling regulatory environment supporting integrated quality assurance and building compliance codes.
Gan et al. (2018) - similarly emphasized need for regulatory environment supporting quality assurance for prefabrication.
Hoonakker et al. (2010) - discussed liability risks to local authorities from inadequate scrutiny of modular components.
Lee and Kim (2017) - investigated quality assurance and compliance issues for off-site construction.
Arashpour et al. (2015) - studied quality assurance and compliance for off-site construction.
Park et al. (2011) - described Singapore's buildability score regulation as a product authentication mechanism.
Yin et al. (2009) - discussed product identification/tracking technologies for quality assurance and risk allocation among supply chain parties.
Barbosa and Woetzel (2017) / McKinsey & Company (2019) - highlighted social value and market scale of prefabrication and quality concerns as major hindrance.
findings: The manufacturer's self-certification approach is predominant for meeting code of compliance requirements across most countries studied (Sweden, Switzerland, Australia, China), while the UK and Singapore primarily use independent third-party certification. A fit-for-purpose regulatory compliance system requires fair allocation of risks and liabilities across the supply chain. A healthy, functional regulatory system for off-site compliance requires third-party certification for products/factories combined with a traceability system, forming a 'chain of custody' approach. The role of lending agencies/insurance companies in compliance remained unclear from survey data.

ideas.idea: Self-certification by manufacturers is the dominant compliance mechanism across most surveyed countries, placing responsibility for quality on individual companies.
ideas.quote: the manufacturer’s self-certification approach appears predominant for meeting code of compliance requirements

ideas.idea: A functional regulatory system needs third-party certification of products and factories plus traceability, not self-certification alone.
ideas.quote: a healthy and functional regulatory system for off-site compliance requires a third-party certification for products/factories and traceability

ideas.idea: Fair and proportionate allocation of risk and liability across the supply chain (manufacturer, builder, authority) is essential for a workable compliance system.
ideas.quote: More than half of the respondents thought it was essential to allocate risks and liabilities evenly across the supply chain by taking a proportionate risk-based approach to dealing with quality compliance issues.

ideas.idea: A 'chain of custody' approach—where each supply chain party takes due responsibility—is proposed as the key enabling condition for compliance regimes.
ideas.quote: one of the essential enabling conditions for a compliance regime is establishing a chain of custody in the supply chain, where each party takes due responsibility

ideas.idea: Product identification and traceability technologies (RFID, GPS, barcodes) support quality control and defect tracking throughout manufacturing and assembly.
ideas.quote: Product identification and tracking technologies are often used to ensure quality assurance for manufactured building products and systems

ideas.idea: Industry-led quality assurance schemes, sometimes combined with government accreditation, create a two-fold responsibility system between industry and regulators.
ideas.quote: The two-fold quality assurance scheme requires both the prefabrication manufacturer industry and the government to take responsibility for producing high-quality prefabricated systems

ideas.idea: Regulatory authentication mechanisms such as Singapore's buildability score can be used to enforce minimum design/manufacturing standards for prefabricated components.
ideas.quote: government policymakers can enforce a buildability score regulation to facilitate the authentication process for prefabricated products

ideas.idea: Insurance and lending schemes can support defect warranties and build market confidence in prefabrication, though their role in compliance remains underdeveloped.
ideas.quote: a sound lending scheme will boost the confidence of prefabrication manufacturers and builders in expanding their share in the off-site construction market

ideas.idea: Lack of scrutiny of modular components creates significant liability risk for local authorities inspecting assembled buildings.
ideas.quote: Unless building officials and certifying agencies scrutinize each modular component, using those components in one assembled building would be considered a significant liability risk to local authorities

ideas.idea: A national/regional register of certified compliant products, verified by accredited third parties, could streamline compliance processes for architects, importers and suppliers.
ideas.quote: there is a need for a national or regional register of compliant building products and systems which are certified by internationally accredited third parties

objectives: To differentiate net cause factors from net effect factors among the most significant readability risks in construction contracts by determining their causal relationships using fuzzy DEMATEL method, in order to improve contract documentation and risk management.
problem_statement: Readability risks in construction contracts are seldom examined and their underlying root causes are rarely analyzed in existing literature, which mostly focuses on operational contractual risks rather than systematic root cause analysis of readability issues that contribute to conflicts, claims and disputes.
methodology: A total of 20 construction industry experts (engineers, architects, contract managers, owners, directors) with varying roles and organizations (owner, contractor, client, subcontractor) were surveyed via face-to-face interviews using pairwise comparisons based on linguistic variables converted to triangular fuzzy numbers. A 10x10 decision matrix of the top ten readability risks (identified from prior fuzzy VIKOR study) was analyzed using fuzzy DEMATEL method to compute a total relation matrix; MPSD and MMDE algorithms determined threshold values; a root cause degree (RCD) diagram was constructed to visualize cause-effect relationships.
key_background_studies: Koc and Gurgun [25] - identified and ranked 18 readability risks in construction contracts using fuzzy VIKOR, forming the basis of this study's top ten risks
Cheung and Yiu [5] - conceptualized construction disputes as having contract provisions, triggering events and conflicts
Broome and Hayes [29] - compared clarity of traditional contracts vs NEC, found standard forms more clear
Rameezdeen and Rajapakse [15] - investigated readability of FIDIC and NEC using readability formula, found positive relationship with commonality in interpretation
Chong and Zin [1] - investigated Malaysian standard contract form, proposed measures for language structure, ranked sentence length top
Rameezdeen and Rodrigo [22] - examined impact of modifications to standard contract forms on readability, found over 50% of clauses remained difficult to read
Besaiso et al. [2] - compared FIDIC and NEC suitability in Palestine, found NEC better at minimizing disputes
Youssef et al. [31] - assessed semantic risks of amended standard contract forms and correlation with contingency pricing
Lee et al. [32] - proposed NLP-based proactive risk assessment model to detect missing contractor-friendly clauses in modified FIDIC conditions
Ameer Ali [41] - critiqued specific poorly drafted contract clauses in Malaysian Government design & build contracts
findings: Poor grammar use (missing nouns, word formation), use of specialized legal vocabulary/jargon, lack of visual representations, and negative language style were identified as the primary net cause factors of readability risks, with poor grammar use being the most significant causal factor. Lengthy documents, abbreviations, scope complexity, controversial legal term uses, repetitions, and ambiguous words were net effect factors rather than root causes. Notably, four of the top five most significant readability risks (by prior VIKOR ranking) were found to be net effects rather than causes, suggesting traditional readability improvement measures (e.g., shortening sentences) may be ineffective without addressing underlying grammatical and terminology causes. Scope complexity, ambiguity, and incoherence formed a triangular dyadic relationship reinforcing each other.

ideas.idea: Standard contract forms (FIDIC, NEC) are generally considered more readable than traditional contracts, but modifications to them tend to reduce readability and clarity.
ideas.quote: Rameezdeen and Rodrigo [22] found that modifications to standard contract forms generally make the contracts more difficult to read.

ideas.idea: NEC drafters deliberately abandoned legal jargon to improve simplicity and clarity, though this created other issues like missing nouns.
ideas.quote: It was addressed that drafters of NEC have taken a revolutionary step by abandoning legal language [2].

ideas.idea: Shortening sentence length, a common readability recommendation, may inadvertently increase grammatical errors and missing nouns, undermining its intended benefit.
ideas.quote: while decreasing the number of words in sentences, it failed to propose good grammar use with missing nouns [19], [20].

ideas.idea: Excessive legal terminology and jargon in standard forms like FIDIC has been criticized as unnecessary and reducing document clarity for engineers who use but did not draft the contract.
ideas.quote: FIDIC conditions have been criticized for containing many unnecessary legal expressions [2], [29].

ideas.idea: Contract incompleteness, ambiguity, and poor documentation are central root causes of construction disputes, making contract drafting quality a preventative risk management tool.
ideas.quote: Contract incompleteness with inadequate contract documentation, poor understanding of contracts and improper contract administration processes [6]–[9] are leading factors contributing construction conflicts.

ideas.idea: Modifications made to standard contract clauses by clients to fit project-specific needs often introduce inconsistencies that are a leading cause of disputes.
ideas.quote: It was addressed that inconsistencies between modifications were one of the top causes of construction disputes in Australia [22].

ideas.idea: Poorly drafted clauses in construction contracts (e.g., jurisdiction clauses) illustrate multiple compounding readability risks such as excessive length, ambiguity, and unclear allocation of responsibility between parties.
ideas.quote: First, the sentence is too long (69 words, threefold of what has been suggested by Chong and Zin [1]), legalese and redundant [41].

ideas.idea: Visual representation and diagrams in contracts can increase transparency and reduce reliance on lengthy textual descriptions of scope and technical details.
ideas.quote: Visual representation of the contracts can increase the transparency of construction contracts, ensuring that the contracts are handled by project managers adequately [24].

ideas.idea: Root cause analysis of contractual readability problems, rather than simple ranking of risks, is necessary because contract drafting interventions aimed at one risk factor can worsen another (a butterfly-effect type interaction).
ideas.quote: With the butterfly effect in mind [71], estimating the consequences of any positive steps on the other readability risks is essential for improved contract drafting process.

ideas.idea: Findings are intended to directly inform practitioners drafting or modifying standard forms such as FIDIC and NEC to prioritize root causes rather than surface symptoms during contract drafting.
ideas.quote: The findings of this study are useful for contract drafters, dealing with traditional, standard contract forms such as FIDIC and NEC, or contract modifications, by emphasizing the most effective measures to improve the quality of contract documents.

objectives: To conduct a systematic literature review of studies on causes of project delays (CPD) published between 1985 and 2018, identifying research trends (publications, countries, institutions, researchers) and compiling a comprehensive, common set of CPDs.
problem_statement: Construction project delays remain a chronic, worldwide problem, and while numerous studies have identified causes of delay in various contexts, prior reviews (e.g., Ramanathan et al. 2012; Zidane and Andersen 2018) are limited in scope, coverage, or geographic bias, leaving a gap for a longitudinal, comprehensive, and reproducible review synthesizing the full body of CPD literature.
methodology: Systematic literature review following Sandelowski and Barroso (2007) approach, using Scopus database searches with keywords 'delay', 'delays', 'overrun', 'overruns', limited to journal articles/reviews in top construction, engineering, and management journals archived by Web of Science. Initial search yielded 2,019/2,020 results, narrowed to 532 by journal title, then to 123 after abstract/full-text review, and finally validated to 100 articles (97 after excluding reviews) from 19 academic journals for detailed analysis. Contribution scores for countries, institutions, and authors were calculated using a weighted authorship formula from Howard et al. (1987).
key_background_studies: Ansah and Sorooshian (2018) - proposed the '4P' theoretical framework grouping project delays by shared characteristics
Adam et al. (2017) - literature analysis providing an aggregated ranking of project delays, limited to 40 articles on publicly funded projects
Eizakshiri et al. (2015) - reviewed studies on project delays to identify gaps and propose future research questions
Ramanathan et al. (2012) - one of the most comprehensive prior reviews, but limited to studies published before 2010
Zidane and Andersen (2018) - comprehensive review of top delay factors but biased toward Norway and underrepresented some regions
Sambasivan and Soon (2007) - identified inadequate planning, poor site management, contractor experience, subcontractors, and client financial capability as prominent causes
Al-Kharashi and Skitmore (2009) - identified client's financial capability and payment delays as most critical causes in Saudi Arabia
Doloi, Sawhney and Iyer (2012); Doloi, Sawhney, Iyer and Rentala (2012) - applied factor analysis/structural equation modeling to Indian construction delays
Lindhard and Wandahl (2014) - examined CPDs in Denmark, highlighting resource shortages and design issues
Durdyev et al. (2017) - studied causes of delay in residential construction projects in Cambodia
findings: The review identified 149 causes of delay from 97 studies, with the ten most common being: weather/climate conditions, poor communication/coordination/conflicts among stakeholders, ineffective/improper planning, material shortage, financial problems, payment delays, equipment/plant shortage, lack of stakeholder experience/qualification/competence, construction labour shortage, and poor site management. Developing countries' researchers and institutions contributed most to CPD research, though UK and USA showed high scores due to collaboration rather than delay frequency. Publication output increased dramatically after 2010 (71% of studies in the last decade). The study found that although many causes are similar across contexts, country- and project-specific factors create variation; about 20 causes affect both developed and developing countries. Gaps identified include: insufficient exploration of interrelated/reciprocal causes (suggesting social network analysis for future work), and unexamined implications of advanced technologies, off-site manufacturing, integrated project delivery, lean construction, and BIM on schedule performance, as well as contractual relationships and project culture being largely ignored in prior research.

ideas.idea: The study notes a research gap regarding how innovative and collaborative delivery methods such as integrated project delivery, lean construction, and BIM might reduce delay-causing issues, an area directly relevant to modern construction methods and contracts.
ideas.quote: The study shows that the implications of innovative and collaborative delivery methods, such as integrated project delivery, lean construction and building information modelling should be examined, and the influence of these methods on project schedule performance could be evaluated.

ideas.idea: The authors explicitly identify that contractual relationship issues have been largely neglected in the delay literature, pointing to an area needing further contractual research.
ideas.quote: the research findings reveal that issues related to the contractual relationship, project culture and project delivery methods have largely been ignored by the previous studies.

ideas.idea: Material shortages, a major delay cause, are linked to off-site manufacturing and supply chain issues, and the paper notes that off-site manufacturing implications for delay are still unexamined in the literature.
ideas.quote: Finally, it was also noted that the implications of advanced technologies, construction automation and off-site manufacturing are yet to be examined and reported in the literature.

ideas.idea: Weather/climate-related delays are recommended to be addressed contractually, suggesting contracts should explicitly account for such risks as excusable delays.
ideas.quote: Furthermore, contractual agreements between the project stakeholders should include any possible delays caused by the weather conditions (Apipattanavis et al., 2010).

ideas.idea: Poor communication and coordination among fragmented stakeholders is a leading cause of delay, and technologies like BIM are proposed as tools to mitigate this by improving information flow and reducing disputes.
ideas.quote: Building information modelling provides a digital environment for each project stakeholder, regardless of his/her location, with clear information, and has been proven to offer dynamic interaction at all stages of the project for better coordination, effective communication and reduction of potential disputes.

ideas.idea: Ineffective or improper planning, often due to unrealistic project schedules imposed by clients, is identified as a major and non-excusable delay cause within the contractor's control, indicating a contractual/responsibility dimension.
ideas.quote: Delays in any of the project milestones, depending on their severity and the floating time of each project activity, will definitely hinder project schedule performance, which is not excusable as the planned milestones are within the contractor’s control.

ideas.idea: Design changes are highlighted as a factor contributing to material shortages and delays, implicating the design-change process and its contractual handling as a recurring issue.
ideas.quote: changes in design (C13); delays in material delivery/supply/manufacturing (C17); changes/increases in material prices (C31); procurement of materials (C40); resource allocation/management (C55); political factors (C64); theft/vandalism (C105); failure in testing (C109) and unreliable suppliers (C114).

ideas.idea: Lack of skilled/qualified workforce, including limited institutional training and unattractive industry image, is a persistent cause of delay tied to workforce development and procurement of competent labour—an issue relevant to prefabrication/MMC skill requirements.
ideas.quote: This is a particularly problematic issue in developing countries, due to the limited number of institutions offering construction training... and the unavailability and unaffordability of skilled foreign forepersons.

ideas.idea: The study calls for future research to model interrelationships between delay causes using techniques like social network analysis, suggesting that isolated treatment of causes (including contractual ones) is an oversimplification.
ideas.quote: there are several interrelated causes that influence another identified cause(s); therefore, investigating the influence of each cause separately is an oversimplification of the problem, a gap in the knowledge that needs to be filled.

objectives: To develop a robust framework for integrating Offsite Construction (OSC) and Building Information Modelling (BIM) in the New Zealand construction industry by identifying integration challenges and proposing strategies to overcome them, through evaluating current research, identifying OSC and BIM challenges, reviewing integration strategies, and applying these findings to the New Zealand context.
problem_statement: Although research exists separately on OSC and BIM, their integration remains ambiguous, complex, undocumented and lacks structure, particularly in New Zealand, leaving stakeholders without practical guidance on how to combine the two to improve productivity.
methodology: A mixed-methods triangulation approach with three stages: (1) scientometric analysis using VOSViewer and Citespace on OSC/BIM-related keywords to map research trends and pioneer countries; (2) a systematic literature review (PRISMA-guided) of 53 articles from SCOPUS, coded for OSC challenges, BIM implementation challenges, and integration strategies, scored using criticality, citation and significance-in-literature indices via NVivo 12; (3) nine semi-structured interviews with New Zealand construction industry experts (10+ years' experience) analysed with NVivo 12 using descriptive and pattern coding to validate and contextualise findings for New Zealand, culminating in an integration framework.
key_background_studies: Abanda et al. (2017) - highlighted OSC as part of Industry 4.0 and BIM's potential for offsite manufacturing, and noted integration remains rudimentary and undocumented
Yin et al. (2019) - identified future research directions for OSC and BIM integration including generative design and cloud BIM
Li et al. (2019) - proposed a conceptual framework integrating BIM and prefabricated housing production (SBP, SWPs, SPOs)
Liu et al. (2021) - studied integration of BIM and steel fabrication machine codes using open BIM standards for better data interoperability
Goulding et al. (2015) - indicated BIM adoption in OSC is significant but did not propose integration strategies
Li et al. (2017) - designed RFID-enabled real-time BIM platform for prefabrication to mitigate schedule risks
Tang et al. (2019) - showed strong link between BIM deployment and OSC performance through integrative management
Kamali and Hewage (2016) - described OSC benefits including time savings of 30-50% compared to traditional construction
findings: The study identified six clusters of OSC challenges (transportation, training and experience, planning and design, financial, collaboration and commitment, industry/innovation/process) and six clusters of BIM implementation challenges (lack of knowledge, human resources, financial, legal constraints, interoperability and collaboration, lack of standardisation). Six integration strategy clusters emerged from literature, with two additional clusters (policy documentation and technology management) identified through interviews. New Zealand lags behind OECD countries in OSC-BIM integration research. The developed framework consists of 23 strategies across 8 clusters (policy document, training and professional development, documentation, technology management, governmental development, contract development, accurate definition and detailing, communication), applicable at organisational (3 clusters) and project (5 clusters) levels, serving as a diagnostic tool for practitioners and policymakers.

ideas.idea: Contract development, including new contract language, is identified as a necessary strategy to support BIM collaboration with OSC integration.
ideas.quote: It has been identified that contract language and clause alterations are also necessary to support BIM collaboration with OSC (Jin et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2021).

ideas.idea: Legal constraints such as data ownership, proprietary issues and risk-sharing must be addressed within contract documents when using BIM.
ideas.quote: Teams utilising BIM should be cognisant of legal constraints such as data ownership, proprietary issues and risk-sharing. Such difficulties must be addressed in contract documents (Azhar, 2011).

ideas.idea: Legal and contractual commitments frequently hamper potential collaboration with third parties in BIM-enabled projects.
ideas.quote: On the other hand, potential collaboration with third parties is frequently hampered by legal and contractual commitments (Liu et al., 2017b).

ideas.idea: The dominance of traditional project delivery processes and historically robust tendering frameworks is a barrier to OSC adoption.
ideas.quote: Dominance of traditional project process and historically robust tendering framework

ideas.idea: Fragmented project delivery and tendering models prohibit full collaboration among stakeholders in OSC projects.
ideas.quote: This is due to the fragmented nature of construction projects and the tendering models which prohibit full collaboration (Table 5).

ideas.idea: Lack of standard project procurement methods is identified as an industry-level challenge for OSC implementation.
ideas.quote: Lack of project procurement methods

ideas.idea: Government mandatory regulations and incentives are seen as more effective drivers for BIM/OSC adoption than voluntary standards.
ideas.quote: Contrary to expectation, this study found that the mandated requirement by the government (Table 6) for applying BIM is much more significant than any standards or training.

ideas.idea: Early stakeholder engagement and collaboration from the earliest project stages is recommended to reduce rework and requires new forms of contract enabling multi-party involvement.
ideas.quote: Engaging in the early stages require new forms of contract that enable the involvement of different parties. Contract development by its own is another identified strategy cluster in the framework.

ideas.idea: Lack of a mature BIM contract is cited as a specific legal constraint hindering BIM implementation.
ideas.quote: Legal issues, legal barriers, intellectual property rights concerns and lack of a mature BIM contract

ideas.idea: Higher initial capital investment required for OSC, despite long-term cost savings, creates industry resistance and financial risk allocation concerns relevant to contracting.
ideas.quote: Although one of the significant benefits of OSC is reducing the overall cost of the project (Darko et al., 2020), high initial capital is needed (Ayalp and Ay, 2020).

objectives: To identify and characterize the supply chain relationships developed among architects, engineers, builders and timber element suppliers within massive timber construction projects, and to identify enablers—such as networking, collaboration, procurement modes and prefabrication—that facilitate greater use of timber as a structural material.
problem_statement: Despite the growing structural use of engineered timber, market adoption remains limited partly due to the complexity of designing, contracting and building timber structures, and specifically due to an underexplored 'culture of the industry' barrier—namely, the relationships, knowledge and experience shared among supply chain stakeholders—which has not been fully addressed in prior literature.
methodology: A qualitative, multi-method case study using 27 semi-structured interviews with architects, structural engineers, builders, timber element suppliers, supplier-builders and academics from nine countries involved in 15 notable European timber buildings; complemented by participant observation (site and plant visits over three months) and secondary data (company reports, websites); data analyzed via qualitative content analysis with coding to identify relationship types, following a grounded, post-positivist research design.
key_background_studies: Gosselin et al. (barriers to timber use categorized into six groups, including 'culture of the industry')
Meng et al. (developed eight criteria—procurement, trust, collaboration, etc.—to evaluate construction supply chain maturity)
Broft et al. and Behera et al. (mapped linear procurement and construction phase structures)
Rogers (1962) (diffusion of innovation theory used to explain early-stage adoption behavior in timber construction)
Dubois and Gadde (described construction relationships as 'loose couplings' of temporary firm coalitions)
Akintoye et al./Akintoye and Main (examined collaboration and partnership agreements among UK contractors and barriers from industry culture)
Cox et al. (identified obstacles to prefabrication adoption, including poor education, distrust, and lack of holistic evaluation tools)
Rosner et al. (compared Design-Build vs Design-Bid-Build performance in cost growth and modifications)
findings: The study identified three levels of stakeholder relationships in timber construction supply chains—Contractual, Timber Building Project, and Structural Timber Building Industry Development—showing that timber projects require closer, more frequent, and more collaborative relationships (a network rather than a linear chain) than typical construction supply chains. Early involvement of suppliers with architects and engineers reduces design risk and cost. Procurement methods that integrate design and construction phases (e.g., Design-Build) and prefabrication both facilitate collaboration by reducing the number of independent stakeholders and enabling knowledge sharing, thus acting as accelerators for timber structural adoption.

ideas.idea: Prefabricated/integrated supplier-builder systems reduce the number of contractual relationships needed in a project, simplifying coordination.
ideas.quote: prefabricated systems allow for smoother relationships by limiting the number of stakeholders while promoting innovative thinking.

ideas.idea: Early involvement of prefabrication suppliers during design (even unpaid) prevents costly or unbuildable designs later.
ideas.quote: if they told the engineers and architects that you have to make the plans without any influence of any supplier or installer at all, then it would have been very likely that the design would have been too expensive or maybe too risky to price

ideas.idea: Design-Build and similar integrated procurement methods increase proximity between design and construction parties, improving performance compared to traditional Design-Bid-Build.
ideas.quote: Rosner et al. [70] demonstrated that performance is significantly better in terms of cost growth and the number of modifications per million dollars when using Design-Build compared to the traditional Design-Bid-Build contract type.

ideas.idea: Two structural engineers—one for design, one for the supplier/fabricator—must coordinate to ensure specified elements are producible, reflecting a division of design responsibility tied to prefabrication.
ideas.quote: The suppliers are responsible for the production of the structural elements designed by these structural engineers... the two engineers will exchange until they reach an agreement.

ideas.idea: Traditional linear procurement (Design-Bid-Build) is less suited to innovative construction methods like timber/prefabrication, which benefit from less traditional contract structures.
ideas.quote: the more innovative a project is, the less traditional contract procurement modes are needed. For example, Traditional modes do not help LEED or Zero energy 1 innovative philosophies.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication reduces field/construction time compared to conventional materials, a key advantage relevant to project delivery method choice.
ideas.quote: Waugh [79] specifically mentioned how construction projects using Crossed Laminated Timber (CLT) as the structural material allow field times to be reduced if compared to the use of concrete and steel.

ideas.idea: Industry-wide obstacles to prefabrication adoption include lack of education, distrust, and absence of reliable comparison tools between methods—issues relevant to contract and risk allocation.
ideas.quote: poor current education within the industry regarding prefabricated practices, the archaic nature of the industry lacking trust, reluctance to embrace new and innovative techniques and the absence of a proven holistic and encompassing evaluation technique to provide accurate and reliable comparisons between differing construction methods.

ideas.idea: When a single firm integrates supply and building services (supplier-builder), collaboration is easier because it occurs within one organization rather than across separate contracted parties.
ideas.quote: If a company decides to incorporate building services into its value proposition, the number of actors involved in the supply chain becomes limited and collaboration can be optimized with client relationships existing within the same entity.

objectives: To conceptually explore the potential of blockchain-based smart contracts for automating and optimizing infrastructure asset management and maintenance processes, extending their application beyond design/construction into maintenance, emergency response, and decommissioning phases.
problem_statement: While smart contracts have been widely applied to construction-phase payment and procurement processes, their use in long-term asset management, maintenance, and emergency response remains largely unexplored, leaving a gap regarding how automation and blockchain traceability could improve resilience and reduce administrative/bureaucratic delays in infrastructure operations.
methodology: Conceptual study (non-quantitative) involving a literature review on smart contracts and blockchain, followed by development of a conceptual framework and a simulated emergency-management scenario. A smart contract named 'EmergencyManagement' was coded in Solidity for the Ethereum blockchain, using IoT sensor data as an external oracle to trigger automated actions (alert notification, data logging, infrastructure closure, and payment). Code efficiency was verified using the SolidityScan tool, and results were discussed via KPI, resilience, and CPM cost frameworks.
key_background_studies: Szabo (1990s) – first introduced the concept of smart contracts as automated digital agreements.
Kim and Kim (2024) – analyzed blockchain's role in optimizing procurement and contract management in construction.
Ahmadisheykhsarmast et al. (2023) – proposed decentralized blockchain for tendering to eliminate intermediaries.
Sonmez et al. (2022) – integrated BIM with smart contract progress payment administration systems.
Wu et al. (2022) – investigated smart contracts to ensure payment continuity at project milestones for material supply.
Wang et al. – developed an automatic incentive-penalty enforcement system for modular construction projects.
Zhong et al. – applied Shapley value-based smart contracts for equitable reward/penalty allocation in modular construction.
findings: The conceptual framework demonstrates that smart contracts can automate emergency detection, alerting, documentation, and payment processes in infrastructure maintenance, achieving a high code efficiency score (86.75/100) with no critical issues. Smart contracts can reduce response times, administrative and legal disputes, and costs while enhancing transparency, traceability, and stakeholder trust. They shorten but do not eliminate bureaucratic and administrative phases, and human oversight remains essential for validation and quality control. The approach also shows potential to improve infrastructure resilience by reducing recovery time and cost overruns associated with governance inefficiencies.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts have mainly been studied and applied for payment automation and procurement during design and construction phases, not maintenance or asset management.
ideas.quote: these works have primarily investigated and demonstrated the benefits of using smart contracts during the design and construction phases, particularly concerning the management and payment during the procurement of construction materials

ideas.idea: The study extends smart contract application to maintenance, emergency response, and decommissioning phases of the infrastructure lifecycle.
ideas.quote: this study extends their application to integrate not only the design and construction phases but also maintenance operations.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate emergency responses such as alerts, data logging, and infrastructure closure once IoT-monitored thresholds are exceeded.
ideas.quote: When the thresholds are exceeded, the smart contract executes three distinct actions, which, as previously mentioned, are carried out autonomously and automatically.

ideas.idea: Human oversight remains essential even with automated smart contracts to prevent errors such as false positives.
ideas.quote: human oversight remains essential to prevent errors, such as false positives or misinterpretations of automated signals.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts reduce legal disputes and administrative delays by encoding pre-agreed interventions and payment conditions.
ideas.quote: Adopting a smart contract improves emergency response and ensures that management operations are carried out in the correct order and manner, simultaneously reducing potential legal disputes that often follow critical events.

ideas.idea: Governance inefficiencies such as funding delays and permit approvals negatively affect cost performance, which smart contracts can mitigate through automation.
ideas.quote: The cost performance index (CPI), a key metric for budget deviation, highlights how governance inefficiencies—such as funding delays, permit approvals, and certification processes—negatively impact overall costs.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can shorten but not eliminate bureaucratic and administrative phases in infrastructure recovery and maintenance.
ideas.quote: smart contracts shorten but do not eliminate administrative and bureaucratic phases, ensuring both efficiency and control.

ideas.idea: Financial operations within smart contracts are safeguarded through pre-allocated funds and require verification by qualified technicians before payment execution.
ideas.quote: Financial operations are safeguarded through pre-allocated funds and verification mechanisms, ensuring payments are executed only after approval from qualified technicians.

ideas.idea: Distinguishing between smart contract code (technical implementation) and smart legal contract (legal enforceability) is essential to understand adoption challenges.
ideas.quote: this concept has often been divided into two distinct parts, specifically referring to smart contract code and smart legal contract.

ideas.idea: Widespread adoption of smart contracts in infrastructure management requires addressing regulatory, technical interoperability, and cost challenges.
ideas.quote: The widespread adoption of smart contracts in asset management requires addressing regulatory concerns, technical interoperability, and initial investment costs.

objectives: To develop an in-depth understanding of contractual challenges in Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) by identifying major causes of conflicts, claims, and disputes in IPD projects, investigating how popular US standard IPD contracts (AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300) address these issues, and providing contractual guidelines/checklists to help parties negotiate IPD agreements.
problem_statement: Despite documented performance benefits of IPD, its adoption remains slow in the US construction industry, partly due to a lack of contractual understanding and implementation of IPD agreements, leaving contracting parties uncertain about how to manage risks, liabilities, termination, insurance, data sharing, and disputes under multiparty IPD contracts.
methodology: An interdependent, three-step qualitative research methodology: (1) selection of representative national IPD standard contracts (AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300) based on consultation with a focus group of construction attorneys; (2) identification of IPD issues of concern through analysis of seven IPD case studies (project case studies and law cases) collected via keyword searches of legal and project databases, supplemented by focus group input; and (3) comparative analysis of contractual provisions relevant to the identified issues under the two standard forms. Outcomes (comparative analysis and a 42-question checklist) were verified by a second focus group of construction attorneys from a legal firm with over 125 years of practice.
key_background_studies: Kent and Becerik-Gerber (2010) - survey-based study of industry experience/attitudes toward IPD, highlighting contract understanding as a constraint
El Asmar et al. (2013) - compared IPD project performance to other delivery methods, showing statistically significant improvements
Lee et al. (2013) - case study of energy risk management in IPD hospital project
Azhar et al. (2015) - surveyed relationship between IPD and ICT
Hanna (2016) - statistical evaluation of IPD performance on building projects
Teng et al. (2017) - game-theory model for profit distribution under IPD
Xie and Liu (2017) - studied IPD case studies' implementation of shared responsibility and incentive clauses
El-adaway et al. (2017) - proposed multiparty relational contracting framework addressing conflicts and disputes
Manata et al. (2018) - studied communication behaviors in IPD teams
Laurent and Leicht (2019) - practices for cross-functional IPD teams
Choi et al. (2019) - compared team integration/owner satisfaction between IPD and CMAR
Ibrahim et al. (2020) - compared project performance across DBB, DB, CM, and IPD delivery methods
Sive and Hays (2009) - noted IPD contracts not fully tested or understood
Bilbo et al. (2014) - identified non-understood contracts as obstacle to IPD adoption
Roy et al. (2018) - identified noncomprehensive contract understanding as challenge for IPD adoption
Viana et al. (2020) - bibliometric review identifying contractual topics as key future IPD research trend
Johnson et al. (2013) - identified AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300 as major commercial IPD contracts
Harper and Molenaar (2014) - noted AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300 as most commonly used IPD contracts
Maemura et al. (2018) - analyzed five case studies for root causes of contractual conflicts in international construction
Assaad et al. (2020b) - analyzed six case studies on commercial/legal considerations of off-site construction
findings: The study identified six major IPD issues of concern: risks and incentives; liabilities and indemnification; suspension and termination; insurance; data sharing; and dispute resolution. Comparative analysis of AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300 revealed differing approaches: ConsensusDocs 300 provides more explicit risk assessment techniques and a formal risk pool/incentive structure putting profits at risk, while AIA C-191 is more silent on techniques but structures incentives through target cost savings and achievement compensation; both include waivers and indemnification provisions but differ in scope; both allow owner discretion to suspend/terminate but differ in notice periods and categories of termination; insurance and data-sharing provisions differ in detail and requirement for consultants/BIM protocols; dispute resolution processes both use tiered escalation to mediation then binding methods, but differ in timelines and procedural specifics. The authors developed a 42-question checklist to guide contracting parties in negotiating and drafting clearer IPD agreements, verified by legal experts, and concluded that improved contractual understanding could help expand IPD adoption in the US.

ideas.idea: Selection of an appropriate project delivery method significantly affects project success, and traditional methods rigidly allocate risk, often leading to suboptimal outcomes.
ideas.quote: traditional contracts combined with these project delivery methods rigidly allocate responsibilities and risks among contractual parties, and as a result, they often lead to suboptimal project outcomes.

ideas.idea: IPD is defined by multiparty agreements, shared risk/reward, and early involvement of all parties, integrating people and processes to optimize project results.
ideas.quote: the main characteristics of IPD are as follows: (1) multiparty agreement, (2) shared risk and reward, and (3) early involvement of all parties.

ideas.idea: A key contractual issue in IPD is how risk is identified, managed, and allocated proactively rather than reactively among parties.
ideas.quote: The risk associated with a project is the same whether it is delivered conventionally or with an IPD arrangement. However, what is different is that risk is managed either proactively or reactively.

ideas.idea: Lack of clear allocation of liabilities among parties is a major cause of disputes in project delivery, emphasizing the need for well-defined indemnification provisions.
ideas.quote: The main reason of dispute was the lack of clear allocation of liabilities among the contracting parties.

ideas.idea: Ambiguity in suspension and termination provisions, including rights to reimbursement of overhead and profit, is a recurring source of contractual disputes.
ideas.quote: The main reason of this dispute was attributed to the ambiguity and lack of understanding the rights and obligations of the parties regarding suspension and termination under the negotiated IPD agreement.

ideas.idea: Standard IPD contracts require early joint risk assessment and development of a risk matrix or risk management plan, though the level of prescribed technique varies between forms.
ideas.quote: Under both standard forms of IPD contract, the parties are required to conduct risk assessment during the early stages of the project and subsequently develop a risk matrix or risk management plan.

ideas.idea: Incentive/risk-pool mechanisms tie compensation to cost savings or place profits at risk for cost overruns, intended to align contractor and owner interests.
ideas.quote: the incentive program should be funded with the shared savings from contingency preservation or reduction in the costs... The risk pool is defined as the collective profits put at risk by the risk pool members in case the project is delivered... with more than the estimated maximum price.

ideas.idea: Both major standard forms allow the owner broad discretion to suspend work without cause, with differing notice period requirements, affecting fairness and predictability for other parties.
ideas.quote: AIA C-191 gives discretion to the owner to suspend, even without cause, the project as a whole or any subset of project activities... ConsensusDocs 300 does not state any time frame in regard to the submission of the written notice prior to suspension.

ideas.idea: Termination provisions differ significantly between standard forms in terms of categories, notice requirements, and consequences, affecting risk allocation among parties.
ideas.quote: unlike AIA C-191, ConsensusDocs 300 gives the owner the discretion to terminate the contract as a whole or one of the parties and without any time restrictions on notice submission, which definitely places the other parties at a disadvantage.

ideas.idea: Data sharing and BIM protocols are formalized contractual mechanisms to ensure collaborative information exchange central to IPD's success.
ideas.quote: sharing of timely and relevant project information is essential to ensure the success of the project... the contracting parties shall meet, as earliest as practically possible, to decide and agree on the software platforms that shall be used on the project for sharing information.

ideas.idea: Insurance requirements under IPD contracts are structured differently for each party (owner, contractor, architect/engineer) and require careful specification of coverage types and durations to avoid gaps.
ideas.quote: Both IPD contracts have certain requirements that should be attained in relation to insurance under IPD construction projects.

ideas.idea: Dispute resolution under IPD contracts follows a tiered escalation process—internal committees, then mediation, then binding methods—intended to minimize costly disputes.
ideas.quote: the parties should refer to the binding dispute resolution methods stipulated in the contract... disputes should be subjected to mediation prior to proceeding with binding dispute resolution methods.

ideas.idea: A practical checklist of contractual questions can help new adopters negotiate and draft clearer IPD agreements, reducing ambiguity and potential disputes.
ideas.quote: the authors developed a checklist consisting of 42 questions addressing the identified IPD issues of concern... Answering these questions shall result in a more comprehensive and clearer IPD contracts.

objectives: To establish a cost assessment framework for construction robots and, using it, compare and analyze the construction costs of robotic and traditional construction methods, in order to systematically identify cost increases/decreases from using robots versus traditional methods and analyze possible reasons.
problem_statement: Construction robots are proposed as a solution to skilled labor shortages and low productivity, but their adoption remains in early stages due to a lack of data on economic performance, uncertainty about costs (especially life-cycle costs), inconsistent cost component definitions in prior literature, and insufficient confidence among construction companies to invest in them, particularly in China where such data are scarce and confidential.
methodology: A case study approach using data from four Chinese construction robot manufacturers (Bright Dream Robotics, Shanghai Weijian Technology, UNRE AI Limited, Henan Pameier) obtained via interviews and publicly shared cases. Five real-world cases were grouped into two sets: a first group (5 cases, 14 robot products) comparing individual robot types' costs to traditional construction, and a second group (Case 5 only) comparing robot groups under coordinated deployment. A Cost Index (CI = CR/CT) was calculated using labor cost and apportioned investment cost data, efficiency, and human demand for each robot versus traditional methods. A cost assessment framework and cost decomposition structure were also developed through literature review, referencing TCO models and industrial robot cost models, supplemented by expert interviews.
key_background_studies: Warszawski (1985) - one of the first to analyze economic effects of construction robots via direct/indirect costs and benefits using cash flow analysis.
Skibniewski and Hendrickson (1988) - defined robot component, operating, and system engineering costs for construction robots.
Kim et al. (2010) and Lee et al. (2013) - compared automated construction system costs with traditional methods including labor and material costs for high-rise buildings.

de Soto et al. (2018) - proposed method for assigning robot system costs to structures; found robotic 3D printing more productive for complex concrete walls but traditional methods better for simple walls.

Brosque et al. (2020, 2021) and Brosque and Fischer (2022a, b) - considered purchase vs. robot-as-a-service models and coordination costs; found only 5 of 10 robot types outperformed traditional construction across safety, quality, schedule, cost.
Hu et al. (2021) - analyzed cash flows of Hephaestus cable-driven robot system over a 5-year life cycle, finding it worthwhile for UK and G20 countries.
Berlak et al. (2021) - assessed 3D printing, BIM, and robotics impacts on productivity and cost.
Warszawski and Rosenfeld (1994) - examined labor inputs/costs for multipurpose interior robots versus manual operations, finding significant skilled labor savings.
Pan et al. (2020) and Mahbub (2008) - identified lack of economic benefit as the main barrier to construction robot adoption.
Bock (2015) - described construction automation adoption using S-curve paradigm shift theory.
findings: The current cost of robotic construction does not have an economic advantage over traditional construction in most individual cases (7 of 14 robot products cost less than traditional methods). However, all construction robots cheaper than traditional methods were more than 2.9 times more efficient than human workers, and high efficiency was the key driver of lower costs. Certain robots reduce the number and skill requirements of construction workers, lowering labor costs, though human-robot collaboration remains necessary. Rationally arranged robot groups had lower costs than traditional construction even when individual robots were costlier, due to improved linkage between construction sequences and higher utilization. The main barriers to adoption were high purchase cost and uncertain life-cycle costs, compounded by technical and management barriers. Despite current cost disadvantages, the socio-environmental benefits (safety, health, waste reduction, job satisfaction) justify continued investment, and the industry is expected to transition gradually from traditional to robotic construction as costs decline and labor costs rise.

ideas.idea: Robotic and traditional construction differ mainly in labor and equipment cost structures, with other cost items being similar depending on robot type and scenario.
ideas.quote: In summary, the cost difference between robotic and traditional construction is mainly expressed in labor and equipment costs.

ideas.idea: Because robots cannot fully replace workers, human-robot collaboration is expected to persist for construction tasks for a long time, affecting labor allocation and contractual staffing needs.
ideas.quote: construction robots and workers are currently in and will be in human–robot collaboration work mode for a long time (Ma et al. 2022).

ideas.idea: The high purchase and uncertain life-cycle costs of construction robots are major economic barriers affecting investment decisions and risk allocation for contractors.
ideas.quote: Further research indicated that the high purchase cost and uncertainty of the life-cycle cost are the main barriers to the application of construction robots.

ideas.idea: Robotic construction requires additional cost items not present in traditional construction, such as installation/disassembly, off-site freight, transfer, overhauling and maintenance costs, reflecting a more complex cost/responsibility structure that would need contractual treatment.
ideas.quote: more cost items should be obtained for robotic construction than for traditional construction (Lee et al. 2013).

ideas.idea: Construction robots impose stricter material specification and site condition requirements than traditional methods, which could create new contractual obligations regarding material supply and site preparation.
ideas.quote: construction robots have a strong dependence on materials. The shape, size, weight, and position of the material will influence the construction effect.

ideas.idea: Deploying robots in coordinated groups rather than individually can lower overall costs by improving process linkage and utilization, suggesting that project delivery/sequencing arrangements matter for robotic construction economics.
ideas.quote: rationally arranging robot groups for construction strengthens the linkage between construction sequences, which in turn increases the utilization of construction robots and accelerates the construction schedule.

ideas.idea: Frequent interfacing with robot manufacturers increases management complexity and can complicate subcontracting arrangements, a factor relevant to contract administration.
ideas.quote: Frequent interfacing with construction robot manufacturers is required, which is more demanding on managers and makes subcontracting more challenging.

ideas.idea: No current construction management/contracting system is well adapted to accommodate robotic construction, implying a gap that contracts and organizational practices need to address.
ideas.quote: Currently, no construction system effectively adapts to construction robots (Xiao et al. 2023).

ideas.idea: Government incentive mechanisms, including mandates and contractual provisions, are seen as necessary to drive adoption of construction robots.
ideas.quote: Specific methods include fostering collaboration with academia and research institutes, economic incentives, adoption and demonstration in public projects or pilot projects, and additional provisions in contracts all the way to mandates (Delgado et al. 2019; Pan and Pan 2020).

ideas.idea: Choice between robotic and traditional construction methods should be guided by schedule flexibility versus cost considerations, informing project delivery decisions.
ideas.quote: Traditional construction methods are recommended for tight project schedules because they allow for multiple crews working together and have more flexibility... From a cost perspective, traditional construction is recommended at this stage.

objectives: To design cost-minimized, just-in-time (JIT) transport plans for prefabricated modular integrated construction (MiC) modules using a mathematical (integer) programming model and tailored solution method, validated with two real Hong Kong building projects.
problem_statement: Module transport planning in MiC projects is typically decided intuitively by contractors, which cannot guarantee JIT delivery and results in additional costs from early or late delivery, storage, double handling, and inefficient logistics; existing literature and heuristic methods focus mainly on 2D prefabricated components rather than bulky 3D MiC modules, and exact optimization approaches for JIT MiC module delivery are lacking.
methodology: The study formulates an integer programming model that minimizes total transportation costs (fuel, vehicle rental, driver salary) plus penalties for early/late delivery, subject to constraints on vehicle capacity, routing, travel time, and time windows. A preprocessing approach enables the model to be solved to optimality using commercial solvers (CPLEX) without heuristic algorithms. The model is validated using real-world data from two MiC projects in Hong Kong (Kowloon and Tai Po), including module and vehicle specifications, road network data, and cost parameters, with sensitivity analysis on penalty costs.
key_background_studies: Hsu et al. (2018) - investigated integrated planning for MiC modules from production to installation, one of few studies on 3D module transport.
Fang and Ng (2019) - used genetic algorithm to minimize transportation costs for prefabricated components, providing heuristic (suboptimal) solutions.
Yi et al. (2020) - first exact solution method minimizing truck rentals and inventory costs for prefabricated components.
Hussein and Zayed (2021) - qualitative analysis of 42 factors affecting JIT implementation and MiC logistics challenges, the only study directly addressing JIT delivery of MiC modules.
Kong et al. (2017) - developed JIT production scheduling model highlighting drawbacks of intuitive approaches in off-site construction.
Si et al. (2021) - proposed decision framework for JIT component delivery using genetic algorithm.
Zhang and Yu (2020) - examined stakeholder interactions in JIT component delivery via particle swarm optimization.
Kong et al. (2018) - developed algorithm for batch delivery problem minimizing delivery earliness/tardiness and environmental impacts.
Bertram et al. (2019) - McKinsey report noting ineffective module transport planning can offset MiC cost benefits, causing up to 10% cost premiums.
Koskela (1992) - foundational lean production/JIT philosophy applied to construction.
findings: The proposed optimal transportation plans achieved zero early/late delivery penalties (full JIT compliance) with high vehicle load utilization (84% average). Compared to non-JIT planning, actual transportation costs were 21.74% higher than expected when JIT was not considered, demonstrating the significance of JIT implementation. The proposed methodology reduced overall transportation costs by 10.13% compared to non-JIT planning. Sensitivity analysis showed that as unit penalty costs for early/late delivery increase, the number of non-compliant deliveries decreases, indicating a trade-off between cost savings from flexible delivery and penalty avoidance. The model efficiently computed optimal solutions for real-world scale problems (over 400 modules) in under 4 minutes.

ideas.idea: Transportation of prefabricated modules is a major obstacle to wider adoption of MiC due to high complexity and cost compared to traditional materials.
ideas.quote: It is acknowledged within the construction industry that the transportation of MiC modules is more costly and complicated than the transportation of raw materials in cast-in-situ construction

ideas.idea: Transportation planning decisions are typically made intuitively by contractors rather than through optimization, leading to inefficiencies.
ideas.quote: In practice, transport planning of prefabricated modules is usually intuitively decided by general contractors based on experience. Intuitive decisions cannot ensure the just-in-time (JIT) module delivery, thereby incurring additional costs of early and late delivery.

ideas.idea: Failure to implement JIT strategies in module delivery leads to additional costs from storage, double handling, and schedule delays, while strict JIT increases logistics costs from more frequent deliveries.
ideas.quote: Failure to consider the JIT strategy can result in additional costs for module storage, double handling, and schedule delays, while strict adherence to the JIT strategy requires more frequent deliveries to transport all the modules, thereby incurring high logistics costs.

ideas.idea: Cost is a top priority for practitioners, with transportation representing a significant portion of total prefabrication costs (procurement 60%, transportation and assembly 20% each).
ideas.quote: procurement cost represents 60% of the total costs, while transportation and assembly of MiC modules account for 20% each

ideas.idea: High-density urban environments like Hong Kong lack space for temporary on-site storage of modules, making JIT delivery essential rather than optional.
ideas.quote: in high-density cities like Hong Kong, there is a lack of available space for temporarily storing the MiC modules between production and installation. Therefore, it is necessary to consider the JIT strategy in module transport planning until temporary storage yards for MiC modules are established

ideas.idea: There is a research gap in exact (optimal) solution methods for JIT transport planning of 3D volumetric MiC modules, as most prior work addresses 2D components using heuristic algorithms.
ideas.quote: the current literature has mainly focused on the supply chain management of two-dimensional (2D) prefabricated components (such as slabs and panels), rather than that of 3D volumetric modules... there is a dearth of proposed exact solution methods that can calculate optimal transport plans to ensure the JIT delivery of MiC modules.

ideas.idea: Optimized JIT transport planning can substantially reduce costs compared to intuitive/rule-of-thumb approaches, quantifying the value of formal contractual/process planning for prefabrication logistics.
ideas.quote: A well-designed module transportation plan is expected to reduce the total project costs by 10%–30%, compared to the subjective rule-of-thumb approach

ideas.idea: The trade-off between transportation cost efficiency and delivery punctuality is a key contractual/operational tension in MiC projects that needs explicit modeling.
ideas.quote: the successful implementation of MiC projects is intricately intertwined with effective cost management, JIT implementation, and a comprehensive understanding of their interdependencies.

ideas.idea: Empirical case studies demonstrate that non-JIT planning creates a gap between expected and actual costs, exposing contractors to unplanned financial risk from delivery timing failures.
ideas.quote: if decision makers do not consider JIT, they will incur actual costs that are 21.74% higher than expected

objectives: To increase understanding of the logistics service value co-creation process in construction, specifically how value is manifested from different actors' perspectives and what drives and maintains the value co-creation process of construction logistics setups (CLS).
