problem_statement: There is a lack of awareness among construction actors regarding the importance of logistics and how it creates value, and while modularised logistics services (CLS) have become common, prior research has not analyzed these setups from a value co-creation perspective nor examined the actual implementation of value co-creation processes involving multiple actors (main contractors, subcontractors, TPL providers) in a loosely coupled system like construction.
methodology: Single in-depth case study of a modularised CLS at a major office building construction project in Gothenburg, Sweden, consisting of three logistics service modules (material management, on-site VMI, and waste management) operated by different third-party logistics (TPL) providers. Data collection combined service blueprinting (developed through four workshops with main contractor logistics managers and a project supervisor) with five semi-structured interviews with main contractor, subcontractor, and TPL provider representatives, supplemented by annual reports, news articles, and websites. Analysis used a conceptual framework combining value co-creation phases (learning, innovation/execution, outcome) and three value dimensions (technical, monetary, perceived value), coding interview data against the service blueprints.
key_background_studies: Ekeskär and Rudberg 2016 - argue TPL outsourcing improves coordination between construction site and supply chain
Janne and Fredriksson 2019/2021 - discuss common outsourcing of logistics by main contractors and early TPL integration benefits and issues of forced/non-voluntary use by subcontractors
Eriksson et al. 2021 - conceptualize CLS as complex service systems and note different actors value different services
Fredriksson et al. 2021 - define CLS as governance structure controlling flow of materials, waste, machinery and personnel, and categorize on-site/off-site logistics services
Bygballe and Ingemansson 2014 - highlight importance of collaboration and knowledge sharing among construction actors for innovation
Crespin-Mazet et al. 2015 - stress resource adaptation and mutual trust reduce risk and streamline processes in construction relationships
Bygballe and Jahre 2009 - describe strategic alignment of project goals with supply chain capabilities requiring adaptive, project-centric approaches
Dubois and Gadde 2002b - characterize construction logistics system as a loosely coupled system
Bankvall et al. 2010 - identify pooled and reciprocal interdependencies in construction requiring coordination
Sundquist et al. 2018 - identify problems of acceptance of CLS among main contractors and subcontractors
Ekeskär et al. 2022 - propose CLS boosts supply chain performance through coordination structures managed by TPL providers
Yazdanparast et al. 2010 - propose three-phase value creation model (learning, innovation/execution, outcome) used as conceptual basis
Håkansson and Ingemansson 2013 - emphasize studying change in supplier interface/innovation in supplier relationships
findings: In a loosely coupled system like construction, value co-creation is driven by trust and commitment, which provide the time needed for learning. Service blueprinting effectively visualises the connection between service design and the value of different service modules, helping build shared understanding among actors. However, risks include delayed involvement of downstream actors (especially subcontractors, who are often non-voluntary users) in the co-creation process, which slows value recognition and commitment, and a lack of coordination between service modules when multiple TPL providers are involved. Modularisation simplifies designing and implementing service content but does not simplify the service value creation or co-creation process itself, and increases the number of actors requiring coordination. The main contractor plays a dual role as both customer and supplier (convincing subcontractors to adopt modules). Technical value was high for material management and on-site VMI modules; monetary value was generally perceived as low, especially by subcontractors who bear costs without seeing full benefits initially; perceived value increased over time as actors became accustomed to the modules.

ideas.idea: Contracts in construction often stipulate mandatory use of certain logistics service modules by subcontractors, making them non-voluntary customers.
ideas.quote: Its use by subcontractors is stipulated as part of their contract with the main contractor.

ideas.idea: The uncertain nature of construction projects makes contracts unclear about who bears responsibility for unpredictable resource demands and related risks.
ideas.quote: The uncertain nature of construction projects renders resource demands unpredictable, which is a risk, and contracts render the responsibilities for these events uncertain (Loosemore, 1999).

ideas.idea: There is a tendency in construction supply chains to transfer value chain/supply chain risks upstream to subcontractors, damaging trust and reliability.
ideas.quote: Deep et al. (2022) identify from the literature review that there is a tendency to transfer the value chain or supply chain risks upstream, which leads to a breach of trust, and lack of reliability and commitment.

ideas.idea: Subcontractors, forced to use logistics modules via contract, show lower trust and commitment because they are excluded from the initial design/co-creation phase.
ideas.quote: The subcontractors were non-voluntary customers for two of the three modules, as they had to use them as part of the contract established in the project. Hence, they were not involved in the initial part of the co-creation process.

ideas.idea: Modularisation of logistics services simplifies designing and implementing service content but increases the number of actors that must be coordinated, complicating overall value creation.
ideas.quote: the modularisation simplified the service content but not the service value creation or the value co-creation process.

ideas.idea: Poor coordination among multiple TPL providers of different modules creates a lack of coherence, requiring an actor with authority (e.g., main contractor) to coordinate them.
ideas.quote: The fourth contribution is the identification of a lack of coherence and coordination between different service modules and the TPL providers of these modules.

ideas.idea: The main contractor plays a dual contractual/relational role as both customer of TPL services and de facto supplier who must convince/persuade subcontractors to adopt and pay for logistics modules imposed on them.
ideas.quote: identifying the role of the main contractor as both a customer (user of logistics service modules) and a supplier (convincing the subcontractor to use the logistics service modules) in the co-creation process.

ideas.idea: Subcontractors, being smaller and cost-focused, perceive lower monetary value from mandated logistics modules because they must pay for services imposed by contract without controlling their design.
ideas.quote: With the implementation of the material management module and the waste management module, the subcontractors were forced to use these logistics service modules, which also meant that they had to pay for them. Thus, they do not see the monetary value as high.

ideas.idea: Because construction projects are temporary and re-procure logistics service providers each time, the value co-creation and trust-building process must restart with each new project, limiting continuity of contractual relationships.
ideas.quote: the construction setting once again introduced hurdles by procuring a new set of modules in the next project, and the co-creation process must start over again.

ideas.idea: The developer, main contractor, or municipality can each act as initiator of a CLS, and the contractual initiator's needs shape the design, which may not align with the needs of other contractual users like subcontractors.
ideas.quote: A CLS can be introduced by developer, main contractor, and municipality (Fredriksson et al. 2021). The actors have different needs depending on their role and activities in the system and value separate services included in a CLS differently.

objectives: To systematically review studies on the critical success factors (CSFs) for implementing modular integrated construction (MiC) projects published between 1993 and 2019, identifying publication trends, geographical distribution, a consolidated checklist of CSFs, and a conceptual model of their interlinkages.
problem_statement: Although MiC has gained increasing attention as a means of improving construction performance, a systematic review establishing a common framework of the CSFs for implementing MiC projects is lacking, making it difficult for researchers and practitioners to identify shared CSFs across project types, stages, and territories.
methodology: A systematic literature review grounded in a realist research paradigm, using Elsevier's Scopus database combined with a snowballing search strategy. Inclusion/exclusion criteria restricted the sample to empirical studies on MiC CSFs published in peer-reviewed journals or rated conference proceedings; 55 documents (1993-2019) were included after full-text evaluation. Meta-synthesis and thematic content analysis were used to extract and rank 35 CSFs by frequency of citation, followed by development of a stage-gate framework and a conceptual causal loop model using systems dynamics (Vensim).
key_background_studies: O'Connor, O'Brien, and Choi (2014) - identified CSFs for industrial MiC projects including timely design freeze and early planning
Murtaza, Fisher, and Skibniewski (1993) - identified CSFs for petrochemical MiC projects including early design freeze and standardization
Kamar, Alshawi, and Hamid (2009) - identified top CSFs for residential MiC projects in Malaysia
Rockart (1982) - formalized the concept of critical success factors in management
Osei-Kyei and Chan (2015) - reviewed CSFs for public-private partnership projects, providing a methodological precedent
Antwi-Afari et al. (2018) - reviewed CSFs for building information modelling implementation, another methodological precedent
Gibb (2001) - classified degrees of pre-assembly in offsite construction
Jonsson and Rudberg (2015) - refined Gibb's classification of production systems and highlighted differences between MiC and cast-in-situ construction
Choi, O'Connor, and Kim (2016) - examined risk and stakeholder management in MiC projects
Rentschler, Mulrooney, and Shahani (2016) - discussed procurement, supply chain, and fabricator selection strategies for MiC
findings: The review identified 35 CSFs for implementing MiC projects, with the six most frequently cited being: (1) good working collaboration, effective communication and information sharing among project participants; (2) improved supply chain coordination and management; (3) accurate design, early design freeze and timely owner approval; (4) fully-integrated approach and involvement of key participants throughout the project; (5) suitable procurement strategy and contracting; and (6) standardization and benchmarking of best practices. These CSFs were mapped onto a stage-gate framework across conception & planning, design & procurement, and construction phases, and a conceptual causal loop model revealed mostly reinforcing feedback loops among CSFs, indicating that certain factors (e.g., effective collaboration, systematic economic analysis, early design freeze) both influence and are influenced by other CSFs. The US, UK, Malaysia, Australia, and Hong Kong were identified as the largest contributors to MiC CSF research.

ideas.idea: Suitable procurement strategy and contracting, including early involvement of manufacturers and suppliers in decision-making, is a critical success factor for MiC projects.
ideas.quote: Pan et al. (2007) argued that irrespective of the strategy adopted, procurement in MiC projects could be improved through the improved cooperation between project parties and effective integration of manufacturers and suppliers in the project decision-making process as early as a possible.

ideas.idea: The design-build delivery method is highlighted as particularly beneficial for MiC projects because it unites design and construction under a single contractual entity, fostering collaboration and accountability.
ideas.quote: Tam et al. (2007) expounded on virtues of using the design-build delivery method for residential MiC projects and highlighted the necessity of involving contractors at the design stage of MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Once module fabricators are selected, contracts should grant them a wide scope of responsibility with minimal interference, since their performance drives overall project success.
ideas.quote: Rentschler et al. (2016) recommended that module fabricators should be offered a greater scope of buying all production materials and manufacturing of the modules in a case where the schedule is critical to avoid the emergence of hindrances to performance.

ideas.idea: Early design freeze, enforced through contractual discipline on timely owner approvals, is essential to enable manufacturing to proceed without costly changes.
ideas.quote: The discipline of contractors and timely approval of the designs are required to allow for the early design freeze to make room for the operations of the modules fabricator (Choi & O'Connor, 2014).

ideas.idea: Full integration and continuous involvement of key participants (owner, designer, fabricator, contractor) throughout all project phases, not just at initial stages, is necessary for MiC success, implying contractual arrangements must support ongoing collaboration.
ideas.quote: Involvement of owners, designers, vendor, and contractors throughout the project phases was also cited in 11 publications as critical to the success of MiC projects... the emphasis here is the involvement of the key project participants at all stages of the MiC project.

ideas.idea: Effective risk management across stakeholders, supply chain, and project execution is a recurring success factor, indicating that contracts need mechanisms to allocate and manage these risks.
ideas.quote: Effective management of stakeholder, supply chain and project execution risks... Choi (2014), Choi and O'Connor (2014), Choi et al. (2016), Hjort et al. (2014), Ismail et al. (2012), Kamar et al. (2009, 2010), O'Connor, O'Brien, and Choi (2014), Rashidi and Ibrahim (2017)

ideas.idea: Standardization of modules and best-practice benchmarking can reduce costs and improve efficiency, suggesting contractual specifications should support standardized design approaches.
ideas.quote: Standardization reduces the tendency of producing unique modules to meet the specification of each MiC project. Warszawski (1999) concurred that standardization of the design and modules allow for efficient allocation of resources.

ideas.idea: Cross-border procurement of modules in regions with incomplete local supply chains requires careful planning and coordination, implying additional contractual complexity for international supply arrangements.
ideas.quote: This extensive coordination becomes mandatory in regions where the supply chain is incomplete, instructing the engagement of overseas suppliers and expertise (Pan & Hon, 2018).

objectives: To identify and rank the critical success factors (CSFs) for project planning and control (PP&C) in prefabrication housing production (PHP), explore the underlying relationships among these factors, and provide a reference for key stakeholders to achieve effective PP&C in PHP.
problem_statement: Although PHP has grown rapidly, especially in China, its planning and control are complicated by increased stakeholder involvement, coordination demands, and information exchange needs; while many studies have examined CSFs for general construction projects, few have systematically explored CSFs specific to PP&C in PHP, leaving a research gap this study aims to fill.
methodology: A mixed-method approach combining literature review, in-depth interviews with five PHP experts, and a pilot study to derive 23 preliminary CSFs; a questionnaire survey (five-point Likert scale) distributed to 400 designers, manufacturers, and contractors in China via snowball sampling, yielding 136 valid responses (34% response rate); data analyzed using mean score (MS) ranking, one-sample t-tests, and exploratory factor analysis (principal component analysis with varimax rotation) using SPSS 19.0.
key_background_studies: Ismail et al. (2012) – identified management-related factors for PHP, but overlooked supply chain, technical, and industry-related factors, motivating this study's broader scope.
Chan et al. (2004) – identified five groups of CSFs for construction project success (project-related, procedures, management actions, human-related, external environment).
Zwikael and Globerson (2006) – examined 16 planning processes and identified the most sensitive ones for project success.
Ling et al. (2009) – established 24 project practices correlated with Singaporean firms' performance in China, especially risk management.
Li et al. (2011) – grouped CSFs for green building projects into five components including project manager's competence and coordination of designers.
Liu et al. (2014) – identified CSFs for PPP infrastructure projects such as feasibility analysis and interface/conflict management.
O'Connor et al. (2014) – presented 21 CSFs for modularization projects including owner's planning resources and fabricator capability.
Heravi et al. (2015) – identified four critical stakeholder groups (owner, developer, designers, contractors) influencing project success.
Deng et al. – provided the research framework (mean score and factor analysis) used to explore inhibiting factors in SI system building.
Arif et al. – provided the research framework identifying key variables through literature review and pilot study, using factor analysis and average scores.
Haller et al. – proposed the sequence deviation quotient (SDQ) method to control design iteration risks in PHP.
Jensen et al. – proposed a configuration system supporting design automation by integrating CAD tools and information sharing via XML.
findings: 23 CSFs were identified and validated as significant (mean scores above 3.00). The top five CSFs were: designers' experience of PHP, manufacturers' experience of PHP, project manager's ability to solve problems, maturity of techniques used in the detailed design phase, and persistent policies and incentives. Exploratory factor analysis grouped the 23 CSFs into five clusters: (1) technology and method (28.55% variance, the most dominant cluster), (2) information, communication and collaboration, (3) external environment, (4) experience and knowledge, and (5) competence of the project manager, together explaining 67.2% of variance. The study concludes that a holistic, multi-stakeholder approach (designers, manufacturers, contractors) is needed to understand and manage PP&C in PHP, and that technology/method issues are the most critical dimension.

ideas.idea: Designers must largely finalize detailed design prior to production, and design changes are costly because they undermine the speed and cost benefits of prefabrication.
ideas.quote: the design must be largely finished prior to the production. The fast production and assembly of building components need accurate design.

ideas.idea: In China, architectural design and detailed component design are institutionally separated, with manufacturers acting merely as subcontractors for detailed design input.
ideas.quote: The architectural design and the detailed design of prefabricated components in PHP projects are clearly separate in China. This is evidenced by the fact that the manufacturer is only a subcontractor.

ideas.idea: Manufacturing is an extra project stage compared to traditional construction, and late delivery by precast component manufacturers is a common cause of contractor delays.
ideas.quote: The manufacturing phase is an extra stage compared with the traditional construction method... late delivery by the precast components’ manufacturers is the most common issue for the main contractors.

ideas.idea: The project manager plays a coordinating role between on-site and off-site activities and must manage vertical transportation constraints affecting schedule control.
ideas.quote: The project manager is the person in the PHP project who coordinates on-site and off-site activities and is responsible for the project objectives.

ideas.idea: Detailed design in PHP is a distinct, time-consuming multidisciplinary process converting construction drawings into assembly drawings, complicated by reliance on 2D CAD tools in China.
ideas.quote: the detailed design process is very time-consuming as the detailed design process is based on two-dimensional computer-aided design (CAD) drawings.

ideas.idea: BIM adoption in detailed design is limited by data interoperability problems between architectural design software and manufacturing CAD/CAM software formats.
ideas.quote: numerous limitations related to the information exchange in both geometric shape information and other semantically meaningful information between architects (the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format) and fabricators (the Standard ACIS Text (SAT) format) have impeded the BIM technology in the detailed design phase.

ideas.idea: Government policy incentives are critical to overcoming contractor reluctance to adopt prefabrication technology in developing markets lacking mature technical systems.
ideas.quote: When the PHP is still in its infancy, contractors are more willing to choose a mature method rather than new ones without incentives from local government.

ideas.idea: Push-based planning (common in China) causes site congestion and inefficiency compared to pull-based lean construction delivery of prefabricated components.
ideas.quote: Most contractors in China adopted the push method. Consequently, all the prefabricated components have been produced beforehand and delivered to the construction site... they will block the construction site.

ideas.idea: Early and close coordination and communication among designers, manufacturers, and contractors is essential to avoid rework, delays, and constructability problems in PHP.
ideas.quote: Only when good coordination is achieved among all the key stakeholders involved in a project can problems such as delays in production, erection schedules, and constructability be avoided.

ideas.idea: Involvement of contractors and manufacturers during the design stage, and of designers during production/construction, is a recurring success factor reflecting the need for integrated project delivery approaches.
ideas.quote: (1) involvement of the designer during the production and construction stage, (2) involvement of contractors and manufacturers during the design stage, (3) information sharing among participants, (4) efficient coordination between off-site and on-site, and (5) effective communication among participants.

ideas.idea: Lack of designer and manufacturer expertise/experience can generate conflicts, delays, and eliminate the scheduling advantages that prefabrication is supposed to provide.
ideas.quote: a lack of expertise in components design may cause severe conflicts between manufacturers and designers; a lack of manufacturing experience can cause delays in the flow of deliveries to the construction site; a lack of competence on the part of the contractor can lead to delays in the installation schedule.

ideas.idea: Well-developed specifications, regulations, and sufficient qualified manufacturers/suppliers form part of the external environment critical to successful PHP implementation, alongside government-driven sustainability requirements.
ideas.quote: Well-developed specifications and regulations are also key to the successful implementation of PHP... The specifications and regulations provide the basis for the design of prefabricated buildings, prefabricated components production, quality checking, and evaluation.

objectives: To examine the factors affecting the adoption of Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA) technologies in Singapore's construction industry, in order to better understand strategies needed to encourage private sector uptake, aligned with the 2017 Industry Transformation Map.
problem_statement: Despite strong government promotion of prefabrication and DfMA, private sector adoption remains low (only 11.2% of national prefabrication level as of 2001), and firms are reluctant to be early adopters given high costs; the factors influencing DfMA adoption in this context are not well understood.
methodology: A questionnaire survey was developed based on a literature review that identified 17 influencing factors across six categories (industry, government, stakeholder, design, performance-driven, project-specific factors). A pilot interview validated the survey. It was distributed via email to 124 developers, contractors, consultants, architects, engineers and project managers sampled from Singapore industry directories (BCA, SIA, Singapore Contractors' Association, Society of Project Managers), yielding 30 valid responses (24.2% response rate). One-sample t-tests were used to assess statistical significance of factor importance ratings.
key_background_studies: Boothroyd (2005) - originator of DfMA methodological procedures for manufacturing/assembly evaluation
Bogue (2012) - distinguished DfM and DfA approaches and three methods of applying DfMA
Ballard and Howell (1998) - described on-site construction as fabrication and assembly, framing construction as a design process
Gibb and Isack (2003) - classified four levels of off-site production and client understanding barriers
Park, Yashada, Kim, and Ham (2011) - studied Singapore buildability regulations and prefabrication uptake
Mao, Shen, Pan, and Ye (2015) - identified obstacles to prefabrication development in China including lack of supporting organizations and legal frameworks
Kamar, Alshawi, and Hamid (2009) - examined knowledge and incentive factors for IBS/prefabrication adoption
Zakaria, Gajendran, Rose, and Brewer (2018a, 2018b) - reviewed factors influencing Industrialized Building Systems adoption decisions
Jaillon and Poon (2008, 2010, 2014) - studied barriers including client support, design limitations, site constraints in Hong Kong
Gerth, Boqvist, Bjelkemyr, and Lindberg (2013) - proposed 'Design for Construction' method as four-step evaluation process
Fox, Marsh, and Cockerham (2001) - examined collaboration issues among manufacturing, assembly, and plant companies
Blismas and Wakefield (2009) / Pan, Gibb, and Dainty (2007) - identified reduction in construction time as key driver in Australia/UK contexts
findings: Most of the 17 identified factors significantly and positively influence DfMA adoption in Singapore. 'Reduction in construction time' was the most important factor, followed by 'Site constraints and storage' and 'Integration of project team.' Government-related factors (legislation and incentives) were rated least important, likely because Singapore already enforces mandatory DfMA requirements, reducing the marginal influence of additional incentives or legislation. Standardization-related design limitations were also rated low in importance, suggesting respondents did not see this as a major barrier given Singapore's flexible buildable design system.

ideas.idea: DfMA is often equated with prefabrication and off-site construction in industry practice, blurring conceptual boundaries between design process and physical technology.
ideas.quote: DfMA has been equated with prefabrication (O’Rourke, 2013), in which a bundle of game-changing technologies can be applied (BCA, 2016a).

ideas.idea: DfMA should ideally be integrated early in the design phase rather than applied late, unlike traditional value engineering which is often applied after design is largely finalized.
ideas.quote: The former is usually applied in construction after the design stage, when the design has largely been developed, thus missing out on the maximum savings... DfMA should therefore be applied as part of the design phase (O’Brien et al., 2000).

ideas.idea: Early design freeze is critical for successful prefabrication/DfMA projects because modular units require early specification, increasing risk for the design team.
ideas.quote: Early design freeze is especially critical in a project involving prefabrication, due to the need for specifications of modular units early on, to ensure timely project completion.

ideas.idea: Fragmentation among manufacturers, assemblers, and plant companies in construction limits the collaborative design needed for successful DfMA, unlike in manufacturing industries.
ideas.quote: a study undertaken by Fox et al. (2001) revealed that manufacturing companies, assembly companies, and building plant companies seldom collaborated with each other.

ideas.idea: Standardization for DfMA creates tension with architectural creativity and design flexibility, though this tension can be managed through appraisal systems.
ideas.quote: the conflict between standardization and flexibility has still not been resolved; as Gibb (2001, pg. 308) put it, ‘it remains as a tension that sometimes leads to design impotence, but should be used to ensure optimal implementation’.

ideas.idea: Government legislation and mandatory scoring systems (like the Buildable Design Appraisal System) can enforce and incentivize prefabrication adoption more effectively than voluntary incentives alone.
ideas.quote: by progressively raising the required minimum buildable score within the technical limits, it would have more direct impact on promoting the use of prefabrication than the foreign labour control policy in Singapore.

ideas.idea: Client and developer decision-making authority is a critical determinant of prefabrication adoption, as demand ultimately rests with them rather than end customers.
ideas.quote: the final demand for prefabrication is determined by developers and clients, rather than by customers (Kamar et al., 2009; Mao et al., 2015).

ideas.idea: Contractors' willingness to invest capital upfront in prefabrication facilities is a key enabler or barrier to adoption, with financial risk borne unevenly across the supply chain.
ideas.quote: if contractors are unwilling to put the capital upfront to establish specialized prefabrication factories for the adoption of prefabrication technology, the process will be slowed down (Szwarc, 2013).

ideas.idea: Site constraints and lack of storage space in dense urban environments pose a major practical barrier to adopting prefabricated/modular construction, requiring solutions like just-in-time delivery.
ideas.quote: Restricted site layouts pose challenges for the placement of prefabricated modules, which results in the project team being reluctant to adopt prefabrication (Blismas et al., 2005).

ideas.idea: Multidisciplinary team integration from the design phase onward, including manufacturers and suppliers, is essential for successful DfMA implementation given the fragmented nature of construction delivery.
ideas.quote: for construction projects to carry forward the practice of DfMA, a multidisciplinary team including building design engineers, architects, contractors, and specialists is needed and these experts must share a common level of commitment and willingness to engage with DfMA technology.

ideas.idea: Cost distribution among contracting parties (main contractor, prefabricator, MEP subcontractors) under DfMA/PPVC can discourage smaller firms from adoption despite available government subsidies.
ideas.quote: about 40% of the contract sum would be taken by the main building contractors, with the rest going to the prefabricator and MEP... subcontractors. This seems to explain the hesitation of SMEs to consider adopting DfMA technologies.

ideas.idea: Government mandates (e.g., mandatory PPVC/PBU requirements on Government Land Sale sites) directly shape the project delivery process and contractual obligations for developers.
ideas.quote: For selected sites under the GLS Programme, developers will be required to adopt a minimum level of PPVC which shall be at least 65% of the total constructed floor area of the building.

objectives: To design an optimal government subsidy allocation policy that promotes contractor adoption of modular construction (MC) by explicitly incorporating uncertainties in MC price, cast-in-situ cost, MCM supply, and future construction volume, using a bilevel stochastic programming approach validated with Hong Kong data.
problem_statement: Existing government subsidy policies for promoting MC adoption are designed under deterministic assumptions about future prices, costs, supply, and demand, which can produce suboptimal subsidy plans given real-world uncertainty; there is also a gap in exact (non-heuristic) solution methods for the resulting complex bilevel subsidy allocation problem.
methodology: The study formulates a bilevel stochastic program with the government as leader (choosing a unit subsidy price under a budget constraint) and contractors as followers (choosing quantities of MC modules vs cast-in-situ work to minimize costs) across multiple stochastic scenarios of price, cost, supply and demand. A theoretical property (Proposition 1) showing monotonicity of MC adoption in subsidy price is proved and used to build an exact bisection search algorithm (Proposition 2) solved via CPLEX. The model is validated using a real-world case study of Hong Kong, using data on 18 districts, four modular manufacturing factories in the Greater Bay Area, public/private housing forecasts, and price/transportation/assembly cost data, with 20 randomly generated scenarios; sensitivity analyses on budget and MC cost are also performed.
key_background_studies: Gao and Tian (2020) - empirically showed prefabrication policies affect labor productivity/material conservation and argued for more incentive schemes over guidelines
Jiang et al. (2019) - found financial subsidies more effective than other supportive strategies, especially in early MC development stage
Du et al. (2023) - used agent-based modeling to compare procurement restriction, carbon credit, and subsidy policies, identifying subsidies as primary motivator
Wang et al. (2021) - identified reputational and financial incentives among 16 factors influencing contractors' construction method choice
Yi et al. (2021) - proposed Stackelberg government-manufacturer subsidy policy, showing poorly designed subsidies can increase emissions and reduce MC adoption
Yi et al. (2023a) - developed subsidy scheme via government-manufacturer-contractor relationships, validated with Hong Kong data using heuristic algorithms
Du et al. (2022) - coordinated precast component supply chain under government subsidies in decentralized/centralized scenarios
Jiang and Qi (2022) - evaluated government subsidy effects on manufacturers, contractors, assemblers using evolutionary game theory
Bertram et al. (2019) - provided data on MC cost premiums, productivity gains, and potential cost savings over cast-in-situ construction
findings: Without subsidy, only 10.2% of construction work would use MCMs; with an optimal subsidy of HKD166/t under a HKD100 million budget, MC adoption rises to 52.3%, a fivefold increase. Considering uncertainty (stochastic model) improves the government's objective by 38% compared to a deterministic mean-value approach. Sensitivity analysis shows increasing marginal budget requirements to achieve higher adoption rates, and that reducing MC costs lowers the required subsidy price while increasing adoption. Government subsidies also diversify contractors' sourcing strategies across factories, fostering longer-term supply-demand relationships. The bisection search algorithm solves the bilevel stochastic problem exactly and efficiently (under 1 second).

ideas.idea: High costs, including cross-border logistics costs, are the primary barrier preventing contractors from adopting MC absent subsidies.
ideas.quote: the cross-border transportation of MCMs incurs extremely high logistics costs, and therefore contractors in Hong Kong have little incentive to adopt this new method

ideas.idea: Financial subsidies are more effective than technical guidelines or compulsory regulations in driving MC adoption, especially in early development stages.
ideas.quote: financial subsidies are more effective than other types of supportive strategies, especially during the initial encouraging stage of MC development

ideas.idea: Government subsidy policy formulation and contractor procurement decisions are interdependent, requiring a bilevel decision framework where the government anticipates contractor responses.
ideas.quote: the government, acting as the leader, makes the decision about the unit subsidy price offered to contractors for using MCMs and anticipates the reactions of contractors to its optimal decision

ideas.idea: Contractors choose between MC and cast-in-situ methods (or a mix) purely to minimize their own costs, treating subsidy as a direct cost offset per ton of MCM used.
ideas.quote: contractors decide whether to adopt MC, cast-in-situ method, or a mixture of these two methods to perform construction work to minimize their overall costs

ideas.idea: Uncertainty in future construction volume, MC/cast-in-situ costs, and supply significantly affects the optimal design and effectiveness of subsidy policy, and ignoring it leads to suboptimal outcomes.
ideas.quote: Neglecting these factors can result in suboptimal subsidy plans for governments and further influence the supply chain related decisions made by contractors.

ideas.idea: Transportation distance and logistics costs from off-site factories to construction sites materially influence contractors' willingness and ability to adopt MC, leading to geographic disparities in adoption.
ideas.quote: contractors in the southern area of Hong Kong ... still rely predominantly on the traditional construction due to the very high costs of transporting MCMs

ideas.idea: Well-designed subsidies can promote diversified and more resilient supply chain sourcing strategies among contractors rather than reliance on a single supplier.
ideas.quote: government subsidies provide diversified procurement strategies for contractors and facilitate a long-term supply-demand relationship between GBA manufacturers and the Hong Kong contractors

ideas.idea: A ceiling on the unit subsidy price is necessary to prevent contractors from profiting purely from subsidies rather than from genuine construction activity.
ideas.quote: The unit subsidy price α should have a reasonable upper limit ... implying that all contractors are not allowed to profit by relying on government subsidies in all scenarios.

ideas.idea: There are increasing marginal budget requirements for governments to achieve successive increases in MC adoption rate, informing practical budget-setting for subsidy programs.
ideas.quote: The minimum amount of subsidy budget required to increase every 10% of the MC adoption rate progressively increases

ideas.idea: Reductions in the overall cost of MCMs (through technology improvement) reduce dependence on subsidies and increase voluntary MC adoption by contractors.
ideas.quote: as a result of cost reduction, contractors proactively will adopt MC, thereby reducing their dependence on government subsidies

objectives: To identify and categorize the principal challenges to implementing design for manufacture and assembly (DfMA) in construction projects, and to develop a construction-oriented DfMA framework with recommendations for tackling these challenges.
problem_statement: Although DfMA has been successfully applied in manufacturing for decades, its adoption in construction remains limited and stifled by various constraints; existing literature lacks a comprehensive identification of challenges and corresponding organizational, contractual, and operational strategies to address them.
methodology: A design science research (DSR) approach combining a systematic literature review (SLR) of 52 selected journal articles (from 232 initial hits) using qualitative content analysis to extract and categorize challenges; two focus group discussions (10 and 14 Canadian construction industry experts) to validate challenges and develop/validate a conceptual framework; and verification of the framework through observation and stakeholder discussions on two real off-site construction case study projects (a multi-residential building in British Columbia, Canada, and a structural steel facility in Ohio, USA).
key_background_studies: Boothroyd and Dewhurst (1960s-70s) - pioneers of formal DfMA research in manufacturing
RIBA (2013, 2020) - introduced DfMA overlay to the Plan of Work, providing implementation guidelines used as framework basis
Gao et al. (2019) - categorized DfMA interpretations in construction into three groups (philosophy, design process, evaluation system)
Wuni et al. - identified challenges in design-for-excellence/industrialized construction, notably limited knowledge and experience
Studies on integrated project delivery (IPD) - early contractor engagement improves organizational integration
Studies discussing shared practices of DfMA with lean and digital fabrication (concluding 'design to target value' and 'concurrent engineering' are shared practices)
2020 review study on DfMA development in manufacturing and construction, categorizing research into implementation strategies, frameworks, and applications
2021 systematic review identifying analogies between prefabrication and manufacturing and future opportunities for DfMA in construction
2022 review identifying main benefits and barriers of DfMA implementation including traditional contracting strategies as a barrier
findings: The study identified 45 challenges to DfMA implementation in construction, categorized into eight groups: contractual, technological, procedural, cultural, commercial, geographical, financial, and technical/cognitive. Contractual and operational challenges were found to be most significant. A construction-oriented DfMA framework based on the RIBA Plan of Work 2020 was developed and verified on two case study projects, showing that integrated business models, relational project delivery methods (e.g., IPD), lean-based operational tools, and digital/I4.0 technologies (BIM, IoT, AI) create environments more conducive to successful DfMA implementation, whereas traditional delivery methods (e.g., design-bid-build) hinder integration and DfMA adoption.

ideas.idea: Traditional contract forms create fragmentation among stakeholders that inhibits DfMA implementation.
ideas.quote: traditional forms of contracts that create vertical, horizontal, and longitudinal fragmentations (i.e., design–bid–build)

ideas.idea: Lack of risk/reward sharing provisions in contracts is a barrier to DfMA adoption.
ideas.quote: Lack of risk/reward sharing consideration in the contract

ideas.idea: Contracts often lack clarity regarding guarantees and insurance, hindering DfMA.
ideas.quote: Lack of clarity in terms of guarantees and insurance

ideas.idea: Existing DfMA platforms do not conform with standard contracts such as CCDC, limiting their use.
ideas.quote: Lack of DfMA platforms which conform with the CCDC contracts

ideas.idea: Contracts often fail to reference multiple manufacturers, constraining flexibility in sourcing.
ideas.quote: Lack of references to several manufacturers in the contract

ideas.idea: Unclear scope of work in contracts leads to confusion and duplication of effort.
ideas.quote: Lack of clear scope of work, confusions, and duplications

ideas.idea: Contracts often fail to define clear roles and responsibilities among stakeholders, impeding integration.
ideas.quote: Lack of clear roles and responsibilities of stakeholders

ideas.idea: Traditional contracting leads to complex litigation and prolonged negotiations between key stakeholders.
ideas.quote: Complex litigation and long negotiations between key stakeholders

ideas.idea: Contracts often lack the agility and flexibility needed to accommodate DfMA processes.
ideas.quote: Lack of agility and flexibility in the contract

ideas.idea: A contractual framework should align stakeholder objectives with project goals through compensation structures and risk allocation, which is essential for integration.
ideas.quote: A contractual framework refers to the regulative guidelines that align the stakeholders’ goals and objectives with the overall project’s objectives through framing compensation structures and addressing risk allocations among project participants.

ideas.idea: Relational/integrated delivery methods such as IPD, which use multi-party contracts with shared risk and reward, better support DfMA implementation than traditional delivery methods.
ideas.quote: integrated project delivery is a formal approach to integration through signing multi-party contracts and sharing the associated risks and rewards of the project

ideas.idea: DfMA needs to be paired with an integrative contractual framework like IPD because DfMA focuses on product/process integration while IPD focuses on people integration.
ideas.quote: While DfMA focuses on product/process integration, it needs to be accompanied by a contractual framework such as IPD, which focuses on people integration.

ideas.idea: Case study evidence shows that projects using traditional delivery/subcontracting (design-bid-build portions) faced greater difficulty implementing DfMA and experienced cost overruns from change orders.
ideas.quote: Due to the traditional nature of project delivery methods and business models, there was a lack of integration between organizational structures of project stakeholders, and from the planning to delivery stages, project teams were not motivated to collaborate.

ideas.idea: A project using a hybrid design-build/IPD delivery model experienced smoother DfMA implementation, improved performance metrics, and fewer change orders, illustrating the value of integrated contracting.
ideas.quote: The IPD-type project delivery method provided incentives for stakeholders to collaborate during all phases of the project. For instance, the shared risks and rewards and joint decision-making principles fostered a collaborative project environment.

ideas.idea: Standard IPD contract forms exist in North America, including CCDC30 in Canada, but further research is needed to develop optimal IPD contractual guidelines that reinforce synergy with DfMA.
ideas.quote: several standard forms of IPD contracting are available in North America (i.e., CCDC30 in Canada and AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300 in the U.S.). Further study is needed on the synergic impact of IPD and construction-oriented DfMA to enhance off-site construction projects, in particular, to develop an optimal IPD contractual guideline for reinforcing this synergic impact.

ideas.idea: Lack of legislative frameworks, codes, guidelines and standards for DfMA implementation is a significant barrier.
ideas.quote: The third most-cited challenge concerns the lack of legislative frameworks of specified codes, guidelines, and standards for the implementation of construction-oriented DfMA methods

ideas.idea: Higher design costs relative to traditional methods act as a barrier to DfMA adoption, linked to specialized labor, prototyping, and compliance costs.
ideas.quote: Some scholars have identified “higher design costs” compared to the cost of traditional methods as a barrier to the proper implementation of construction-oriented DfMA methods in construction projects

ideas.idea: Complex code compliance and inspection processes add difficulty to implementing DfMA/off-site methods.
ideas.quote: Complex code compliance and inspection process

ideas.idea: Lack of prefabrication and industrialized construction consideration in tender documents is a barrier identified by industry experts.
ideas.quote: Lack of prefab and IC consideration in tenders

objectives: To develop an ethnography-based methodological framework for prefabricated construction projects (PCPs) that evaluates, analyzes, and improves dynamic organizational resilience (efficiency, flexibility, robustness) from a project life cycle perspective, and to validate this framework using a case study of an EPC-contract PCP in China.
problem_statement: PCPs are interorganizational and highly vulnerable to disruptions (e.g., COVID-19, supply chain issues, fragmented processes) due to complex stakeholder relationships, yet existing research has focused on risk from a project perspective rather than organizational resilience, and there is a lack of quantitative methods to evaluate how stakeholder relationships across the project life cycle affect organizational resilience in PCPs.
methodology: A two-part mixed-method framework: (1) a qualitative ethnographic method (in-depth interviews, participant observation) to identify stakeholder roles and relationship types (coordination, power, control) across five project life cycle stages (planning, designing, manufacturing/storage/transportation, assembling onsite, operation); (2) a quantitative graph theory method to calculate performance metrics and compute flexibility, robustness, and efficiency indicators, aggregated into an overall organizational resilience score. The framework was applied to a real 2-year EPC-contract PCP case (Poly Real Estate Group, Changsha, China), using interviews with eight experienced participants, followed by disfunction analysis (removing key stakeholder links) and comparative analysis of alternative collaboration technologies (league among GC/DS/M, BIM, decentralized collaboration platform/blockchain).
key_background_studies: Coutu (2002) - first defined organizational resilience as capacity to resist and recover from shocks/disasters
McManus et al. (2008) - proposed organizational resilience as function of situation awareness, keystone vulnerability, and adaptive capacity
Bhamra et al. (2011) - defined resilience in organization theory as ability to return to stable condition after disruption, adopted as the study's working definition
Sydow and Braun (2018) - conceptualized projects as temporary organizations to manage interorganizational relations, emphasizing stakeholder relationships in resilience
Li et al. (2016) - identified network of stakeholder-associated risk factors in prefabricated housing projects
Luo et al. (2019) - examined supply chain risks associated with stakeholders across project phases affecting PCP performance; used in disfunction analysis selection (PC, GC, M)

Yahia et al. (2021) - provided graph theory-based relationship types (coordination, power, control) and metrics for organizational resilience of collaborative networks, central to quantitative framework
Grossi et al. (2007) and Penserini et al. (2009) - source of performance criteria and equations for measuring flexibility, robustness, efficiency via graph theory
Nguyen et al. (2021) - systematically reviewed stakeholder relationships in off-site construction, categorizing relationship patterns

Ekanayake et al. (2021a,b) - identified supply chain capabilities critical to resilience in industrialized construction in Hong Kong, compared as SNA-based approach lacking individual relationship characterization
Teng et al. (2017) - highlighted complexity of managing cooperation relationships among stakeholders including GC, designers, manufacturer, corroborating centrality of GC finding
findings: The organizational resilience of the case PCP followed a bowl-shaped pattern across the five life cycle stages, being weakest during the planning stage (P1) due to unclear project information and unformalized contracts, and strongest during manufacturing/storage/transportation (P3). Efficiency performed best among the three dimensions, while robustness and flexibility required improvement, suggesting the need to manage redundant personnel/resources and improve communication and workflow control. Disfunction analysis showed the general contractor (GC) held the most central and important role, with its disfunction most severely undermining resilience in P2, P3, and P4; the prefabrication consultant (PC) was important in design and assembly stages, and the manufacturer (M) was important in manufacturing stage. Comparative analysis showed that partial relational upgrades (a league among GC, DS, M) had little impact on resilience, whereas systematic improvements via BIM and especially a blockchain-based decentralized collaboration platform (DCP) significantly improved organizational resilience by enhancing both communication efficiency and workflow control/delegation-supervision structures.

ideas.idea: Under EPC contracts, the general contractor holds a centralized role encompassing both design and construction responsibilities, unlike traditional contracts where design and construction responsibilities are split between owner and contractor.
ideas.quote: Under an EPC-contract PCP, on the other hand, the general contractor is responsible for both design and construction.

ideas.idea: Contract type shapes stakeholder relationships and role allocation across project phases, meaning organizational resilience and stakeholder structures may differ by delivery method.
ideas.quote: The stakeholders and their relationships within PCPs vary case by case. For example, in a traditional-contract PCP, general contractor is responsible for construction, and the owner/developer takes charge of early design work.

ideas.idea: Contractual delegation and supervision relationships (power and control) between stakeholders such as GC, designer, and manufacturer can be restructured through informal alliances, but this alone does little to improve project resilience.
ideas.quote: Under a league among GC, DS, and M in a PCP, the GC trains their own DS and P (Zhang et al. 2018b)... Firstly, it is seen that a league among GC, DS, and M has little impact on the project’s organizational resilience.

ideas.idea: Digital collaboration technologies like BIM and blockchain-based platforms can alter contractual/organizational structures of delegation, supervision and communication among stakeholders in prefabricated projects, improving resilience beyond what informal restructuring achieves.
ideas.quote: DCP not only improves information communication, but also upgrades delegation and supervision relationship of stakeholders.

ideas.idea: The project's contractual and information structures are least defined and most fragile during the planning stage, before key contract documents are formalized, indicating that early contractual clarity is critical to resilience.
ideas.quote: This result shows that this PCP is fragile at planning stage, which makes sense because considerable volumes of project information and contract issues remain unclear and veiled at this stage.

ideas.idea: The general contractor's central position, established through numerous relationships in design, manufacturing and assembly stages, means its disfunction (e.g., due to disputes or contractual breakdown) has outsized negative impact on the whole project's resilience.
ideas.quote: It can be concluded that the disfunction of the GC decreases this PCP’s organizational resilience to a great extent, which reflects the central position of the GC in this project.

ideas.idea: Managing supply chain relationships (with suppliers, manufacturers, logistics enterprises) is a key contractual concern in PCPs given the lengthened supply chain and reliance on multiple subcontracted parties.
ideas.quote: the M had to find a reliable material supplier (S) and an efficient logistics enterprise (LE).

ideas.idea: The GC subcontracts assembly work to multiple parties, creating a fragmented contractual network at the assembly stage that requires coordination among many stakeholders.
ideas.quote: In the assembling onsite stage, the GC subcontracted certain assembly works to subcontractors (SCs), as well as to some participating stakeholders, such as the D, M, and PC, who also collaborated with each other to facilitate the onsite modular assembly work.

objectives: To develop a scoring framework that assesses the feasibility (or infeasibility) of using the design-build (DB) project delivery method for bundled infrastructure projects, based on quantified project bundling objectives derived from expert surveys and statistical weighting.
problem_statement: Agencies bundling multiple infrastructure projects into a single contract face difficulty selecting an appropriate project delivery method (PDM), particularly deciding whether DB is feasible for their bundle. No prior framework or tool exists to assess DB feasibility specifically for bundled projects, as existing PDM feasibility tools were developed for single, non-bundled projects and do not account for the unique risks (e.g., mutual dependence) and complexities of bundled contracts.
methodology: A mixed quantitative methodology was used: (1) a Delphi process using literature and 37 bundled-project case studies to derive 25 project bundling objectives; (2) a Likert-scale survey of 51 US industry experts (owners, contractors, architects/engineers) to rate the importance of each objective for DB feasibility, validated via sample size calculation, Cronbach's alpha (internal reliability), and ICC (external reliability); (3) Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with data standardization, KMO/Bartlett's tests, Kaiser criterion, and Varimax rotation to calculate weights for each objective; (4) calculation of objective scores (importance × weight), ranking, and Mann-Whitney U tests to identify seven statistically distinct DB feasibility tiers with cutoff scores; (5) development of a user-friendly Excel/VBA-based scoring tool that computes a Project DB Feasibility Score (PDFS) and Industry DB Feasibility Score (IDFS) based on user inputs.
key_background_studies: FHWA (2019) - primary source describing project bundling practices, PDM options, and DB benefits for bundled projects, central to establishing gap
Gransberg (2020) - discusses project bundling challenges and risk/complexity differences from single projects
Qiao et al. (2018, 2019a,b,c) - identify decision-making factors, benefits, and thresholds for project bundling
Shan et al. (2023) - case study (DelDOT) illustrating mutual dependence issues in bundled DBB projects and shift to DB
Tran and Molenaar (2013, 2015) - developed risk-based PDM selection frameworks and matrices for single highway projects (DBB, DB, CM/GC)
Al Khalil (2002) - developed AHP-based model for PDM selection for single projects
Khwaja et al. (2018) - developed decision-support tool comparing DBB and DB based on user rankings
Zeng et al. (2014) - fuzzy simulation optimization for PDM selection minimizing cost/duration
Assaf and Assaad (2023); Assaf et al. (2024) - prior studies on bundling decision-making factors and challenges, direct predecessors to this study's gap identification
FHWA/Colorado DOT Project Delivery Selection Matrix (PDSM) (FHWA 2017; Tran et al. 2013) - existing risk-based, qualitative PDM selection tool used as comparison baseline for the proposed framework
findings: The study identified seven feasibility tiers for DB delivery of bundled projects, with Tier 1 representing highest feasibility. The three objectives most strongly associated with high DB feasibility (Tier 1) were: (1) having specific scheduling, sequencing, staging, and phasing; (2) meeting tight milestones or deadlines; and (3) completing the overall project on schedule—all schedule-related objectives, reflecting DB's fast-track nature from design-construction concurrency. A user-friendly Excel/VBA tool was developed allowing project owners to input selected objectives and importance ratings to calculate a Project DB Feasibility Score (PDFS) and benchmark it against an Industry DB Feasibility Score (IDFS), supporting go/no-go PDM decisions. The framework differs from existing tools (e.g., PDSM) by being tailored to bundled projects, quantitative, objectives-based, and simpler to use.

ideas.idea: In DB delivery, most design-related risk is transferred from the owner to the design-builder, reducing owner risk exposure compared to DBB.
ideas.quote: In the case of the DB delivery method, most of the risks (especially the design-related risks as most of the construction-related risks are already allocated to the contractor) are transferred from the project owner (i.e., the agency) and allocated to the contactor (i.e., the design-builder).

ideas.idea: Bundled projects introduce mutual dependence risk not present in single projects, since all project elements (permits, ROW, utilities) must clear before advertisement under DBB, and a problem at one site can delay the entire bundle.
ideas.quote: an engineering problem (such as geotechnical or hydrological) or environmental issue at one project location of the bundled projects can prevent the entire package from being advertised under the DBB delivery method since clearance/approval must be obtained for all projects in the bundled contract before the agency’s advertises the contract.

ideas.idea: DB delivery can overcome the mutual dependence problem of bundled projects because the design-builder can take on responsibilities (ROW, permits, utility coordination) that would otherwise delay the entire bundled contract under DBB.
ideas.quote: the design-builder (i.e., DB team) was responsible for all aspects of the project, including plan preparation, utility coordination, permit acquisition, and ROW negotiations.

ideas.idea: Under DB, the contractor provides constructability feedback and input to the design, reducing change orders and delays during execution.
ideas.quote: in DB projects, the owner can benefit from constructability feedback and analysis since the contractor provides inputs to the design, which helps in reducing change orders and delays later in the project execution phase.

ideas.idea: DB allows construction to start before design completion, enabling fast-tracked project delivery through concurrency of design and construction.
ideas.quote: Under the DB contract, the construction phase can start before the full completion of the design, which ensures a fast-tracked completion of the project.

ideas.idea: Bundled contracts create additional complex construction sequencing responsibilities for the contractor, who must schedule, phase, and sequence multiple project locations to meet an aggressive overall schedule, a challenge not present in single project delivery.
ideas.quote: the contractor has to schedule, phase, sequence, and finish all the projects according to the generally aggressive schedule for the entire bundled contract.

ideas.idea: Bundling increases third-party coordination burden (utilities, ROW, permits, railroads) across multiple project locations under one contract, and this responsibility falls on whichever party (owner or contractor) is designated by the chosen PDM.
ideas.quote: bundled projects increase the requirements for third-party coordination since the project owner or the contractor (depending on the used PDM) has to coordinate with third-party agencies to handle utilities, acquire ROW, apply for permits, or coordinate with railroads for all the different projects under the same bundled contract.

ideas.idea: Existing PDM feasibility/selection tools (e.g., PDSM, AHP models, risk-modeling frameworks) were developed for single, non-bundled contracts and are not directly applicable to bundled projects, which differ substantially in complexity, scope, and risk profile.
ideas.quote: the existing studies provided guidance on selecting a proper PDM for single (i.e., nonbundled) projects/contracts only. However, bundled projects...greatly differ in their properties, complexities, scope, and execution considerations.

ideas.idea: The DB delivery decision for bundled projects is a distinct step in the overall bundling process, occurring after candidate projects are identified for bundling but before contract letting/execution.
ideas.quote: the applicability of the proposed framework in this paper is after the project owner identifies candidate projects to bundle and before the actual letting or execution of the bundled contract.

ideas.idea: Scheduling-related project objectives (specific sequencing/phasing, meeting milestones, overall schedule completion) are the strongest drivers of DB feasibility for bundled projects, reflecting the fast-track, schedule-focused nature of DB contracts.
ideas.quote: these three project bundling objectives are schedule-related objectives, which determines that the DB method is highly feasible for bundling programs that have their main goals directed toward enhancing the overall schedule.

ideas.idea: DB delivery carries known disadvantages for owners, including reduced client control over design, higher costs for owner-requested changes, and loss of realized risk-transfer savings back to the contractor, which owners must weigh in PDM decisions.
ideas.quote: These disadvantages include reduced client control, increased cost of client requested changes, client’s reduced ability to influence the design, potential higher cost since the contractor assumes most of the risks.

objectives: To identify and classify the major sources and causes of construction disputes in Kuwait based on a review of actual litigation cases, rank the severity of these dispute sources, validate findings through expert interviews, and develop a regression model to predict disputed claim values.
problem_statement: Construction disputes are increasing and hindering project completion and court resolution processes, yet most prior research relies on surveys and questionnaires rather than actual litigation cases, and there is a lack of guidelines matching dispute sources to appropriate avoidance measures, particularly in the Gulf region.
methodology: A sample of 177 litigation cases was randomly selected from the Kuwait Ministry of Justice Expert Department records (from over 1,000 cases), covering government and private, building and infrastructure projects under traditional project delivery. Case data (contract value, duration, parties, dispute source) were statistically analyzed and classified into four groups (abnormal conditions, financial, project delay, project management). Ten construction legal experts were interviewed using a Likert scale to validate and rank dispute severity. A linear regression model (using SPSS) was built with claim value as dependent variable and contract value/project duration as independent variables, run on all cases and separately on building-only cases (89 cases).
key_background_studies: Diekmann and Nelson (1985) - identified incomplete contract documentation and change-related uncertainties as dispute sources
Kumaraswamy (1997) - classified disputes into root causes (unfair risk allocation, inappropriate contract types) and proximate causes (design deficiencies, contract administration)
Love et al. (2011) - classified dispute sources into management, organizational, and people systems
Cakmak and Cakmak (2014) - categorized disputes into seven groups including contract-related causes (ambiguities, risk allocation)
Daoud and Azzam (1999) - noted Middle East contracts are often one-sided favoring the owner, causing disputes
Awwad et al. (2016) - found contractual concerns are the most common disputes in the Middle East
Elziny et al. (2016) - identified contract management and contract documentation as top dispute sources in Egypt
Mahamid (2016) - surveyed Saudi contractors, found payment delay and unrealistic contract duration as top dispute causes
Dmaidi et al. (2013) - identified bidding policy and payment delay as key dispute sources in Palestine
Chan and Suen (2005) - proposed recommendations to minimize contractual, cultural, and legal disputes
Mohamed et al. (2014) - proposed measures including risk-sharing understanding to minimize disputes
Al-Humaidi (2004) and Alrasheed et al. (2023) - attempted to estimate litigation/arbitration fees based on claimed values in Kuwait
findings: Payment delay was the most severe and frequent dispute source in both government and private cases. Contractual issues (incomplete information, conflicts of interest, noncompliance, lack of knowledge in contract documents) ranked second, followed by main contractor time delay and owner time delay. The financial dispute group accounted for 40.68% of all cases. Government cases represented 62.71% of cases and 94.83% of total claim value, with main contractor time delay contributing 51.09% of total claim value. Main contractors were identified as the primary dispute offenders, especially in government contracts, while owners were more often blamed in private contracts. The regression model showed only moderate correlation (R2=0.183 for all cases, 0.194 for building-only cases) between claim value and contract value/duration, indicating other factors influence claim value. Expert interviews largely corroborated the case-based findings, particularly regarding payment delay, main contractor time delay, back-to-back payments, and owner time delay as top priorities. The study concludes that outdated contract documents (unchanged since 1971) and politically influenced awarding/bidding practices in Kuwait contribute significantly to disputes, and recommends contractual clause revisions and further regional investigation.

ideas.idea: Contract documents with incomplete information, conflicting interests, and noncompliance are a major recurring source of disputes, ranking second overall.
ideas.quote: Contract documents (incomplete information, conflict of interests in both parties, noncompliance, lack of knowledge)

ideas.idea: Existing standard contract documents in Kuwait have not been updated since 1971, contributing to unfair or unclear contractual terms and disputes.
ideas.quote: It was found that the contracts currently being used are still those that have been designed and referred to since 1971; and as of yet, there have been no upgrades or modifications to make them legitimately acceptable and fair to both contracting parties.

ideas.idea: Payment delay is identified as the most frequent and severe dispute source across both government and private construction contracts, suggesting contractual payment clauses need strengthening.
ideas.quote: Ranked first as a source of dispute was delay in payments for both government and private dispute cases.

ideas.idea: Main contractor-caused time delays represent the largest share of dispute claim value, reflecting risks in project delivery and contractor selection processes.
ideas.quote: The percentage of claim values associated with dispute, stemming from project delay caused by the main contractor, was 51.09% of the total claim values for all cases.

ideas.idea: The lowest-cost bidding award system used in Kuwait's public tenders may contribute to disputes by favoring cost over contractor competence.
ideas.quote: The main criteria to choose the winning bidder is total bidder cost. Many studies discussed and highlighted the problems of using lowest cost bidding; the state of Kuwait is not an exception.

ideas.idea: Contractual clauses should be revised to fairly allocate risk and responsibility between owner and contractor to reduce disputes, particularly regarding financial and payment provisions.
ideas.quote: It is timely and urgent that certain agreement clauses should be introduced and perhaps made more impartially stringent and properly screened by legal advisers of both government and private entities.

ideas.idea: Vague or ambiguous contract documentation and inadequate contractual clarity are recurring proximate causes of disputes noted in the broader literature, relevant to how standard contracts should be drafted.
ideas.quote: proximate causes, they include sketchy design information, vague design documentation, inadequate briefs, incompetent contract administration, inappropriate contract forms, erratic contractor selection process, and sluggish client responses.

ideas.idea: Variation orders and scope changes are identified as contract-related dispute triggers, underscoring the need for clear change management provisions in contracts.
ideas.quote: Documenting all changes, applying for proper design review, and having claims in writing.

ideas.idea: Work stoppage disputes highlight the need for contracts to clearly specify compensation and documentation procedures when work is halted.
ideas.quote: Contract terms should clearly mention details on the compensation of the affected party and recording the reasons for the work stoppage.

ideas.idea: Recommendations for mitigating financial disputes include applying explicit contract payment terms such as back-to-back payment clauses and penalties for late payment.
ideas.quote: Applying contract payment terms, to include contract terms for back-to-back payments, judicious selection of contractors, applying for bank letter of credit (LC). payments, and being cautious relative to penalties for late payments.

objectives: To evaluate procurement systems that enable early contractor involvement (ECI) in terms of how well they support off-site manufacturing (OSM), and to develop a conceptual two-stage ECI process model for New Zealand that addresses design buildability barriers to OSM adoption.
problem_statement: OSM/MMC uptake in New Zealand is hindered by industry culture, skills, logistics, cost, procurement and design/buildability barriers, and there is currently no standard model for two-stage ECI procurement in NZ to overcome these issues, particularly the risk that designs commissioned under single-stage procurement may be difficult or impossible to build using OSM.
methodology: Literature review combined with three ethnographic case studies of construction projects in Dunedin, Otago, NZ (2006-2017, costing NZ$10-20 million), document analysis, open coding of pre-construction services from ECI literature, and legal doctrine analysis distinguishing design buildability obligations from design code compliance. The resulting conceptual model was presented at a conference and refined based on feedback.
key_background_studies: Jorgensen and Emmitt (2007) - ethnographic case studies identifying factors for effective lean integration including project delivery framework
Mosey (2011) - promotes the 'conditional' pre-construction contract and two-stage ECI concept, recognising commercial interests of parties
Shahzad (2011) - classifies main barriers to OSM adoption in NZ into seven categories including industry culture and design/process issues
Whitehead (2009) - describes hybrid ECI models in Australia with partnering first stage and DB second stage
Pheng et al. (2015) - describes two-stage ECI approach maintaining competitive pricing via notional then firm bill of quantities
Rahmani et al. (2013/2014) - describes two-stage model with non-price contractor selection and open-book target cost
Laryea and Watermeyer (2016) - case studies of two-stage ECI at Wits University, South Africa, showing contractors received no remuneration for design involvement
Francis and Kiroff (2015) - research on perceptions of ECI in NZ, asserting DB is most common ECI form in NZ commercial construction
Jergeas and Put (2001) - found owner risk aversion and lack of knowledge as key barriers to innovation, argue for early contractor involvement from 'day one'
Kirkham (2007) - demonstrates diminishing value and increasing cost of change as design develops, informing procurement decision criteria
findings: ECI offers significant advantages for OSM projects by enabling collaborative design development, risk and value management, and subcontractor procurement, allowing contractors to evaluate buildability and costs of OSM versus traditional assemblies. A two-stage ECI conceptual process model is proposed comprising a first-stage pre-construction contract and second-stage standard-form construction contract, with key variables including scope of pre-construction services, payment/reimbursement options, termination grounds, direct works pricing, allocation of design/buildability obligations, IP ownership, milestones, and collaborative contract provisions. Legal doctrine analysis shows that contractors under lump sum contracts bear buildability risk (implied fitness for purpose once undertaking design), while designers/consultants are held to reasonable skill and care; standard NZ contracts (NZS 3910, NZIA SCC, SA-2009) reduce contractor design liability to reasonable skill and care. A standard first-stage pre-construction contract could reduce buildability risk, overcome conservative market culture barriers to OSM adoption, and potentially expose consultants to negligence claims for failing to recommend ECI on complex projects.

ideas.idea: OSM inherently requires design finalisation earlier, reducing flexibility for changes during construction and increasing risk of connectivity/tolerance issues.
ideas.quote: The design must be finalised earlier, making changes during the construction phase more difficult.

ideas.idea: Design-related constraints, including mismatches between design and manufacturing process, are prominent barriers to OSM adoption.
ideas.quote: the potential ‘mismatch between design and the manufacturing process’

ideas.idea: Involving contractors early in design reduces the risk of commissioning unbuildable designs, a key risk under traditional single-stage procurement.
ideas.quote: Under single-stage procurement, clients risk commissioning a design which, when tendered, is found to be unnecessarily difficult or even impossible to build. Involving the constructor in design development may reduce this risk.

ideas.idea: Standard forms of contract, by being familiar and legally tested, may help overcome market/cultural resistance to OSM adoption.
ideas.quote: standard forms of contract provide familiarity and can be tried and tested over time

ideas.idea: Two-stage ECI models can maintain competitive lump sum pricing even though scope is not fully defined at the time of early engagement, using notional bills of quantities later remeasured against detailed design.
ideas.quote: Contractors can be invited to tender a price based on a notional bill of quantities, and then once the design is finalised, a firm bill of quantities is developed by applying the rates from the original tender.

ideas.idea: There is no existing standard contractual model for two-stage ECI in New Zealand, unlike other jurisdictions with published pre-construction service agreements.
ideas.quote: There is currently no standard model for two-stage ECI in NZ.

ideas.idea: Existing UK standard forms (JCT PCSA, NEC ECI clause) provide bespoke pre-construction provisions but are limited to specific contract types and not universally suited to lump sum arrangements.
ideas.quote: the NEC’s FAQs webpage (NEC, 2014b) clarifies that the ECI clause is not suitable for use with lump sum contracts.

ideas.idea: Consultants/construction managers owe a duty of reasonable skill and care, while head contractors under lump sum/DB face a stricter fitness-for-purpose standard, affecting risk allocation for design/buildability defects.
ideas.quote: The implied legal duty imposed for construction work is fitness for purpose. Fitness for purpose imposes a higher standard than that of reasonable skill and care.
