findings: The top five significant constraints to PPVC adoption were: extensive coordination required prior to and during construction, need for additional project planning and design efforts, increased transportation and logistics considerations, requirement for early commitment, and higher initial cost than conventional construction methods. The top three most effective mitigation strategies were: encouraging close collaborations between project stakeholders during the early phase of the project, use of BIM to improve coordination and facilitate communication among stakeholders, and offering training courses for project teams and workers. The case study of a real PPVC project corroborated these survey findings, particularly regarding cost, planning/design effort, coordination, and transportation constraints.

ideas.idea: PPVC requires extensive multidisciplinary coordination throughout design, manufacturing, transportation, and installation stages, which is hindered by the industry's fragmented and conservative nature.
ideas.quote: PPVC involves multidisciplinary professionals to work in parallel and collaboratively in every stage of the project, which means that extensive coordination among the different project stakeholders is required, to handle the design, manufacturing, transportation, and installation of the prefabricated modules.

ideas.idea: PPVC demands significantly more upfront project planning and design effort than conventional construction because design must be reinvented for each unique project and finalized early.
ideas.quote: The planning and design processes of PPVC projects demand early collaboration among different parties such as architects, contractors, and manufacturers, which normally requires additional efforts from different project stakeholders.

ideas.idea: Transportation of prefabricated modules is constrained by regulations, module size limits, and logistics considerations that must be assessed before design begins.
ideas.quote: Normally, before taking any design step, the modular project team needs to examine the limitations of module transportation in the relevant area, because in most cases there is some special traffic control requirement on transporting heavy and bulky articles in densely populated areas.

ideas.idea: PPVC's need for early commitment and inflexibility for later changes is a critical constraint because modules must be manufactured before construction starts, reducing the ability to accommodate later design changes.
ideas.quote: PPVC requires early involvement of project design and planning because the precast components and modules need to be manufactured before construction starts. However, the respondents attending the survey maintained that the intensive upfront commitment in PPVC projects was inflexible.

ideas.idea: PPVC projects have higher initial costs than conventional construction due to expensive prefinished modules and costly shipping, exacerbated by damage risk from large module size.
ideas.quote: The initial cost for PPVC projects mainly refers to the expenses for the purchase of prefinished modules as well as for the shipping, which is normally higher than those for projects constructed with traditional methods.

ideas.idea: Close collaboration among project stakeholders in the early project phase is the most effective strategy to mitigate PPVC constraints, since concurrent work by multidisciplinary professionals requires it.
ideas.quote: in a PPVC project, multidisciplinary professionals to work concurrently during the early project phases such as planning and design, which makes close and effective collaborations from different project stakeholders a necessity rather than an option for PPVC projects.

ideas.idea: Building Information Modeling (BIM) serves as a key tool to bridge communication gaps and enhance interdisciplinary coordination among stakeholders in PPVC projects.
ideas.quote: it gives rise to the adoption of BIM, which serves as an information platform to bridge the communication gaps between project stakeholders and enhance the interdisciplinary coordination.

ideas.idea: Increased organizational requirements from PPVC adoption include changing roles of project participants and increased complexity of procurement and contracting issues.
ideas.quote: Increased organizational requirements (e.g. changing roles of project participants/increased complexity of procurement and contracting issues)

ideas.idea: Real-world case evidence shows contractual inspection requirements are used to ensure module compliance with binding contract terms across multiple overseas manufacturing locations.
ideas.quote: inspectors were hired to do inspections at the manufacturing factories and Jurong temporary site to ensure the compliance of the completed modules to the requirements stipulated in the binding contract.

ideas.idea: Mock-up modules are produced and require client approval before actual production begins, functioning as a risk-avoidance and dispute-prevention mechanism in PPVC delivery.
ideas.quote: Mock-up modules were manufactured first before the actual production of modules to obtain the approval from the client in order to avoid the possible disputes in the future.

objectives: To develop an automatic incentive-penalty enforcement system (smart contract) for modular construction that (i) establishes relationships between participants' work plan reliability and project performance to derive smart contract rules, (ii) builds a blockchain platform to enforce these rules, and (iii) integrates on-site images as oracles for progress tracking and smart contract verification.
problem_statement: Current construction practices lack an effective, real-time mechanism to enforce rewards and penalties for schedule/work plan reliability in modular construction; rewards/penalties are typically only enforced at or near project completion, making it difficult to encourage adherence and to trace causes of delay. There is also a gap in research on integrating real-time progress inspection with smart contract rules tailored to modular construction's coordination challenges among fabricators, suppliers, and contractors.
methodology: Case study of a residential high-rise project in Singapore using prefabricated bathroom units (PBUs). Two-phase framework: Phase A—data collection on PBU delivery and installation (74 PBU loading platform assembly durations, 139 hoist-up durations) and construction of a STROBOSCOPE discrete-event simulation model to test scenarios of PBU delivery variability, crane availability, and worker assignment (100 runs per scenario), producing cost/schedule outputs used to derive incentive/penalty rules; Phase B—development of an Ethereum-based smart contract (built in Remix) encoding these rules, plus an IPFS-based decentralized image-sharing application (using Web3.js and React) serving as a blockchain oracle to verify real-world performance and trigger payments.
key_background_studies: Peters and Panayi (2015) - defined smart contracts as self-enforcing mechanisms monitoring external inputs to settle contract stipulations, used as the study's working definition.

Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez (2020) - linked cost/schedule data to Ethereum smart contracts for secure payments but failed to automate progress payments due to centralized data governance, motivating the current study's automation goal.

Hamledari and Fischer (2021a, 2021b) - proposed using reality capture technologies (e.g., UAVs) to fetch as-built data to trigger smart contract payments, but did not develop concrete smart contract rules for real project performance scenarios.
Lee et al. (2021) - integrated digital twins and blockchain for traceable as-built information but lacked concrete smart contract rules based on performance scenarios.
Lu et al. (2021) - explored smart construction objects as blockchain oracles to enhance supply chain collaboration, informing this study's oracle design.
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - investigated digital twin-based oracles for performance-based smart contracts to financially incentivize parties, relevant to incentive design.
Tao et al. (2021) - developed an integrated blockchain-IPFS method for storing BIM design files, informing the decentralized storage approach used in this study.
Bamana et al. (2019) and Goh and Goh (2019) - used simulation to show JIT delivery reduces cycle time and improves labor productivity, informing simulation approach.
Liu et al. (2020) - used discrete event simulation to evaluate supply chain configurations' impact on project performance, informing simulation methodology.
Jung et al. (2018) - showed construction and material supply should be viewed as one system, informing the integrated delivery-installation simulation approach.
findings: The STROBOSCOPE simulation showed that PBU delivery sequence variability, crane availability, and worker assignment significantly affect project duration, idle times, and total cost. Under the benchmark scenario, project duration was 41.54 working days; best-case delivery variability (0-6) reduced duration to 40.93 days and saved US$2562 (translating to 1502 ETH incentive), while worst-case variability (22-24) increased duration to 50.79 days and incurred penalties up to 18,358 ETH. The developed smart contract successfully automated enforcement of rewards and penalties across all 19 scenarios (5 for PBU delivery, 7 for crane, 7 for workers) without third-party intervention, and correctly rejected/flagged erroneous inputs (false alarms). The IPFS-based image-sharing oracle allowed managers to upload timestamped, hashed images as evidence for triggering payments, improving transparency, traceability, and documentation. Overall, if the PBU fabricator performed at the highest reliability level per the smart contract rules, the project could save 4.7% of overall cost compared to the benchmark. The study concludes that smart contracts can provide objective, instant performance feedback, better anchor understanding of how subcontractor performance affects schedule/cost, and improve documentation for retrospective review, though limitations remain regarding decentralization, flexibility for change orders, and automated image interpretation.

ideas.idea: Modular/prefabricated construction requires significant coordination among multiple participants (designers, suppliers, prefabricators, contractors), and this coordination challenge is a key contractual issue addressed by the study.
ideas.quote: the success of modular construction requires additional effort in the form of coordination among multiple participants, such as designers, suppliers, prefabricators, and contractors.

ideas.idea: Traditional contract enforcement in construction typically only applies rewards/penalties at or near project completion, delaying incentive effects and making retrospective delay analysis difficult.
ideas.quote: rewards for on-time performance and penalties for delayed completion are usually not enforced until a project is either completed or near completion, making it difficult to encourage adherence to the schedule and work plan during the project.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automatically execute contractual payment clauses based on real-time verified data, reducing reliance on third-party authentication and administrative costs, which is directly relevant to modernizing contractual payment mechanisms for MMC/prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Blockchain and smart contracts are rising technologies that can be used to solve problems within the construction industry due to their ability to create, verify, and audit contract obligations in real time between companies, without the need for third-party authentication.

ideas.idea: There is a recognized gap in linking individual participant reliability to project-level performance in a way that can inform contractual incentive/penalty rule design for modular construction.
ideas.quote: There is a gap in the body of knowledge in understanding the relationship between an individual participant’s work plan reliability and project performance, and developing smart contract rules to motivate reliable completion based on various possible scenarios.

ideas.idea: Because smart contract executions are irreversible, contractual rules must anticipate all possible performance scenarios in advance, highlighting a need for detailed contractual specification akin to what standard contracts would need to address for MMC.
ideas.quote: Because smart contract executions are irreversible and immutable, it is important to consider all possible scenarios and outcomes when implementing smart contracts in the ever-changing construction environment.

ideas.idea: Off-site fabrication delivery sequencing and variability directly affect project schedule and cost, suggesting that contracts governing MMC/prefabrication should explicitly address delivery performance as a contractual risk allocation issue.
ideas.quote: The simulation results show that the arrival sequence had a significant impact on project success... The accumulated effects of out-of-sequence deliveries disrupted the balance of unloading, hoisting, and installing, and had the potential to endanger the completion of the project itself.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts function as an attachment to conventional contracts rather than a replacement, indicating that current contractual frameworks (such as CCDC) may need supplementary mechanisms to handle automated performance-based payments for MMC.
ideas.quote: the developed smart contract functions as the attachment to the conventional contract; it lacks the flexibility to deal with multiple change order scenarios.

ideas.idea: The lack of flexibility of smart contracts to handle change orders is identified as a limitation, pointing to a broader contractual gap in accommodating variations common in prefabricated/modular projects.
ideas.quote: It is recommended to develop the future research to support more rigorous and efficient contract design from human logic.

ideas.idea: Objective, image-based documentation via blockchain oracles can reduce disputes over performance and payment conditions, addressing a documentation/evidentiary gap relevant to contractual administration in MMC projects.
ideas.quote: Due to the uniqueness of the images, it is difficult for subcontractors to argue about what has been clearly recorded in the images.

ideas.idea: Conventional construction management suffers from poor, easily-lost documentation, which smart contract/blockchain systems can remedy by providing an immutable, chronological record relevant to contract compliance verification.
ideas.quote: improving the poor conventional documentation processes for construction data, wherein records are often defectively filed and simply lost after project completion.

ideas.idea: Standard practice for subcontractor performance appraisal is largely subjective and qualitative, whereas the study proposes quantified, scenario-based incentive/penalty structures as a more objective contractual mechanism applicable to prefabrication supply chains.
ideas.quote: In many current practices, subcontractor performance appraisal tends to be subjective and qualitative, and it is difficult to customize the incentives and penalties to reflect various performance levels.

objectives: To identify and rank liability factors involved in the process from digital design to digital fabrication, and to develop a conceptual framework for contract design that considers these factors, including recommendations for how existing project delivery models can incorporate them.
problem_statement: The adoption of digital fabrication in construction projects introduces new liability uncertainties in the process from digital design to digital fabrication, which can increase disputes; however, these liability factors have received little scholarly attention, leaving project stakeholders without guidance on how to design contracts to address them.
methodology: A two-stage single case study research design: Stage 1 involved a descriptive case study of Case R within Project Q (a Taiwanese theater project using DBB delivery), including document review and 21 semi-structured interviews, with process mapping via swimlane diagrams. Stage 2 involved a three-round Delphi survey of 14 project stakeholders to identify, rate, and rank 163 liability factors across eight categories (actors, resources, conditions, attributes, processes, artifacts, values, risks), followed by development of a conceptual contractual framework with four provisions (A-D) based on statistical thresholds (quartiles of mean and standard deviation).
key_background_studies: Hamdi and Leite (2014) - identified liability factors for conflicts in BIM implementation, including model ownership, cost control, and accuracy in BIM for facility management
Alwash et al. (2017) - presented legal uncertainties in BIM adoption, including dissipation of shared information, limited liability in collaborative virtual space, and negligence from professionals
Celoza et al. (2021a) - identified legal factors for information management including risk allocation in contracts, data transition, and standard of care
Celoza et al. (2021b) - found necessary conditions for BIM cost success including contractual BIM requirements and BIM execution plans
Bock and Linner (2015) - foundational work on digital fabrication and construction automation, robot-oriented design (ROD)
Ng et al. (2021) - developed design for digital fabrication (DfDFAB) concept and studied integration between design and construction value chains
Hall and Bonanomi (2021) - explored Ostrom's common pool resource governance theory to manage collaborative resources in IPD projects
Dalkey (1969) - established the Delphi method methodology used in this study
Okoli and Pawlowski (2004) - provided Delphi survey design steps followed in this research
Sullivan et al. (2017) - described characteristics of DBB and CM project delivery models
Touran et al. (2011) - discussed financial liability and risk allocation across DBB, CM, and DB delivery models
Fischer et al. (2017) - described IPD delivery model characteristics and multiparty relational contracting
findings: The study identified 163 liability factors across eight categories through the Delphi survey, with 85 factors deemed important (above the second quartile mean). The two most important liability factors were resource-related: management capability and BIM expertise, followed by general contractor (actor), BIM modeling coordination platform (resource), and reduce errors (value). A conceptual framework for contract design was developed comprising four contractual provisions (A, B, C, D) based on importance and variability of ratings. Provision A, containing 22 highly important factors, is recommended for inclusion in contracts between all parties as general conditions. The study found that among the four project delivery models, IPD requires fewer supplementary contractual considerations for digital fabrication, while DBB and CM require more supplementary agreements like PCSA and BIM protocols due to lack of early contractor involvement.

ideas.idea: Digital fabrication creates new liability uncertainties because faulty fabrication downstream may stem from inadequately constructed digital design models upstream, requiring clear contractual understanding of responsibility.
ideas.quote: a faulty digital fabrication operated by a downstream contractor could be due to a poorly constructed three-dimensional (3D) design model with inadequate design information passed from upstream design teams.

ideas.idea: General contractor is identified as the most important actor bearing liability because they manage the overall construction process including digital fabrication planning.
ideas.quote: the general contractor is responsible for the overall construction process including planning and managing digital fabrication.

ideas.idea: Early contractor involvement is a critical condition for successful digital fabrication design, relevant to enabling design for constructability across delivery models.
ideas.quote: The condition of early contractor involvement is relevant to "design for constructability," as stated by one surveyed expert.

ideas.idea: Traditional DBB delivery, lacking early contractor involvement, tends to allocate risk poorly and presumes excessive foresight in design compared to construction realities.
ideas.quote: DBB can "improperly presume a high degree of clairvoyance when allocating risk" (O’Connor 2009), but there are also cases when contractors "tend to be claim-oriented"

ideas.idea: Design-Build delivery, while enabling faster delivery and cost certainty through early contractor involvement, can restrict design flexibility partly due to insurance policy limitations covering design dissatisfaction.
ideas.quote: DB can lead to restricted design flexibility because the typical design professional liability insurance policy, commonly known as an E&O policy in the US, might not cover dissatisfaction of design

ideas.idea: IPD's target-value design and risk/reward sharing mechanisms foster innovation and cost control conducive to digital fabrication and prefabrication adoption, though collaborative resource mismanagement can cause disputes.
ideas.quote: The early contractor involvement and risk-and-reward sharing mechanism foster systemic innovation across disciplines and adoption of digital fabrication with cost control (Ng and Hall 2021).

ideas.idea: IPD contracts often explicitly specify innovative construction methods such as prefabrication and modular construction as part of the agreement structure.
ideas.quote: innovative construction methods such as prefabrication and modular construction are usually specified in IPD contracts such as the Integrated Form of Agreement (IFOA).

ideas.idea: Management capability and BIM expertise are identified as the two most critical liability resources needed to successfully manage integration between digital design and digital fabrication.
ideas.quote: The resources of management capability and building information modeling (BIM) expertise rank as the two most important liability factors.

ideas.idea: On-site constructability is the most important condition liability factor because digitally fabricated components must integrate properly with other building parts during on-site assembly.
ideas.quote: a system fabricated digitally off-site should be integrable with other building parts during on-site assembly.

ideas.idea: Preconstruction services agreements (PCSA) and BIM protocols are recommended supplementary contractual mechanisms to bring early contractor involvement and address liability factors in DBB and CM delivery models lacking inherent early integration.
ideas.quote: PCSA is recommended for a DBB or CM project to enable the early involvement of the digital fabrication trade contractor to participate in the design process.

ideas.idea: IPD requires fewer supplementary contractual provisions than other delivery models for digital fabrication because its structure already integrates early contractor involvement and collaborative design processes.
ideas.quote: the authors evaluated that, among the other three project delivery models, IPD requires fewer supplementary considerations when designing the contract for design for digital fabrication.

ideas.idea: Fragmented understanding of fabrication machine constraints among project teams is a source of liability uncertainty that contracts should address through improved information sharing.
ideas.quote: Such liability uncertainty could be caused by the fragmented understanding of, for example, fabrication machine constraints among the project teams (Celoza et al. 2021a).

ideas.idea: Design/BIM and on-site misalignment is ranked as the top risk factor, reflecting the danger of digital design fragmenting from actual on-site construction conditions.
ideas.quote: digital design [in BIM] and off-site digital fabrication could be fragmented with the situation on-site.

objectives: To develop a machine learning–driven text classification model to analyze particular conditions of FIDIC contracts from a multifunctional (Control, Coordination, Adaptation) and risk perspective, and to determine what aspects good particular conditions focus on when modifying general conditions to avert risks.
problem_statement: While FIDIC general conditions have been analyzed under a multifunctional perspective, particular conditions—which modify general conditions to fit specific project circumstances—can introduce additional or uneven risks, and prior research on particular conditions has been practice-oriented, narrowly focused on single aspects, and has not applied contract theory or efficient automated analysis to understand how particular conditions affect overall contract function distribution.
methodology: Content analysis and supervised machine learning classification of contract sentences based on the 11-subfunction coding scheme of Chen et al. (2018b). Human coders (three postgraduates supervised by experts) coded FIDIC 1999 Red Book, FIDIC 2017 Suite of Contracts, and five particular conditions based on the FIDIC 1999 Silver Book (5,785 sentences total). Four machine learning algorithms (NB, SVM, LR, RF) were compared using TF-IDF feature extraction with N-gram variations; SVM with linear kernel, C=10, and unigram&bigram&trigram features was selected as optimal. This model was used to code four additional particular conditions. Statistics on functional complexity were computed across nine 'good' contracts (five human-coded, four machine-coded) and compared to general conditions using chi-square tests.
key_background_studies: Chen et al. (2018b) - first applied the three-function/eleven-subfunction coding scheme via content analysis to FIDIC 1999 general conditions, providing the coding scheme and baseline this study extends to particular conditions.

Mellewigt et al. (2012) and Schepker et al. (2014) - introduced/established the multifunctional (Control, Coordination, Adaptation) perspective of contracts that underlies this study's theoretical framework.

Lawrence (2017) - argued particular conditions can inadvertently transfer risks (e.g., nominated subcontractor risks) to one party, motivating the study's focus on risk allocation via particular conditions.
Lee et al. (2020b) - used rule-based NLP to measure how risk allocation is modified by employers in FIDIC particular conditions, a related but narrower practice-oriented study.
Lee et al. (2019) - built an NLP system to extract 'poisonous clauses' in contracts to help contractors identify risks, illustrating prior single-aspect, practice-oriented approaches.
Bodea and Purnus (2016) - analyzed how particular conditions affect financial arrangement/management of contractors, another narrow-focus prior study.

You et al. (2018) and Yao et al. (2021) - empirical (questionnaire-based) studies linking Control/Adaptation/Coordination clauses to relational and performance risk mitigation, providing theoretical grounding on function-risk relationships.
Hassan and Le (2020) - used NLP to distinguish requirement vs non-requirement clauses, a simpler dichotomous and practice-oriented classification contrasted with this study's more elaborate approach.
findings: The SVM model with TF-IDF (unigram+bigram+trigram, linear kernel, C=10) achieved the best and most stable accuracy among tested algorithms for coding particular conditions. Chi-square tests showed no significant difference in functional (Control/Coordination/Adaptation) or subfunctional distributions between the nine full contracts (general + particular conditions) and the general conditions alone, indicating particular conditions are coherent extensions rather than substantial redistributions of contract functions. Particular conditions most heavily add/modify Obligations and Task Descriptions (Coordination and Control subfunctions) to explicitly clarify parties' responsibilities and tasks, mitigating risk of misunderstanding and unilateral risk transfer. Interpretations subfunction sentences are most numerously modified, reflecting particular conditions' role in clarifying project-specific terms. Adaptation function is least adjusted, since future contingencies remain hard to foresee even when drafting particular conditions, and general conditions' Adaptation provisions are treated as already mature/flexible.

ideas.idea: Particular conditions serve as project-specific modifications to standard general conditions, and this modification process itself can introduce additional risks if drafted unevenly.
ideas.quote: However, the particular conditions of contracts present specific requirements closely related to projects, which can generate additional risks for both parties.

ideas.idea: Contracts perform three distinct functions—Control, Coordination, Adaptation—that map onto different risk types (relational risk from opportunism, performance risk from task complexity, and performance risk from future uncertainty).
ideas.quote: Contracts can serve three functions—Control, Coordination, and Adaptation—to mitigate different risks.

ideas.idea: Modifying standard contract clauses (deleting fair clauses or adding unbalanced ones) can shift risk burden disproportionately onto one contracting party.
ideas.quote: some particular conditions can set certain contractual and legal pitfalls to bring additional risks to the employer or contractor by deleting some fair clauses or adding some clauses to distribute risks unevenly

ideas.idea: There is no significant difference in the overall functional distribution between a full contract (general + particular conditions) and its underlying general conditions, meaning particular conditions do not fundamentally alter risk allocation logic.
ideas.quote: no significant differences are found in the functional distributions between a whole contract (containing both general and particular conditions) and its general conditions... particular conditions of contracts are coherent extensions of general conditions without significantly changing the overall functional distribution of general conditions.

ideas.idea: Good particular conditions primarily add clarity to obligations and task descriptions, reducing ambiguity about who is responsible for what, which helps prevent disputes and risk transfer.
ideas.quote: particular conditions should concentrate more on explicitly illustrating both parties' obligations and tasks prudently to mitigate potential risks.

ideas.idea: Frequent detailed amendments in the Coordination function (task descriptions, interpretations) should not be seen as a sign of distrust between parties but rather as efforts to reduce misunderstanding and build trust.
ideas.quote: these amendments in Task Descriptions contradict the traditional thoughts that too many amendments in particular conditions are the root of a poor relationship... contract managers distinguish between different changes.

ideas.idea: The Adaptation function, dealing with unforeseeable future events, is least modified in particular conditions because contract drafters cannot anticipate all contingencies even at the project-specific level, so general boilerplate provisions for adaptation remain largely intact.
ideas.quote: Adaptation is the least adjusted function. This is because future contingency is difficult to foresee at any time, including when drafting particular conditions.

ideas.idea: Standard/model contracts (like FIDIC) are widely reused with minor modifications rather than drafting entirely new contracts, reflecting efficiency in contract creation across projects.
ideas.quote: Different transactions might have something in common, so there is no need to prepare a totally new contract for every new transaction.

ideas.idea: Task Changes provisions (e.g., variation procedures) are essentially never altered in particular conditions, suggesting these procedural mechanisms are treated as fixed regardless of project specifics.
ideas.quote: The number of Task Changes adjusted by particular conditions is all zero, indicating that the Task Changes subfunction of construction contracts, such as value engineering and variation procedures, has been rigorously set in general conditions and their modification is tightly restricted.

ideas.idea: Machine learning-based coding of contract text can improve efficiency and objectivity in contract management, aiding practitioners in identifying and codifying risk-related clauses across many projects.
ideas.quote: The machine learning model can help them efficiently analyze the contracts of the projects they have done, which contributes to knowledge management for writing and understanding particular conditions.

objectives: To quantify the marginal benefits (cost, time, productivity) of prefabrication over traditional building systems (TBS) in Auckland building projects, and to examine whether 'building type' significantly affects these observed benefits.
problem_statement: While prefabrication is widely credited with benefits over traditional construction, existing evidence is largely anecdotal or based on isolated case studies, lacking statistically robust, evidence-based quantification across building types, which contributes to the technology's low industry uptake.
methodology: A mixed archival research and case study method was used, drawing on historical records of 66 completed prefab building projects in Auckland (houses, commercial, educational, community, apartment buildings). Final contract sums, completion dates, gross floor areas and number of floors were collected via purposive sampling through contracting/consulting firms and the Registered Master Builders Federation. Equivalent TBS costs and durations were derived from the Rawlinsons Construction Handbook and designer/contractor feedback. Marginal cost saving, marginal time saving, and productivity improvement (product of cost and time savings) were computed per project and averaged by building type; single-factor ANOVA was used to test the effect of building type on these outcomes.
key_background_studies: Shahzad and Mbachu [1] - discuss diminishing differentiation between conventional and prefab building types and classification thresholds based on prefab value proportion
Lu [14] - notes prefab offers more reliable upfront cost estimates and investment returns
Bell [3] - discusses socio-cultural stigma and misperceptions about prefab quality from post-WWII era
Egan [26] - argues prefab yields speed, cost, and productivity benefits (~30-40% improvement)

Burgess et al. [27] - New Zealand case study finding prefab did not yield superior economic benefits, citing Kaufmann and Remick [28], Atkin and Wing [29], and Bell [3] on residential time savings of 30-60%
Mbachu and Shahzad [7] - distinguish strategic productivity (cost/schedule based) from economist's input-output productivity measures
findings: Prefabrication delivered average 19% cost savings and 34% time savings over TBS, translating to 7% overall productivity improvement. House projects showed the highest productivity gain (11%) and time savings (50%), while community buildings had the highest cost savings (24%). ANOVA results showed building type had no significant effect on cost or productivity improvement outcomes but had a significant effect on time savings, indicating that claims of superior time-saving benefits should be building-type specific rather than generalized, while cost and productivity benefits can be generalized across building types.

ideas.idea: Conventional buildings already contain componentized/panelized prefab elements, blurring the distinction between prefab and traditional systems, especially for non-residential buildings.
ideas.quote: there is increasingly little differentiation between the conventional building types and the “componentized” and the “panelized” prefabrication types.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication limits the flexibility for bespoke design changes compared to traditional construction, which can negate cost and time benefits if late changes occur.
ideas.quote: the prefab approach usually limits the extent of the owner’s changes to the standard designs. If significant changes are made, especially at the construction phase, the outcomes for the prefab technology in terms of costs, speed and wastage will be less desirable

ideas.idea: Logistics and site conditions (e.g., traffic congestion, interface problems, variability from design assumptions) can make traditional construction preferable to prefab in certain circumstances.
ideas.quote: Other issues include the logistic challenge (especially for projects located in traffic congested areas), onsite connection or interface problems, and the reality that construction-phase changes are bound to be made due to the variability of site conditions from the initial design assumptions.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication provides more reliable and predictable cost estimation for upfront investment and returns compared to traditional building, a key contractual/financial consideration.
ideas.quote: Lu [14] observes that prefab does not only save construction costs but also offers more reliable estimates of the upfront costs, total investment outlay and overall returns on investments.

ideas.idea: Time-saving benefits of prefabrication are not uniform across building types and should be reported specifically per building type rather than generalized, which has implications for contractual scheduling expectations.
ideas.quote: claims about the superior benefits of prefab can only be generalised in respect of cost and productivity improvements across all building types, whereas claims about time savings should be cautiously applied to specific building types.

ideas.idea: Standardized house designs (off standard plans) enable faster manufacture and installation, suggesting procurement strategy influences achievable prefab benefits.
ideas.quote: majority of the houses being developed off standard plans provided by group home builders. Such houses lend readily to standard components, which make for faster manufacture and installation, thereby enhancing speed of construction.

ideas.idea: Small market scale can limit the economic benefits of prefabrication compared to larger markets, indicating context-dependent viability of prefab adoption.
ideas.quote: This can be associated to small size of the New Zealand market and its inability to exploit the scale efficiencies offered by mechanized bulk production of similar products.

objectives: To develop, pilot and validate a robust, empirically-based early-stage decision-support tool that helps clients and decision makers determine a project's suitability for offsite modular construction in the engineering construction sector.
problem_statement: Existing decision-support tools for assessing offsite modular construction suitability are limited, outdated, or not tailored to the engineering construction sector, leading decisions to be based on capital cost, experience or intuition rather than holistic, value-based evaluation.
methodology: A mixed-method study conducted in two phases (2014-2016) with engineering construction clients, contractors, consultants and suppliers across Europe via the European Construction Institute (ECI). Phase 1 used an explanatory sequential mixed method: web-based questionnaire (n=18), semi-structured phone interviews (n=12), Delphi-style plenary questionnaire (n=46) and workshop focus groups (n=28). Phase 2 used a convergent parallel mixed method: additional literature review, workshop 2 (n=12), an online questionnaire to the ECI modularisation task force (n=10), and workshop 3 (n=25) to trial and evaluate the resulting Excel/VBA-based Ecimod tool.
key_background_studies: Tatum et al. (1987) - seminal work defining modularisation and modules in engineering construction, treated as foundational definition source
Gibb (1999) - established the importance of early project-wide offsite strategy development and terminology of offsite/modularisation
Emes (1992) - argued offsite strategy must be evaluated from an overall project view rather than element view
Pan et al. (2008) - developed a decision-support matrix for build system selection in housing construction, cited as existing but limited tool
Haas and Fagerlund (2002) - developed Modex, the earliest identifiable decision-support tool related to modularisation, used as basis for rating technique (Smart)
Cigolini and Castellano (2002) - discussed modularisation tools and offshore sector's influence on modularisation practices
Blismas et al. (2006) - noted that benefits of offsite depend on project specifics and cannot simply be listed as guaranteed
Padron et al. (2007) - developed Autmod3 planning tool for modular building systems, aimed at implementation stage rather than early decision-making
findings: The study identified 46 drivers and 41 constraints for adopting modularisation in engineering construction, categorised into client objectives, site characteristics, project execution/management approach, and EPC/contractor/industry player status. These were used to build the Ecimod decision-support tool with three levels (initial selection, applicability, feasibility) using a Simple Multi-Attribute Rating Technique (Smart) scoring system. The tool was validated through workshops with acceptable disagreement levels (20-22%), refined based on feedback (e.g., allowing user-specified drivers/constraints), and implemented as an Excel/VBA-based tool. It is presented as the first globally-applicable, empirically-based decision-support tool for modularisation decisions in engineering construction, though limited by sample size and lacking real-world case study validation.

ideas.idea: Early strategic decision-making about whether to use offsite/modular approaches is critical and should occur at the earliest possible project stage, ideally from an overall project perspective rather than element-by-element.
ideas.quote: to maximise the benefits from offsite...it is essential that a project wide strategy is developed at an early stage in the project

ideas.idea: Decisions about offsite/modular construction are often made based on capital cost, experience or intuition rather than systematic evaluation, due to a lack of adequate decision-support tools.
ideas.quote: Decision-support tools for determining a project’s suitability for offsite modular construction are currently limited or outdated, leading to decisions being based mainly around capital cost, experience or intuition.

ideas.idea: Increased engineering and design effort is both a benefit driver (early freeze of design decisions) and a drawback (higher cost and effort) of modularisation, showing the tension in early design commitment relevant to contractual risk allocation.
ideas.quote: H: Limited late changes due to early freeze of design and decisions... H: High engineering and design effort, mainly detailed engineering, necessity to design for transportation and maturity of the information at the early stage

ideas.idea: Modularisation shifts risk allocation between parties, for example from engineering design to engineering construction, which has implications for contractual risk distribution.
ideas.quote: Risk allocation shift (e.g. from engineering design to engineering construction)

ideas.idea: Transportation and installation of modules introduce significant risks (damage, loss) that must be planned for and mitigated early, which is a contractually relevant risk category distinct from traditional onsite construction risk.
ideas.quote: H: High transportation risk (module damaged or lost)

ideas.idea: The choice to modularise depends heavily on the propensity and economic interests of the EPC contractor, which may conflict with client interests, creating a potential contractual/relationship issue.
ideas.quote: H: Economic interests in advising a modular approach (e.g. design hours payment)... H: Economic interest in advising a stick build approach

ideas.idea: Lack of industry experience, knowledge and consolidated management procedures among contractors is a barrier to adopting modular approaches, which project delivery models and contracts may need to address.
ideas.quote: Lack of consolidate methods and management procedures in facing modular projects... Lack of critical information management... Lack of risk evaluation and mitigation (e.g. during transportation and installation)

ideas.idea: Increased coordination and communication requirements among project operators, suppliers and installers are needed when modularising, implying contractual provisions for enhanced collaboration.
ideas.quote: More effective communication and coordination required between project operators

ideas.idea: Standardisation and early client/key player involvement in engineering and design can support project replication and resolve infeasibilities earlier, a point relevant to procurement and contract structuring for repeat/modular projects.
ideas.quote: Possibility to introduce standardisation for project replication... Early involvement of the client and key project players

objectives: To develop Shapley value–based smart contracts that automatically quantify subcontractors' marginal contributions and assign fair rewards/penalties to motivate reliable task-level collaboration in modular construction, and to implement these rules in a blockchain-based smart contract system.
problem_statement: Construction projects involving modular construction require highly interrelated collaboration among subcontractors (fabricator, crane, workers), but there is a lack of an objective, automatic mechanism to fairly distribute rewards/penalties based on marginal contributions, and existing smart contract/blockchain literature has not demonstrated how to handle multiparty scenarios, derive fair incentive-penalty sharing without human judgment, or decentralize reliable task-level construction management.
methodology: Case study of a high-rise residential building in Singapore using modular construction (prefabricated bathroom units, PBUs). Empirical delivery and installation data (74 PBU loading platform assemblies, 139 hoisting activities) were collected and fitted to distributions. A discrete-event simulation model was built to permutate 27 combinations of reliability levels (high/middle/low) for PBU fabricator, crane, and workers, run 50 times each, to quantify project duration and cost outcomes. Shapley value calculations were applied to the simulation outputs to determine fair marginal-contribution-based reward/penalty allocations for each subcontractor. These payment rules were encoded into Ethereum smart contracts (Solidity) and deployed on a blockchain network (Ganache, MetaMask, Truffle) for validation and testing.
key_background_studies: Shapley (1953) - introduced the Shapley value concept used as the core fairness mechanism for cost/benefit allocation in coalitions.
Pishdad-Bozorgi and Srivastava (2018) - studied IPD contracts and showed financial incentives keep parties in coalition and minimize cost overruns, informing the incentive design rationale.
Hall et al. (2018) - demonstrated IPD's inter-organizational governance enabling collaborative management across firm boundaries.
Hunhevicz et al. (2020, 2021, 2022a, 2022b) - explored blockchain governance, DAO concepts, and performance-based smart contracts with financial incentives, framing the gap this study addresses.
Elghaish et al. (2020) - developed a smart contract framework for IPD projects coding risk/reward transactions, cited as case-based incentive work needing further validation.
Lu et al. (2021a) - recorded reputation scores in blockchain with incentive mechanisms for offsite logistics/onsite assembly, suggesting game theory integration for fairness.
Javanmardi et al. (2018) - linked cooperative game theory to relational contracting, underpinning the fairness/incentive rationale.
Assaad et al. (2020) - argued subcontractor interactions are shaped mainly by contractual relationships, framing the collaboration problem.
Henisz et al. (2012) - argued coercive contractual/hierarchical forces cannot guarantee reliable collaboration, motivating need for incentive-based mechanisms.
findings: The simulation and Shapley value analysis showed that higher subcontractor reliability shortens project duration and reduces costs, but marginal benefits of higher reliability diminish if other parties remain unreliable. Shapley-based payments produced penalties for low reliability, no payment for middle reliability, and rewards for high reliability, incentivizing subcontractors to avoid penalties and encouraging peer negotiation toward higher reliability. Individual high performance was shown to be a dominant strategy that also motivates encouraging others' high performance, creating peer production incentives. Investing in higher reliability, when Shapley value payments are enforced, produced the lowest total cost overall despite higher upfront investment. The smart contract, deployed on an Ethereum blockchain (via Ganache, MetaMask, Truffle), correctly and automatically triggered reward/penalty payments matching Shapley value calculations, and could detect and reject malicious/incorrect payment attempts, demonstrating feasibility of self-enforcing, decentralized, automatic incentive execution without centralized human judgment.

ideas.idea: Traditional centralized contractual management structures create slow, hierarchical decision-making that can be improved through decentralized, blockchain-enabled bottom-up collaboration among subcontractors.
ideas.quote: Ensuring horizontal collaborations can shift centralized control push to decentralized pull (Howell 1999).

ideas.idea: Interactions and responsibilities among subcontractors in construction are primarily defined by contractual relationships, which shape coordination but do not guarantee reliable collaboration.
ideas.quote: The interactions between the different subcontractors are mainly shaped by their contractual relationships (Assaad et al. 2020).

ideas.idea: Coercive contractual or hierarchical authority alone is insufficient to ensure reliable collaboration or prevent opportunistic behavior among subcontractors pursuing individual benefit.
ideas.quote: it has been argued that coercive forces from hierarchical authority or contractual terms cannot guarantee reliable collaboration or reduce opportunistic behaviors (Henisz et al. 2012).

ideas.idea: Relational contracting approaches such as IPD attempt to align subcontractor interests by sharing risk and reward based on joint project outcomes rather than individual contractual terms.
ideas.quote: Project teams jointly take responsibility for completing the projects and share the achievements or failures of the projects based on the "pain-share, gain-share" mentality (Yeung et al. 2007).

ideas.idea: Financial incentive design within contracts (including IPD) can keep parties committed and reduce cost overruns, but determining fair reward/risk sharing remains a persistent contractual challenge.
ideas.quote: determining fair rewards and sharing in the early phases and achieving financial transparency can be challenging (Kahvandi et al. 2019; Rodrigues and Lindhard 2023).

ideas.idea: Smart contracts encoded on blockchain can automate payment, reduce transaction costs, and enforce contractual terms without centralized administration, but struggle to handle unexpected or complex multiparty construction scenarios.
ideas.quote: implementing smart contracts in the construction industry is inherently difficult because smart contracts cannot handle unexpected cases (Li et al. 2023).

ideas.idea: A key contractual challenge is defining coordination and incentive mechanisms within smart contracts that align diverse project participants' interests toward collective project outcomes.
ideas.quote: defining coordination mechanisms in smart contracts that can align human interests to create collective outcomes represents one of the main challenges of implementing blockchains practically (Hunhevicz et al. 2021).

ideas.idea: There remains a fundamental incompatibility between the decentralized nature of smart contracts and the centralized risk/benefit allocation practices still used in current construction contracts.
ideas.quote: Current projects still need a centralized manager to allocate risks and benefits, leading to incompatibility between the decentralized nature of smart contracts and centralized management practices (Lu et al. 2021b).

ideas.idea: Cooperative game theory, and specifically the Shapley value, offers an objective way to allocate contractual rewards and penalties fairly based on each party's marginal contribution to a coalition, rather than relying on subjective central judgment.
ideas.quote: The Shapley value, introduced by Shapley (1953), is a mechanism in cooperative game theory that provides a unique and equitable distribution of additional costs when working in a coalition (Sharafi et al. 2021).

ideas.idea: Embedding objective, quantified incentive rules (rewards for high performance, penalties for low performance) directly into smart contracts can replace subjective, centralized risk allocation with self-enforcing contractual mechanisms.
ideas.quote: There is no need for a central command to allocate risks manually. Therefore, communications and collaborations can occur automatically without human judgment, and a win-win situation can be realized.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts need to be paired with legally enforceable contracts to ensure consistency between automated execution and legal enforcement, and current smart contracts are vulnerable to major unforeseen ('black swan') contractual events.
ideas.quote: it is necessary to pair smart contracts and contracts so that the smart contract can be consistent with legal enforcement... there is no such pledge that it can handle an event that comes as a surprise but has a major effect.

ideas.idea: Contractual reliance on a trustful centralized database for smart contract inputs creates a single point of failure risk, suggesting a need for decentralized data verification mechanisms in future contract systems.
ideas.quote: this study assumed the existence of a trustful central database that is responsible for smart contract data input. However, the central database might also suffer from a single point of failure.

ideas.idea: Blockchain-based instantaneous reward/penalty mechanisms can replace the traditional practice of delaying dispute resolution or litigation until project completion, changing how contractual remedies are administered.
ideas.quote: Blockchain can bring out instantaneousness where reliable completion can be motivated or enforced... Project managers either accept the outcomes if the loss is tolerable or resort to litigation if intolerable.

objectives: To identify and address the obstacles currently preventing further expansion of off-site prefabrication of timber and MEP services, examining coordination between builders and suppliers, evaluating hindering approaches, and simplifying initiatives to integrate off-site and in situ work.
problem_statement: There are limited empirical and qualitative studies addressing the detailed processes and performance obstacles in coordinating off-site prefabrication between builders and suppliers, particularly for timber and MEP services, despite growing interest in innovative off-site technologies.
methodology: Qualitative field research using 40 unstructured, face-to-face interviews with approximately 2 participants from each of four builder organizations and four supplier organizations in Melbourne, Australia. Data were coded and analyzed using NVivo software (v12) through content analysis for builders and suppliers separately, followed by comparative analysis, with internal (literature) and external (industry expert presentations) validation.
key_background_studies: Bildsten (2014) - identified traditional lack of collaboration and coordination between builders and suppliers in construction supply chains
Johnsson and Meiling (2009) - studied defects in completed off-site prefabricated timber modules
Tserng et al. (2011) - developed an algorithm for efficient on-site assembly of modular MEP services, highlighting supplier limitations in design verification
Yunis et al. (2016) - revealed deficiencies between off-site prefabrication and in situ construction, informing interview focus
Salama et al. (2017) - established a 'Modular Suitability Index' to optimize coordination of off-site components with in situ construction
Laurent and Leicht (2019) - defined Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) and cross-functional team management for off-site prefabrication coordination
Masood et al. (2021) - studied supply chain challenges for prefabricated houses in New Zealand, used for comparison with Australian findings
findings: Builders' obstacles include sustainability, quality assurance, mass production, CAD/BIM, technological support, commercial arrangements, system building, buffering in supply, schedule monitoring, productivity, flexibility, engagement, risks, and multiple supply arrangements. Suppliers' obstacles include design, financing and subcontracting, coordination, recognized practices, risks, multiple supply arrangements, and constraints. The study concludes that these obstacles can be addressed through improved collaboration and coordination, as a traditional lack of both exists between builders and suppliers. Early engagement of builders and suppliers in the digital design phase is recommended to enhance project integration and coordination.

ideas.idea: Builders often include contractual clauses such as bank guarantees and insurance certificates to manage cash flow and payment risks associated with prefabrication suppliers.
ideas.quote: Bank guarantees allow the builders to deposit payments, which helps them obtain materials, plant and/or equipment necessary for contending with construction project-specific risks.

ideas.idea: Some large builders subcontract identical prefabrication work to multiple competing suppliers simultaneously to mitigate the risk of delay or non-performance.
ideas.quote: If you fail in what you deliver, it might be cheaper to let in bulk . . . If you can't deliver on time, you'll lose more.

ideas.idea: Tier One builders sometimes impose onerous subcontract terms that leave suppliers with little negotiating power regarding delivery obligations.
ideas.quote: Tier One (1) builders mightn't budge . . . There's no excuse because those contracts blindly say you will deliver.

ideas.idea: Variation orders from project clients disrupt suppliers' prefabrication cycles, affecting quality control, scheduling, and installation efficiency.
ideas.quote: each variation order (VO) by the project client inevitably changed their cycle of preparation, resources invested, QC, as well as coordination, thereby jeopardizing the functions of logistics, scheduling, meeting deadlines, constructability, and installation efficiency.

ideas.idea: Suppliers protect their intellectual property by withholding detailed shop drawings until a formal subcontract is secured, which can create friction with builders and clients.
ideas.quote: Supplier P1 has been dedicated to transparently providing a set of requirements and limitations of different timber species, just falling short of divulging their cost information straight away. The latter is a measure to protect their IP, which would only be divulged if the builder proceeds to subcontract their shop drawing design and off-site timber prefabrication.

ideas.idea: Lack of timely and thorough design information before prefabrication starts creates significant contractual risk exposure for builders, including unforeseen costs, delays, and defects.
ideas.quote: There was a belief amongst each of the builders that all design details must be provided sufficient and thorough, especially before off-site prefabrication of components starts... risks of associated unforeseen costs, delays, defects, OH&S hazards, and project client distress would ensue, which normally require remediation measures through potentially hostile negotiations.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD), a relational multiparty contract, is better suited to off-site prefabrication than traditional procurement because it requires managed cross-functional teams.
ideas.quote: IPD has recently been defined by Laurent and Leicht (2019) [33]... as when "multiple stakeholders from the design and construction team join a relational, multiparty contract".

ideas.idea: Suppliers bear most of the risk in construction supply chains relative to builders, who function primarily as purchasers.
ideas.quote: Hence, it has been the supplier organizations that normally carry most of the risks in the supply chains of construction projects [13,14].

ideas.idea: Some suppliers use nominated subcontractor arrangements and joint trading accounts with clients to manage financial risk in supply contracts.
ideas.quote: Supplier P2 is unique inasmuch that they regularly open a short-term joint trading account with the builders or construction project clients to whom they supply off-site prefabricated timber components. The construction project client would then engage the builder, with Supplier P2 included as a Nominated Subcontractor.

ideas.idea: Earlier supplier involvement in design and planning phases is seen as key to improving contractual and coordination outcomes for off-site prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Supplier P2 wants earlier involvement in projects, ideally within the planning and/or design phases.

ideas.idea: A fully in-house, vertically integrated builder model can bypass many contractual and coordination risks associated with subcontracting off-site prefabrication suppliers.
ideas.quote: The years of investment and efforts by Builder C4 toward establishing their holistic in-house system afforded them the luxury of being able to bypass the abovementioned risks by undertaking all design, prefabrication, logistics, lifting/loading, construction, and fit-out themselves.

objectives: To examine the impact of postpandemic inflation on construction project budgets in Canada and to demonstrate, through a case study, how off-site construction (OSC) can mitigate inflation-driven cost overruns by identifying high-risk inflationary building divisions and quantifying the relationship between inflation and contract claim amounts.
problem_statement: Persistent and volatile inflation following the COVID-19 pandemic has driven up construction material and labor costs in Canada, causing significant cost overruns, budget deviations, and claims on fixed-price contracts, yet there is limited practical guidance on identifying which building divisions are most inflation-sensitive and how off-site construction can be strategically deployed to counter these effects.
methodology: A four-phase mixed-methods case study approach: (1) collection and analysis of historical Building Construction Price Index (BCPI) and material price data for Montréal; (2) elemental cost analysis (ECA) of a real off-site (volumetric modular) case project—a single-story administrative complex in Northern Ontario delivered under a CCDC-14 Design-Build Stipulated Price Contract—using the National Master Specification breakdown; (3) assessment of inflation-triggered change orders and claim amounts against the contract sum; and (4) statistical analysis using Spearman's correlation coefficient and a sensitivity coefficient (SC) to examine the relationship between inflation rate and claim amount by division, with data validated by the project owner, banking institutions, and an external cost consultant.
key_background_studies: Musarat et al. (2020, 2021) - established inflation as a critical driver of construction cost overruns and outlined factors (interest rates, wages, exchange rates) affecting inflation's economic impact.
Ribeirinho et al. 2020 (McKinsey) and Changali et al. 2015 - highlighted that most construction projects suffer cost overruns, often linked to productivity issues.
Bertram et al. 2019 (McKinsey Global Institute) - argued OSC yields efficiency gains, faster completion, and reduced exposure to inflationary pressures over project timelines.

de Laubier et al. 2019 and Goulding and Rahimian 2019 - advocated OSC as a holistic solution for mitigating cost overrun risk from price increases and delays, citing controlled factory environments and stable skilled labor.
Smith and Quale 2017 - defined off-site construction as prefabrication of components before site assembly, foundational to OSC terminology.
Kamar et al. 2011 - defined industrialization/off-site construction as preparation, design, fabrication, and assembly at a location separate from final installation.
Jordà and Nechio 2023 - analyzed post-pandemic inflation surge globally and its causes including supply disruptions and geopolitical events.
Alaloul et al. 2021 - discussed inflation's role in cost estimation and its link to housing/material/labor price increases.
findings: Analysis of the case project revealed a 14% increase in contract sum attributable to inflation, with metals (highest inflation, 42.3% index change) and special construction/prefabricated components showing the greatest cost sensitivity (SC of 0.27 and 0.14 respectively). Spearman's correlation between inflation rate and claim amount was 0.6044, indicating a strong nonlinear positive relationship. Divisions with high sensitivity coefficients (metals, special construction, HVAC) were identified as best suited for off-site construction, since OSC enables bulk purchasing with fixed pricing, reduces material waste and project delays, and allows work to proceed in a controlled factory environment, thereby insulating projects from inflationary volatility. The study concludes OSC is a strategic, collaborative approach—agreed upon by design-build teams, clients, and financiers—for safeguarding budgets against inflation, useful for both immediate project planning and long-term resilience strategy.

ideas.idea: Fixed-price design-build contracts (CCDC-14) shift inflation risk to the contractor unless allowances are pre-negotiated, creating tension when actual inflation exceeds benchmarked estimates.
ideas.quote: A Design–Build Stipulated Price Contract (CCDC-14) was applied to the project, meaning that the contract price was not to be increased due to inflation.

ideas.idea: Change orders driven by inflation require a formal claim and validation process involving multiple stakeholders, showing how contractual administration must adapt to volatile pricing.
ideas.quote: the effect on project cost of change orders triggered by inflation of building material cost was assessed.

ideas.idea: Off-site/prefabricated construction reduces exposure to inflation because centralized factory production allows bulk material purchasing at fixed prices, insulating the project from mid-project price volatility.
ideas.quote: the use of OSC enables bulk purchasing of materials, such as steel, which is highly susceptible to price fluctuations, further insulating projects from inflationary pressures. (Bulk purchasing agreements often come with fixed pricing, which protects against sudden price hikes.)

ideas.idea: OSC is positioned as a risk-mitigation strategy specifically for divisions most sensitive to price escalation, informing decisions on which scopes of work to prefabricate versus build conventionally.
ideas.quote: the divisions most affected by inflation (i.e., those with a high SC), such as metals and special construction, are good candidates to be studied using the OSC approach.

ideas.idea: Successful use of OSC to manage inflation risk depends on collaboration and mutual agreement among design-build teams, project management consultants, clients, and financial institutions, highlighting a multi-party contractual dynamic rather than a purely technical decision.
ideas.quote: various stakeholders, including the design and build team, project management consultants, clients, and financial institutions, mutually agreed on the OSC approach and collaborated closely to minimize the negative impact of inflation on the total project cost.

ideas.idea: OSC's controlled factory environment improves workforce stability and productivity, indirectly reducing schedule-related cost escalation that compounds with inflation.
ideas.quote: The controlled factory environment in OSC enables the use of a more stable and skilled workforce, further enhancing the efficiency and reliability of construction projects.

ideas.idea: Elemental cost analysis combined with inflation indices can be embedded into project budgeting and cash flow models at the outset, enabling proactive contract price adjustments rather than reliance on after-the-fact contingency claims.
ideas.quote: This model should predict price variations over time during the project’s initial stages, allowing for proactive budget adjustments, rather than relying on contingency costs for later modifications.

objectives: To develop a constraint programming based optimization approach that integrates logistics/supply chain data, contract-derived deadlines, and resource availability to generate optimal module assembly schedules that minimize total waiting time of prefabricated modules on the module yard.
problem_statement: Off-shore prefabrication and modular construction increasingly rely on complex, uncertain supply chains where modules are frequently delayed; existing subjective, experience-based scheduling approaches to manage limited assembly yard resources (crews and bays) are inefficient and lead to increased waiting waste and potential project delays, creating a need for a systematic optimization approach.
methodology: The study proposes a constraint programming (CP) based optimization framework combining three data sources—logistics management database (module arrival/supply information), construction contract documents (on-site demand/expected delivery deadlines), and crew/resource availability data. A mathematical model with an objective function (minimizing total module waiting time) and constraints (arrival time, delivery deadline, crew/resource limits) is formulated and solved using IBM ILOG CPLEX Optimization Studio V12.6. A case study abstracted from a real modular construction project in Alberta, Canada, involving 10 large modules assembled from 40 off-shore fabricated small modules, is used to test two supply-delay scenarios and demonstrate the framework's feasibility.
key_background_studies: Ballard and Howell (1998) - introduced lean construction concept underpinning the study's approach
Wu and Lu (2013) - documented benefits of modular construction in Northern Alberta oil sands projects
Choi and Song (2014) - described off-site fabrication, transportation and installation processes for modules
Koskela et al. (2002) - discussed balancing fabrication, transportation and installation to minimize waste
Tommelein et al. (2003) - explained contractor tendency to avoid just-in-time delivery due to delay risk, causing waste
Dubois and Gadde (2002) - noted difficulty of supply chain management in construction versus manufacturing
Liu and Lu (2016) - showed improvised scheduling strategies increase crew idling time and cause further delay
Liu and Wang (2012) - applied constraint programming to linear construction scheduling with multi-skilled crews
Menesi et al. (2013) - demonstrated constraint programming for time-cost trade-off in large-scale projects
findings: The proposed CP-based optimization framework successfully generated optimal assembly schedules (start/finish times) for 10 large modules under two supply-delay scenarios, yielding total waiting times of 298 days (Scenario 1) and 311 days (Scenario 2), demonstrating that supply delays increase idle waiting time for arrived small modules. The framework effectively integrates contract-derived delivery deadlines, logistics supply data, and crew/resource constraints to support decision-making, allowing project managers to update assembly plans dynamically as supply information changes, thereby reducing waiting waste and supporting both crew work planning and logistical planning.

ideas.idea: Contract documents are a key data source defining on-site demand deadlines that constrain module assembly scheduling.
ideas.quote: the pre-set field erection deadlines extracted from construction contract

ideas.idea: Expected delivery times specified in the contract impose hard constraints on when large modules must be finished, directly tying contractual deadlines to yard scheduling decisions.
ideas.quote: The expected delivery time for each large module is extracted from the contract document and listed in Table 3.

ideas.idea: Off-shore prefabrication introduces supply chain complexity and delay risk that contractual and logistical planning must jointly manage.
ideas.quote: As off-shore prefabrication continues to gain momentum, supply chain management becomes increasingly complex for industrial modular construction projects and delays commonly occur to prefabricated modules.

ideas.idea: Contractors tend to front-load delivery of prefabricated materials to mitigate late-delivery risk, which itself generates waste, reflecting a risk-averse contractual/practical response to supply uncertainty.
ideas.quote: instead of adopting a just-in-time (JIT) delivery method, the contractor tends to deliver the materials or pre-fabricated modules at the earliest time in order to mitigate the risk of late delivery

ideas.idea: Module assembly planning must reconcile uncertain off-site fabrication/shipping (an upstream, largely uncontracted process) with on-site demand requirements set by contract, requiring integration of logistics and contractual data.
ideas.quote: By synthesizing information from the logistics management system, contract documents, and resources availability, a constraint programming based optimization algorithm is proposed.

ideas.idea: Reliance on overseas vendors for module fabrication (due to labor cost and material sourcing) creates additional coordination and shipping-related contractual risk layers not present in traditional on-site construction.
ideas.quote: the engineering design and fabrication of modules are usually undertaken by overseas vendors in East Asia, such as South Korea, China

ideas.idea: Subjective, experience-based scheduling decisions made without systematic optimization tools can be contractually costly, increasing delay and idle time rather than mitigating it.
ideas.quote: decisions resulting from subjective experience often turn out to be less efficient and non-optimal... 'improvised' schedule strategies based on common sense to mitigate material delay would actually increase the crews' idling time and lead to further project delay.

objectives: To develop and empirically test a framework identifying which project delivery model (PDM)/collaboration form best overcomes process-related barriers in modular high-rise construction projects.
problem_statement: Although modular high-rise construction offers benefits, process-related barriers—especially lack of integration, cooperation, and communication among stakeholders—persist, and existing research has not examined which collaboration forms/PDMs suit modular high-rise projects.
methodology: Multiple holistic case study research using three international high-rise modular cases (The Fizz Spartaan, Amsterdam; CitizenM Bowery, New York; Mapleton Crescent SW18, London). Data collected via 10 semi-structured interviews with project managers/stakeholders, supplemented by documents and project materials; data analysed via template/open-axial-selective coding in Atlas.ti; PDM selection assessed using 17 criteria and spider-chart comparison (Hosseini et al. 2015; Hombergen et al. 2004).
key_background_studies: Blismas et al. (2005) – identified need for more intensive collaboration and communication, and client reluctance to commit to a single supplier as risk-averse behavior.
Wuni et al. (2019, 2020) – highlighted difficulty of early design freeze and key decision-making in modular projects.
Hosseini et al. (2015) – provided the 17 selection criteria framework for evaluating PDMs.
Jonsson and Rudberg (2014) – discussed modularity and organizational/process implications, and suitability of high-rise for modular methods.
Peltokorpi et al. (2018) – modularity as a concept explaining architecture of products, organizations, and processes.
De Ridder (2011) – proposed idea of a Product Delivery Model with standard contracts tied to modular products.
Hough and Lawson (2019) – discussed suitability of modular buildings for repetitive/cellular building types.
findings: No single PDM universally fits modular high-rise projects; the three cases each used a different PDM (Turnkey, Design-Bid-Built, Design & Build) depending on client characteristics such as willingness to be involved and to take risk. Traditional Design-Bid-Built is poorly suited due to late contractor involvement, whereas more integrated PDMs (ECI, Design & Build, Turnkey) better accommodate modular construction's need for early design freeze and execution knowledge during design. Clients generally wish to minimize execution responsibility and shift risk to contractors/suppliers. No case used long-term/serial tendering or framework agreements, despite modular construction benefiting from continuous improvement and long-term partnerships. The study concludes that current project-based PDMs may not truly meet modular concepts' needs, and a shift toward product-based delivery models with fixed partnerships would better serve modularization, though this requires a fundamentally different industry approach. Until then, the best match should be found by comparing client profiles (17 criteria) against PDM characteristics.

ideas.idea: Modular construction requires early design freeze and extensive pre-engineering before construction, shifting collaboration needs earlier than in conventional projects.
ideas.quote: An extensive pre-engineering at an early phase of the project is required in order to come to an ‘early design freeze’

ideas.idea: Managing the multidisciplinary integrated process across design and manufacturing is the biggest process-related barrier in modular construction.
ideas.quote: Managing this process is seen as the biggest process-related barrier to modular construction.

ideas.idea: Manufacturers should have a larger, more determining role during the design phase to align design with production constraints.
ideas.quote: One way to achieve this is by assigning a larger and more determining role of the manufacturer during the design phase.

ideas.idea: Selection of an appropriate Project Delivery Model (PDM) is central to project success, and no single PDM is a generic match for modular high-rise projects.
ideas.quote: it is not possible to reach a consensus directly from the collaboration forms used in this case studies.

ideas.idea: Traditional Design-Bid-Built contracts are poorly suited to modular construction because the design is often too advanced before tendering for optimization, creating conflict over responsibility for module assembly.
ideas.quote: In general, the traditional DBB model is not particularly well-suited to modular construction methods... this would always lead to discussion, as was in the CitizenM Bowery case.
