ideas.quote: Enterprises should not treat ER as a siloed activity but rather as a joint supply chain goal. Formal collaboration mechanisms, such as green procurement contracts or shared ER targets, can align efforts and reduce inefficiencies.

objectives: To develop and validate a text mining and risk-analysis based model that automatically extracts contractual obligations from the general conditions of a construction contract and quantifies the uncertainty/risk each obligation poses to project objectives (cost, schedule, quality, safety, environment), using the NSW GC21 contract as a case study.
problem_statement: Construction contracts, particularly the general conditions, are a major source of unbalanced risk-sharing between client and contractor, yet risks are not explicitly stated in the text and must be inferred; existing text-mining studies extract obligations or poisonous clauses but do not assess the overall risk balance of general conditions, leaving a gap in comparative risk quantification between parties.
methodology: A two-stage approach: (1) rule-based text mining using a lexicon of promisor-determiner nouns (PDN) and obligation-maker verbs (OMV) derived from FIDIC contracts, implemented in MATLAB Text Analytics Toolbox (POS tagging, preprocessing, tokenization, lemmatization, IF PDN+OMV THEN NP2 rule) to extract obligations from the NSW GC21 (2nd ed.) general conditions; (2) risk analysis using probability x impact scoring by 14 expert respondents across five project objectives, corrected by five lateral latent factors (proximity, controllability, manageability, dormancy, detectability) weighted via expert judgment; results validated against a two-round Delphi expert panel using Precision, Recall, and F-measure metrics.
key_background_studies: Hassan and Le (2020) - NLP/machine-learning rule-based framework to classify contract text into requirements/non-requirements using keyword lexicon, informing rule-based extraction approach.
Marzouk and Enaba (2019) - Three-tier system combining contract analysis, 5D BIM, and correspondence text mining; provided five-stage text mining approach adapted in this study.
Lee et al. (2019) - Model to extract 'poisonous clauses' risky to contractors using lexicon-based extraction rules across 11 risk types; compared as a related but narrower contribution.
Roshnavand et al. (2019) - Text mining method to identify ambiguity/confusion sources in modular construction contracts using NLTK; provided methodological precedent for contract text mining.
Gao et al. (2012) - Model to extract 'exceptions' (indemnities) from contracts using noun-phrase pattern extraction; contributed extraction methodology steps.

Chui and Bai (2010) - Content analysis categorizing general conditions into six categories (rights/obligations, process, quality, cost, administration, others) comparing AIA and Chinese standard forms.
Manderson et al. (2015) - Analyzed general conditions content across ten thematic areas including risk allocation and BIM adaptation.
William and Ashley (1987) - Analyzed >90 clauses across two contract types on six performance indices, showing risk distribution between owners and contractors.
Zou et al. (2007) - Provided the risk analysis methodology (probability x impact) adapted for scoring obligation importance against project objectives.
findings: The model extracted 109 main contractual obligations from GC21 general conditions (76 contractor, 33 principal), achieving Precision 81.55%, Recall 77.06%, F-measure 79.25% against expert panel validation. Risk analysis identified the ten most critical obligations (e.g., paying advance payment, notifying non-compliance with codes, paying scheduled amounts, providing site information, notifying faults in contract documents, design-related duties, site access) that most affect project objectives. Obligation sharing was found fairer for cost and schedule objectives but unequal for quality, safety, and environmental objectives, with the contractor bearing the majority (about 69.7% of total obligations) while the principal's top obligations carried about 15% more importance on average. The study concludes that general conditions clauses vary greatly in importance and that early identification of high-risk obligations can support more balanced contract drafting, tendering, and claims management.

ideas.idea: Most construction contracts are drafted unilaterally by the client/owner without contractor input, which shapes the risk-sharing pattern embedded in the general conditions.
ideas.quote: Studies show that >70% of construction contracts are prepared by the business owner, without any consultation with or contribution from the contractor (Zaghloul and Hartman 2003).

ideas.idea: Risk should be allocated to the party best able to manage it, otherwise unmanaged risk increases costs and schedule overruns.
ideas.quote: previous research underlined that each risk should be assigned to the party who could manage it best (Tao 1994). Otherwise, the consequences of the risk will increase and the project will face cost and time overruns

ideas.idea: The general conditions document is the principal legal instrument for allocating risk, rights and obligations between contracting parties and is a key source of project uncertainty if not clearly drafted.
ideas.quote: The principal legal platform for risk-sharing in a construction contract is the general conditions that have an unexampled role to reduce project uncertainty if they have been drafted clearly (Bubshait and Almohawis 1994).

ideas.idea: Standard forms of contract (e.g., FIDIC, AIA, GC21) promote fairness in risk-sharing, save drafting time/cost, and provide a reliable tendering basis compared to bespoke contracts.
ideas.quote: The use of standard forms of agreement leads to fairness in sharing risks between two parties, facilitates risk management, and establishes a reliable basis for bids during tendering.

ideas.idea: Contract clauses are not equally important; they can be classified into conditions, warranties, and innominate terms based on consequences of breach, and the study focuses on conditions as the main source of obligations.
ideas.quote: The conditions, which are recognized as essential terms... The focal point of this study was the conditions that are the main source of the obligations of the client and the contractor.

ideas.idea: Disclaimer or risk-transferring clauses that shift unpredictable risk onto one party can significantly increase contract costs and negatively affect tendering and claims.
ideas.quote: transferring the unpredictable risks to one party using contractual terms, such as disclaimer clauses that could increase the contract costs between 8% and 20%

ideas.idea: A text-mining lexicon approach (promisor nouns + obligation verbs) can systematically extract contractual obligations, offering a scalable way to analyze how standard contracts assign responsibilities between parties.
ideas.quote: IF ‘promisor + verb’ THEN ‘obligation’; in other words: IF ‘PDN + OMV’ THEN ‘NP2’

ideas.idea: Obligations related to site access, site information provision, and design responsibilities are among the highest-risk clauses affecting schedule and quality objectives, highlighting critical handover and design-review responsibilities in project delivery.
ideas.quote: Granting the contractor access rights to the site proportionate to the work and following the agreed schedule is one of the major commitments of the client. Any delay or deficiency in this activity delays the critical chain of the project schedule

ideas.idea: Distribution of high-risk obligations between contractor and principal is unequal, with the contractor bearing a much larger share of significant obligations, indicating imbalance in standard general conditions.
ideas.quote: the mentioned ratio, for 109 main clauses was 69.7% for the contractor and 30.3% for the principal.

ideas.idea: Beyond probability and impact, lateral latent factors such as controllability, manageability, dormancy, proximity, and detectability materially change the relative risk ranking of contractual obligations, refining understanding of how risks should be managed contractually.
ideas.quote: there are lateral latent (LL) factors for the robust prioritization of risks, such as urgency, manageability, and controllability

ideas.idea: A risk-balanced analysis of general conditions can inform practical contract strategy for both clients and contractors during tendering, drafting, and administration phases.
ideas.quote: the drafting party could assess the contract risk balance to evaluate the general terms and conditions; the contractor could adjust the bid markup and cover the risk exposure during tendering; and the client could ensure that the contract clauses were designed in a balanced manner

objectives: To explore the impact of emerging off-site/industrialized construction technologies (bathroom pods) on construction subcontractors in Australia using the resource based view (RBV) of the firm as a theoretical lens, in order to understand which subcontractor resources are affected and how subcontractors should adapt strategically.
problem_statement: While much research has examined the impacts of industrialized construction/off-site prefabrication on the construction sector generally, there has been little research into its impacts specifically on subcontractors, who operate at the coalface of the industry and face different innovation challenges than larger firms due to their smaller scale and limited resources.
methodology: Qualitative exploratory study using semi-structured interviews with senior executives/directors of six major subcontracting firms (hydraulic, mechanical, electrical trades) in Australia who had worked with off-site bathroom pod technology in residential high-rise projects. Non-probability snowball sampling was used to identify subcontractors experienced with pods. Data were analysed using Leximancer software (automated computational linguistics/concept mapping) combined with narrative analysis of interview transcripts, organized around RBV resource categories (financial, physical, human, intellectual, social, organizational).
key_background_studies: Barney (1991) - foundational RBV theory defining firm resources and sustainable competitive advantage criteria
Gibb and Isack (2003) - hierarchical model of industrialization levels and need for supply chain coordination
Blismas and Wakefield (2009) - drivers, constraints and future of off-site manufacture in Australia, including labour and skills impacts
Koebel et al. (2004) - innovation diffusion in US residential building market, adopter types and firm characteristics
Sexton et al. (2008) - subcontractors' limited resources and technology intensity compared to larger firms
Goulding et al. (2014) - differing adaptability of design/manufacturing stakeholders versus subcontractors to off-site prefabrication
Lu and Liska (2008) - barriers to off-site prefabrication adoption including design inflexibility and skills gaps among on-site workers
Pan et al. (2008) - survey of UK house builders on quality drivers and barriers (cost) for off-site prefabrication, including bathroom/kitchen pods
Loosemore (2014) - industrialization creating winners and losers, disrupting power and reward structures in construction
Barrett et al. (2008) - RBV as resource-push view of construction innovation, relevant to SMEs/subcontractors
findings: The key subcontractor resources affected by bathroom pod adoption are human, financial, intellectual and social resources, while physical and organizational resources were less impacted at this stage. Financial impacts varied by trade (hydraulic subcontractors negatively affected due to loss of scope/materials income, mechanical/electrical more positively affected); competition and traditional subcontract power structures meant savings were often passed up to head contractors rather than retained by subcontractors. Human resources saw reduced numbers of lower-skilled tradesmen but stable management staffing, with new coordination/logistics skills required and concerns about deskilling, apprentice training gaps, and worker motivation in factory settings. Intellectual resources became more important for competitive advantage, with firms adopting different knowledge retention strategies (codification vs. tacit/family knowledge). Social resources/collaboration needs increased significantly, particularly early design involvement and new relationships with manufacturers, though these remained project-based rather than long-term strategic partnerships. Organizational and physical resource impacts were currently minimal, reflecting an early adoption stage. Overall, respondents' experiences were predominantly negative, consistent with prospect theory's loss aversion, but authors conclude industrialization creates opportunities for subcontractors who strategically adapt resource management and pursue collaborative supply chain partnerships.

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication (pods) shifts value and scope of work away from subcontractors, reducing their financial capture even when cost savings are generated.
ideas.quote: Competition is so high we don’t get to retain any of the savings or indirect cost benefits for ourselves. We still end up making the same margin as per usual because everyone just passes the cost savings along.

ideas.idea: Traditional subcontract structures and head contractor power result in savings/benefits from off-site methods being passed up the contracting chain rather than retained by subcontractors.
ideas.quote: in contrast to the relational contracts found in other industries that effectively use OSM (Helper and Henderson 2014), our respondents were hampered by traditional subcontracts which resulted in rewards being passed up the line to head contractors. Until this is resolve the incentive to collaborate will not exist.

ideas.idea: Successful implementation of off-site prefabrication requires high levels of supply chain coordination among designers, manufacturers, and constructors, which is often lacking under current contractual arrangements.
ideas.quote: Gibb and Isack (2003) highlight the need for high levels of supply chain co-ordination between designers, developers, builders, manufacturers and suppliers to enable the benefits of off-site prefabrication to be fully realized.

ideas.idea: Early subcontractor involvement in design and prototyping of prefabricated components is beneficial but is not always reflected in what is delivered, causing communication breakdowns that hinder project success.
ideas.quote: respondents noted that pod designs agreed was not always what arrived on-site, a breakdown in communication which hindered project success and new relationships between subcontractor, head contractor and the pod manufacturer.

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication changes risk allocation for subcontractors, removing traditional sources of income (materials/labour margin) without corresponding adjustment in contract pricing or risk allowance.
ideas.quote: When you take the bathrooms away we then have to make the money on the labour and when it is priced into the materials as a flat rate there is no risk allowance in there. We always lose money on labour, so it going to be a real issue.

ideas.idea: Off-site methods can increase competition among subcontractors by lowering barriers to entry for firms that would not normally bid on larger jobs, intensifying price competition.
ideas.quote: what it [pods] has done is open the door for a lot of other companies that wouldn’t normally look at a big job can now look at the jobs and it will increase competition and the race to the bottom.

ideas.idea: New collaborative relationships and joint ventures with manufacturers are needed to help subcontractors adapt to off-site technologies, but these remain project-based rather than long-term strategic partnerships as seen in other industries.
ideas.quote: our results suggest that these social resources are currently project-based and not held as long-term cooperative strategic relationships.

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication requires early design freeze, which conflicts with the industry's traditional practice of allowing design changes throughout construction, creating contractual and coordination challenges.
ideas.quote: inflexibility of design was a major challenge because off-site prefabrication requires and an early design freeze, whereas the industry has become accustomed to projects progressing with incomplete designs which involve numerous changes and adaptions throughout construction.

ideas.idea: Joint product development between subcontractors, manufacturers and other supply chain participants is identified as key to successful transition to off-site technology, echoing practices in other industries.
ideas.quote: Asanuma (1989), McMillan (1990), Turnbull et al. (1992), McIvor et al. (1998), Subrahmanya (2008) and Helper and Henderson (2014) all support joint product development as a key to the successful transition into off-site technology in other industries.

objectives: To clarify the real meaning and relevance of collaboration for digital transformation in the construction industry, exploring what collaboration looks like in practice on digitalized construction projects.
problem_statement: The term 'collaboration' is vague and inconsistently defined across disciplines and in construction industry gray literature, policy documents, and standards, with no grounded theoretical framework underpinning its use; this creates a gap in understanding what collaboration actually means and how it operates in real-world digitalized construction projects.
methodology: Exploratory qualitative study using content analysis of literature, standards, and guidelines, combined with 13 open-ended semistructured interviews with AEC industry experts (middle and senior management) selected via snowball sampling. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using open, axial, and selective coding in NVivo to generate concept and project maps and themes.
key_background_studies: Hughes et al. (2012) - provides a construction-specific definition of collaboration emphasizing team-based, non-adversarial relationships achieved through appropriate contracts
Schöttle et al. (2014) - defines collaboration as formation of joint project organization with shared risks/rewards and interorganizational trust
Bedwell et al. (2012) - human resources management definition of collaboration as joint activity toward project goals
Hartono and Holsapple (2004) - information systems definition emphasizing participatory, knowledge-based process
Vosman et al. (2023) - discusses collaboration for resilience and contingency planning in infrastructure projects
Ganeshu et al. (2024) - discusses cultural shift from hierarchical to collaborative organizational culture
Xue et al. (2010) - emphasizes behaviors like trust, tension, conflict, incentives influencing AEC project performance
Bouwen and Taillieu (2004) - foundational work on multiple parties' involvement in collaboration
Verheij and Augenbroe (2006) - work on workflows in collaborative processes
Creswell and Poth (2016) - methodological basis for qualitative coding and grounded theory approach
findings: The study identified key themes: collaboration is defined by multiple parties' involvement and workflows in place; collaborative behaviors within alliance/integrated project delivery are characterized by self-managing teams and open-mindedness toward problem resolution; appropriate procurement strategy is associated with the importance of collaboration; technology (BIM, email, cloud environments, Microsoft Teams) is confirmed by all experts as facilitating smooth collaborative workflows; and personality traits integrated into the BIM process emerged as the most influential interdependency for realizing collaboration in project teams.

ideas.idea: Collaboration is closely tied to procurement strategy and contract type, with certain forms of contracts (partnering, alliancing, integrated project delivery) sharing the objective of shared pain/gain among stakeholders.
ideas.quote: partnering, alliancing, and integrated project delivery contracts share the same objective (Hughes et al. 2012): all stakeholders in project teams share both the pain and the gain associated with ultimate project performance

ideas.idea: An appropriate procurement strategy is seen by experts as improving the importance of collaboration on projects.
ideas.quote: 4 out of 13 experts believed that an appropriate procurement strategy seemingly improves the importance of collaboration, which again echoes the existing studies (Eriksson 2017; Akintan and Morledge 2013).

ideas.idea: Collaboration requires a shift from hierarchical decision-making to team-based decision-making where risks and rewards are equally distributed, reflecting a 'best for project' rather than 'best for me' mentality.
ideas.quote: creating a collaborative team where risks and rewards are equally distributed and no decision is made from the hierarchical fashion, and the ultimate decision is changing from best for me to best for project.

ideas.idea: The construction-specific definition of collaboration emphasizes non-adversarial team-based working achieved through the use of appropriate contracts, early involvement of key members, and mutual respect of roles and responsibilities.
ideas.quote: The UK construction sector encourages team-based collaboration that is nonadversarial, where key members are involved early in the process and everyone understands and respects the input of others, their role, and their responsibilities. This is achieved by using the appropriate contract.

ideas.idea: Collaboration in construction involves shared responsibilities, risks, and rewards among participants through interactive, jointly planned processes.
ideas.quote: To maximize the value for the customer, the study aimed to resolve problems mutually through interactive processes that are planned together, and shared responsibilities, risks, and rewards of each participant.

ideas.idea: Self-managing teams and open-mindedness toward problem resolution are the most important collaborative behaviors within alliance work and integrated project delivery, reflecting how contractual/organizational structures shape team autonomy in resolving disputes.
ideas.quote: two themes, i.e., self-managing teams and open-mindedness toward problem resolution, emerged as the most important

ideas.idea: Technology (BIM, cloud environments, communication platforms) is considered a critical enabler of collaborative workflows in digitalized construction projects, which has implications for how contracts should address technology-driven coordination.
ideas.quote: collectively all the experts confirmed that building information modeling (BIM) and email communications, cloud environment and Microsoft Teams facilitated smooth collaborative workflows.

ideas.idea: The personality traits of team members integrated into the BIM process are seen as the most influential interdependency for realizing collaboration, suggesting that human factors interact with digital/contractual processes.
ideas.quote: the most influential theme that emerged was members’ personality traits integrated into the BIM process, which aligns with most studies (Bond-Barnard et al. 2018; Ekung et al. 2015).

objectives: To examine, through observation of two California offsite construction companies, six foundational supply chain management (SCM) perspectives and to propose an outline for a supply chain integration theory that can guide construction companies in realizing the potential of offsite construction projects.
problem_statement: Offsite construction adds complexity to SCM due to the aggregation of parts and materials into building components in offsite facilities, yet construction supply chains remain fragmented, weakly integrated, and prone to myopic, locally optimized decisions. There is a lack of empirical studies on how different companies integrate their supply chains for offsite construction, and no robust theoretical framework exists to guide firms in leveraging SCM strategies for offsite construction's full potential.
methodology: An inductive, case-based theoretical study (following Eisenhardt, 1989) using the Observation-Participation Method, in which the authors—drawing on professional experience and established relationships—directly observed, participated in, and conducted informal interviews with project management teams at two California-based construction companies (Company A and Company B) employing distinct supply chain integration approaches (a 'One Company Policy' portfolio model vs. internal vertical integration). Data were synthesized across six SCM perspectives: target project type, contract type, business strategy, production management methods, SCM practices, and organizational culture.
key_background_studies: Vrijhoef & Koskela (2000) - defined four roles of SCM in construction and highlighted fragmentation and myopic decision-making as central problems
Christopher (2005) - foundational definition of supply chain as a network producing value for end-users
Ballard & Howell (1998) - Last Planner System and lean construction concepts relevant to workflow variation and JIT
Green et al. (2005) - explained slow SCM adoption in construction due to industry fragmentation
Hall et al. (2022) - identified vertical integration as a business strategy enabling coordination of design, manufacturing, transport, and assembly

Lessing & Brege (2018) - argued that high performance in offsite construction requires both internal integration and external supply chain collaboration; introduced Industrialized Construction concept
Prado (2022) - introduced an Operations Management-based integration framework for offsite construction focusing on JIT delivery
Prado & Tommelein (2023) - examined offsite-manufactured facade installation linking production metrics to project cost/schedule
Zhang & Fischer (2024) - optimized inventory levels integrating fabrication and installation planning via Operations Science
Tommelein & Li (1999) - showed Value Stream Mapping enhances JIT delivery for concrete components
Cossio & Cossio (2012) - demonstrated time/cost savings from transitioning facade delivery to offsite via JIT, despite stakeholder resistance
findings: Company A (project-centric, design-build with subcontracted factory under a 'One Company Policy') offers project adaptability and early design input but suffers from separated profit centers, limited production transparency, and late design changes disrupting factory operations. Company B (product-centric, vertically integrated) achieves standardization, repeatability, and JIT delivery efficiency but faces internal fragmentation between engineering/PM and manufacturing departments and reduced flexibility under hard-bid contracts. Comparing six SCM perspectives yields takeaways emphasizing the need to balance customization with scalability, adopt flexible collaborative contracts, combine project- and product-centric strategies, integrate lean and operations management practices, enhance transparency via real-time information exchange, and foster collaborative cross-departmental culture. The study proposes a three-insight theory outline: (1) hybrid business strategy combining project-centric adaptability with product-centric standardization; (2) integration of lean production (offsite) with lean construction (onsite); (3) integrated teams bridging onsite PM and offsite manufacturing. Key enablers include collaborative contracting, digital integration, and cooperative organizational culture. The theory outline requires future empirical validation.

ideas.idea: Traditional subcontracting arrangements between contractors and offsite factories create financial and organizational separation that leads to misaligned incentives and poor information flow, causing late design changes that disrupt factory operations.
ideas.quote: Due to minimal communication during manufacturing, project teams frequently introduce late changes to safeguard project profitability, leading to disruptions in factory operations.

ideas.idea: Design-build contracts with the client combined with lump-sum subcontracts with the offsite factory reinforce financial and operational separation between project and factory teams.
ideas.quote: Typically, the contractor team engages in a design-build contract with the owner and a lump sum contract with the factory, reinforcing their financial and operational separation.

ideas.idea: Hard-bid contracts with early design integration can create internal fragmentation between engineering/PM departments and manufacturing, reducing repeatability and profitability.
ideas.quote: the engineering and project management teams have the "power" to propose fluctuations in the manufacturing and engineering budget to provide "solutions" to the client. This situation can lead to reducing repeatability during manufacturing

ideas.idea: Traditional subcontracting models shift risk to subcontractors and hinder supply chain integration, indicating a need for more collaborative contract frameworks.
ideas.quote: Traditional subcontracting models shift risks to subcontractors, often hindering integration. A transparent, collaboration-driven contract framework is essential to aligning stakeholder incentives across the supply chain.

ideas.idea: Flexible, collaborative contract types are recommended to encourage integration and transparency across the offsite supply chain, contrasting with rigid design-build or hard-bid structures.
ideas.quote: Adopt flexible, collaborative contracts to encourage integration and transparency

ideas.idea: Relational contracts can foster collaboration and reduce adversarial dynamics compared to traditional subcontracting in offsite construction.
ideas.quote: Relational contracts foster collaboration, reducing adversarial dynamics in traditional subcontracting.

ideas.idea: Vertical integration as a business strategy consolidates upstream and downstream processes (design, manufacturing, construction) within a single firm, redefining traditional contractual and operational boundaries.
ideas.quote: By bringing in-house design, construction, and manufacturing, offsite construction firms redefine operational boundaries (Eldamnhoury & Hanna, 2020).

ideas.idea: Lack of visibility and transparency into offsite production processes for the client and GC, resulting from subcontracting structures, hinders collaboration and process integration.
ideas.quote: As a result, both the client and the GC have limited visibility into the offsite production process during manufacturing, which can hinder collaboration and process integration.

ideas.idea: Just-in-time (JIT) delivery of prefabricated components from factory to site reduces onsite risk and time, improving project profitability, but requires buffer planning between manufacturing and erection rates.
ideas.quote: Company B prefers a JIT delivery of the prefabricated components from the plant to the project site as it allows to avoid any issue with these components within the job site and also reduces the time spent on the job site

ideas.idea: Achieving high performance in offsite construction requires both internal integration and external supply chain collaboration, not one alone.
ideas.quote: These findings reinforce the argument by Lessing and Brege (2018) that achieving high performance in offsite construction requires both internal integration and external supply chain collaboration.

ideas.idea: A hybrid contractual and business strategy balancing project-centric flexibility with product-centric standardization is proposed as a way to manage contractual and delivery challenges in offsite construction.
ideas.quote: Combine project-centric flexibility with product-centric efficiency for a hybrid business strategy

ideas.idea: Digital technologies (BIM, digital twins, blockchain) can support contractual and operational integration by enabling real-time information exchange between onsite and offsite parties.
ideas.quote: Seamless coordination between offsite and onsite operations requires digital technologies to facilitate real-time information exchange, reducing communication delays and enhancing efficiency.

ideas.idea: Responsibility for issues arising from external designers' input is sometimes borne by the offsite manufacturer even when the fault originates elsewhere, affecting profitability and risk allocation.
ideas.quote: Unfortunately, when there are issues from other parties that input data into Company B's scope of work (external designers), company B takes responsibility for these issues, and this sometimes generates less profitable results.

objectives: To investigate dispute causation in modular construction projects by (1) determining the most common causes leading to disputes, (2) categorizing the causes based on their interconnectivities, and (3) identifying and quantifying key associations among causes that trigger disputes.
problem_statement: Contractual risks and disputes remain a top factor affecting modular construction performance, yet existing dispute-causation research focuses on traditional construction and fails to address the unique and complex sources of disputes associated with modularization, including the interconnectivities among causal factors.
methodology: An integrated multistep analytical approach using 39 publicly available US legal cases of modular construction disputes collected via Google Scholar. A binary reference matrix of causes versus cases was built, then transformed into a weighted adjacency matrix for social network analysis (degree centrality, network density) to identify common causes; spectral clustering (using silhouette score to determine optimal k=4) grouped 40 causes into four clusters; association rule analysis with the Apriori algorithm (support, confidence, lift thresholds) plus Fisher's exact test identified statistically significant associations of causes within each cluster.
key_background_studies: Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2021) - identified contractual risks and disputes as a top factor affecting cost/schedule performance of modular projects
Arashphour et al. (2017) - considered contractual problems and disputes as a challenge to integrating offsite technologies
Azghandi-Roshnavand (2019) - noted disputes become more critical with modular methods due to unique complex requirements
Kumar Viswanathan et al. (2020) - highlighted limited work on associations/interconnectivities among dispute causal factors and poor communication as key factor
Love et al. (2008) - argued effective dispute minimization requires examining associations, not just identifying causes
Woodley (2019) - stated disputes arise from complex interplay of multiple factors, not single causes
Cakmak and Cakmak (2014), Jahren and Dammeier (1990), Chan and Suen (2005) - documented payment and completion delays as severe dispute causes in general construction
Said (2015) - noted higher cost implications of design/scope changes and labor union issues in modular construction
Choi and Song (2014) - highlighted higher design and engineering requirements in modular construction versus stick-built
Alwisy et al. (2012) - emphasized importance of accounting for onsite conditions early in module design
Duncheva and Bradley (2019) - linked unclear building codes/specifications for modular products to rework and delays
Jaillon and Poon (2010) - stressed early collaboration and coordination of project participants in modular design/construction stages
findings: The four most common causes of disputes in modular construction were payment holds/delays, lack of collaboration between trades, delay in project completion, and poor communication. Network density was 83.8%, indicating disputes are typically triggered by multiple co-occurring causes rather than a single cause. The 40 causes were grouped into four clusters with significant associations: Cluster 1 (design errors, excessive design/scope changes, delays in design completion); Cluster 2 (time extensions, onsite delays, unforeseen site conditions, resource shortages, negligence); Cluster 3 (defective modules, misalignment with codes/specifications, inadequate bidding, payment holds); Cluster 4 (starting construction with incomplete design, lack of collaboration among trades). These findings suggest specific contractual and managerial adjustments needed to mitigate modular construction disputes.

ideas.idea: Modular construction requires new or adjusted contractual models and processes not needed in traditional construction, including addressing lead-time requirements for module delivery.
ideas.quote: For instance, Wong et al. (2017) highlighted the need to address lead-time requirements associated with the delivery of the modules in the project contractual conditions.

ideas.idea: Modular projects need clear contractual continuity across assessment, selection, and design phases to avoid disconnects that cause disputes.
ideas.quote: the success of modular construction projects requires avoiding disconnects in any contractual transition existing between assessment, selection, basic design, or detailed design phases (O’Connor et al. 2014).

ideas.idea: A lack of customized standard contract forms and clear project standards for modular construction is a major contractual/legal challenge contributing to disputes.
ideas.quote: modular construction is associated with many contractual and legal challenges, including the lack of clear project standards and integration strategies as well as the lack of customized standard forms of contracts (Fateh et al. 2017).

ideas.idea: Payment holds/delays and project completion delays are the most common and significant causes of disputes in modular projects, consistent with traditional construction but exacerbated by offsite processes.
ideas.quote: the most common causes of disputes in modular construction projects include C4 (payment holds and delays), C19 (lack of collaboration between various project trades), C2 (delay in project completion), and C38 (poor communication between project participants).

ideas.idea: Poor communication and lack of collaboration between trades are recognized as major barriers to modular construction implementation, and improving them helps prevent disputes.
ideas.quote: the lack of proper communication and collaboration among project stakeholders has been considered one of the main barriers to the implementation of modular construction (Hamzeh et al. 2017).

ideas.idea: Design errors, excessive scope/design changes, and delayed design completion are strongly associated with disputes, and late design changes are especially costly in modular construction due to fabrication commitments.
ideas.quote: higher cost implications are associated with design and scope of work changes in modular construction projects as compared to traditional stick-built methods.

ideas.idea: Early design freeze and adequate allocation of design/engineering lead time are success factors that also reduce dispute likelihood in modular projects.
ideas.quote: early freeze of the design as well as appropriate allocation of design and engineering lead times are considered success factors for modular construction projects (Rahman 2014; Choi et al. 2016).

ideas.idea: Modularization does not eliminate risks from unforeseen site conditions, and contractors' technical capability to manage both offsite and onsite work is critical to avoiding disputes.
ideas.quote: the results show that the modular construction method does not completely eliminate the risks associated with unforeseen site conditions that can lead to disputes and conflicts among the project stakeholders.

ideas.idea: Inadequate bidding/tendering practices combined with misalignment to applicable building codes and specifications for modules are linked to disputes, highlighting a regulatory gap for modular products.
ideas.quote: the lack of clear and unambiguous building regulations and specifications for modular construction is highly associated with rework, drawing revisions, and delays in modular construction projects (Duncheva and Bradley 2019).

ideas.idea: Starting construction with incomplete design (a factor more critical to modular than traditional construction) combined with poor trade collaboration is a key trigger of disputes, underscoring the need for early contractor involvement.
ideas.quote: it is crucial to ensure (1) early involvement of the contractor/supplier/manufacturer in the project; and (2) improved coordination and synchronization between the design team, onsite work, and offsite work.

ideas.idea: Certain dispute causes are unique to modularization (e.g., labor union issues from offsite/out-of-state labor, starting construction before design completion, and interfacing defects between modules), distinguishing modular disputes from traditional stick-built disputes.
ideas.quote: some of the causal factors are unique to modularization, particularly C22 (labor union–related issues)... Another example is C14 (starting construction with incomplete design)... Another causal factor is C34 (interfacing defects).

ideas.idea: Disputes in modular construction are generally caused by multiple co-occurring factors rather than single causes, implying standard contracts should address combinations of interacting risks rather than isolated issues.
ideas.quote: the findings reflected that modular construction disputes are mostly triggered by the occurrence of multiple causes rather than by just a single cause.

objectives: To identify and quantify the key risks affecting cost and schedule performance of modular construction projects, and to examine how these risks are perceived by different project stakeholders (owners, consultants, general contractors, subcontractors).
problem_statement: While modular construction offers well-documented benefits over traditional stick-built construction, lack of understanding and management of unique modular risks leads to suboptimal cost and schedule performance. Prior research has focused on barriers/drivers of modular adoption or specific risk aspects (e.g., tolerances, supply chain), but no study had comprehensively analyzed the key risks impacting cost and schedule performance across stakeholder groups.
methodology: A multistep quantitative survey-based methodology: (1) a list of 50 modular risk factors identified from a prior systematic literature review was used to build an online Qualtrics survey rating likelihood of occurrence and cost/schedule impact on a 5-point CII Likert scale; (2) survey distributed to 190 US construction professionals, 48 valid responses (25.26% response rate) analyzed; (3) Cronbach's alpha reliability test; (4) risk rating calculation (likelihood x impact); (5) Kendall's concordance analysis (chi-squared) to test agreement within stakeholder groups; (6) one-way ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests to compare risk perceptions across stakeholder groups.
key_background_studies: Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2020) - conducted the systematic literature review that identified the 50 modular risk factors used as the basis for this study's survey
Enshassi et al. (2019, 2020a, 2020b) - developed risk management frameworks for tolerance and geometric variability issues in modular construction
Luo et al. (2019) - used social network analysis to study offsite supply chain risk networks in Hong Kong
Arashpour et al. (2017) - conducted risk analysis of infrastructure/hybrid projects covering onsite, coordination and offsite dimensions
CII (2014) - identified critical success enablers for modularization in industrialized projects
Abotaleb et al. (2019) - risk-based approach examining causes of out-of-sequence work and owner/contractor alignment
Russell et al. (2013) - examined causes of time buffers and stakeholder perception differences, informing this study's methodological approach
O'Connor et al. (2014) - highlighted modularization benefits and design principles for successful modular projects
Nadim and Goulding (2011) - discussed contractual and collaborative barriers to modular construction adoption
findings: Eight risk factors were found common to both cost and schedule performance: shortage of skilled/experienced laborers, late design changes, poor site attributes and logistics, unsuitability of design for modularization, contractual risks and disputes, lack of adequate collaboration and coordination, challenges related to tolerances and interfaces, and poor construction activity sequencing/management. Shortage of skilled labor and late design changes ranked as the top two risks for both cost and schedule. Environmental and safety risks were least critical. Significant misalignment existed among stakeholders on 32% of cost risk ratings and 36% of schedule risk ratings, indicating differing risk perceptions across owners, consultants, contractors and subcontractors, underscoring the need for collaborative risk assessment.

ideas.idea: Contractual risks and disputes are among the most critical factors affecting both cost and schedule performance in modular projects, ranking fifth for cost and seventh for schedule.
ideas.quote: Contractual risks and disputes (R47) were perceived by the respondents to be highly critical to cost performance (ranked fifth) and schedule performance (ranked seventh) of modular construction projects.

ideas.idea: Standard contracts and contractual terms need to be specifically adapted to address unique modular construction characteristics such as lead-time requirements for module delivery and collaborative agreements.
ideas.quote: The contractual terms should take into consideration unique modularization characteristics such as those related to lead-time requirements associated with the delivery of the modules and the need for collaborative agreements in offsite construction (Wong et al. 2017; Nadim and Goulding 2011).

ideas.idea: The criticality of contractual risk is heightened in modular construction because new processes and contractual models are needed to fit the method's requirements.
ideas.quote: However, the criticality of such factor is amplified when implementing modular construction methods due to the need for new processes and contractual models that meet the requirements of the construction method (Nadim and Goulding 2011).

ideas.idea: Late design changes are especially damaging in modular projects because early manufacturing start and design inflexibility limit the ability to accommodate change orders, making design freeze a critical success factor.
ideas.quote: In fact, inflexibility of modular design (Zhai et al. 2014) and the necessity for early initiation of modules manufacturing (Blismas and Wakefield 2009) hinders the ability to handle change orders and onsite modifications.

ideas.idea: Poor site attributes and logistics require extensive front-end planning covering site accessibility, storage capacity, and soil conditions, which is a critical driver of successful modular delivery.
ideas.quote: In fact, successful implementation of modular methods requires extensive front-end planning which considers all the previously mentioned site attributes.

ideas.idea: Design suitability for modularization must be established during the design phase using modular design principles, otherwise cost and schedule issues will follow, implying a need for early integrated design coordination across delivery participants.
ideas.quote: To ensure successful modular construction projects, modular design principles should be adopted during the design phase (O’Connor et al. 2014). Otherwise, schedule- and cost-related issues are expected in the project.

ideas.idea: Lack of collaboration and coordination among stakeholders (design, procurement, logistics) is a major barrier to modular construction and negatively affects both cost and schedule outcomes, pointing to the need for collaborative procurement/contractual arrangements.
ideas.quote: Collaboration and coordination among project stakeholders is documented to have a positive impact on modular construction projects by establishing a collaborative procurement method (Zhai et al. 2014), better coordinating shipments from subcontractor and/or contractor warehouses to the site, and improving the coordination of material inventory requirements (Said 2015).

ideas.idea: Tolerance and interface management between modules and onsite elements is a critical technical/contractual issue requiring skilled manufacturers and careful interface design to avoid cost and schedule impacts.
ideas.quote: Therefore, it is important to mitigate such challenges by ensuring appropriate management of the interfaces between the different main components during the design phase, having a manufacturer that is skilled in tight-tolerance modular fabrications, and avoiding small modules with excessive interfaces (O’Connor et al. 2014; Isaac et al. 2016).

ideas.idea: Synchronizing offsite fabrication schedules with onsite construction activity sequencing is essential; delays in either location cascade into schedule delays and cost overruns, highlighting the interdependence of parties and need for coordinated scheduling provisions.
ideas.quote: Therefore, scheduling and planning of construction work at the factory (off site) and on site should be connected and synchronized in modular construction projects to avoid schedule delays and cost overruns (Taghaddos et al. 2014).

ideas.idea: There is significant misalignment among owners, consultants, contractors and subcontractors regarding which risks are most critical, suggesting that contract frameworks should promote shared understanding and risk allocation among parties.
ideas.quote: The results also revealed significant misalignment among project stakeholders in terms of the risks most affecting the performance of their modular construction projects... Therefore, all project stakeholders should work collaboratively to enhance their alignment and minimize the impacts of such risks on their modular projects.

objectives: To develop and validate an automatic decentralized management framework that uses image-based deep learning to detect construction progress, a simulation model to derive risk-based smart contract stipulations, and a web3.js-based decentralized application (dApp) to synchronize detection results and automate smart contract execution in construction.
problem_statement: Smart contracts enabled by blockchain hold promise for automating construction management stipulations (payments, quality checks, scheduling), but they cannot inherently interact with real-world data, and current smart contract applications lack governance mechanisms and validated methods to integrate as-built progress data. It is unclear how to represent as-built data in blockchain, design governance mechanisms to minimize delay, and coordinate as-built data to decentralize smart contract execution.
methodology: A case study of a 33-floor high-rise building constructed under an EPC delivery method. Unordered images of critical path activities were collected on a standard floor, labeled, and augmented (1,492 original images expanded via TensorFlow augmentation to 7,210 training/1,492 testing images) to train a convolutional neural network classifying activity completion status; a Bayesian network refined predictions using schedule prerequisites. A discrete-event simulation (ARENA) using fitted productivity distributions modeled 570 delay/workforce scenarios on the critical path, with Gaussian mixture model clustering used to categorize risk levels (tolerable, recoverable, intolerable, unrecoverable) and identify optimal mitigation policies (workforce reassignment, penalties). These outputs were coded into Solidity smart contracts, compiled via Truffle, deployed on a Ganache Ethereum test blockchain, and connected via a web3.js/React dApp with IPFS image storage and MetaMask wallet interaction to automate payment and penalty execution.
key_background_studies: Ballard (2000) - foundational lean construction work on variation and reliable workflow, and local responsibility assignment used as basis for smart contract design
Hamledari and Fischer (2021a,b,c) - blockchain/smart contract applications for progress payments and information accuracy improvements
Lu et al. (2021a,b) - smart contract oracle concepts and incompatibility of decentralized blockchains with centralized construction practices
Wang et al. (2020) - blockchain-based information management framework for precast supply chain, showing cost reduction potential but lacking construction specifications
Tao et al. (2021) - blockchain framework for collaborative BIM design highlighting storage/cybersecurity limitations
Xue and Lu (2020) - semantic differential approach to reduce blockchain storage needs for BIM changes
Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez (2020) - Microsoft Project add-on conditioning smart contract payments on schedule/payment data
Elghaish et al. (2020) - blockchain framework automating financial transactions across the construction value chain
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - identified challenge of smart contract flexibility and lack of ex-post governance adjustment
Chen et al. (2022) and Li et al. (2023) - prior simulation-based approaches to generate smart contract stipulations for dynamic construction scenarios
Dimitrov and Golparvar-Fard (2014) - image classification of material/surface features for progress tracking
Kropp et al. (2018) - recognizing as-built activity states via computer vision against BIM
Yang et al. (2022) - contracts should serve control, coordination, and adaptation functions
findings: The deep learning model achieved 96.31% accuracy classifying activity completion status from images, improved to 98.93% after Bayesian network refinement using schedule prerequisite logic. Simulation of 570 scenarios showed that delays in B1+B2 and CA1 could be recovered by adding workforce, but delays in CA2 (the schedule bottleneck) could not be recovered; action items should be applied early in the schedule rather than to later minor activities; workforce additions with the best ROI (saved hours per $100) were superior to maximum workforce assignment; and GMM clustering successfully categorized risk scenarios into tolerable, recoverable, intolerable, and unrecoverable categories to guide optimal mitigation selection. The developed dApp prototype successfully synchronized detected progress with smart contract stipulations, automatically triggering payments for on-time completion and both extra workforce assignment plus documented, quantified penalties for delayed completion, validated through an Ethereum/Ganache/IPFS/MetaMask-based prototype. The framework demonstrated potential to automate management intelligence, reduce manual checking/negotiation, and enhance transparency, though private blockchain immutability and lack of a comprehensive governance/quality-compliance mechanism remain limitations.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate payment and penalty enforcement based on detected as-built progress rather than relying on manual, retrospective compliance checking.
ideas.quote: Smart contracts provide a reliable means of automating management stipulations based on certain detected events, such as assigning payments based on the progress of work

ideas.idea: A major barrier to smart contract adoption is the lack of a mature governance model specifying rights, obligations, and sanctions for noncompliance.
ideas.quote: Lacking a mature and consistent governance model is the primary barrier impeding the deployment of smart contracts in the industry (Hamledari and Fischer 2021b).

ideas.idea: Smart contracts inherently struggle to handle unexpected/dynamic situations because there is no mechanism to patch stipulations after deployment.
ideas.quote: Ensuring the flexibility of smart contracts in handling unexpected cases will likely continue to be a significant challenge, because it is impossible to patch ex-post when no governance mechanism for such adjustments is implemented beforehand in the smart contracts

ideas.idea: Traditional construction practice defers delay penalties until near project completion, making it difficult to retrospectively assign responsibility, whereas smart contracts can document and quantify responsibility for delays in real time at the subcontractor level.
ideas.quote: In current construction practice, the penalty for delayed completion is usually not enforced until or near project completion... It is difficult for project managers to retrospectively check and identify who should be held responsible for the delays... The developed smart contract function clearly documents the reasons and quantifies the damages each contracted subcontractor should be responsible for

ideas.idea: Contracts (and by extension smart contracts) should fulfill three functions—control, coordination, and adaptation—to mitigate risks, integrating lean production's focus on local responsibility of the party to whom work is assigned.
ideas.quote: contracts should serve three fundamental functions—Control, Coordination, and Adaptation—to mitigate different risks. The developed smart contracts integrate lean production management to focus on the 'local' responsibility of those to whom the various parts are assigned or contracted

ideas.idea: Simulation-based scenario and risk analysis can be used to derive optimal, situation-aware smart contract stipulations (e.g., workforce reassignment) that adapt automatically to different delay severities, rather than fixed static clauses.
ideas.quote: a simulation model was constructed to predict potential risks given the detected scenarios and determine the optimal survival plans as smart contract precautions. The smart contract could implement corresponding strategies automatically, given the various detected scenarios.

ideas.idea: Immutability of blockchain records is both a strength (preventing manipulation of progress data by managers) and a weakness (errors cannot be corrected), raising the need for more robust governance to ensure fairness and avoid disputes in self-executing contract stipulations.
ideas.quote: the fact that the information contained in the blocks is inviolable also represents a major drawback, since this information cannot be changed when errors occur. This will increase the challenge of designing a more robust smart contract governance mechanism to ensure that all the self-executed stipulations are fair enough to eliminate potential disputes.

ideas.idea: Current smart contract implementations have focused mainly on schedule/workforce optimization and payment, but quality compliance checking is an important governance gap that future contractual mechanisms need to address.
ideas.quote: The developed smart contract stipulations only considered workforce assignment to optimize schedule control. In reality, checking construction quality compliance is also crucial to ensuring the construction processes and products conform to regulations.

objectives: To identify critical contract conditions related to variations across four international standard contract formats (FIDIC Silver Book, AIA A141, NEC4 ECC, PSSCOC), evaluate their importance and contractor favorability through expert survey, and present a systematic risk evaluation process for variation management, illustrated through two case studies.
problem_statement: While prior studies have compared variation/change order provisions across standard contracts, none have systematically identified and evaluated the risks that different contract conditions pose to contractors; this gap leaves contractors without tools to assess variation-related contractual risk during tendering and execution.
methodology: A six-step comparative and empirical approach: (1) comparison of variation-related clauses across FIDIC Silver Book, AIA A141, NEC4 ECC, and Singapore PSSCOC, yielding 30 key contract items in 6 groups; (2) development of a questionnaire with 5-point importance and 7-point favorability Likert scales; (3) survey of 62 experienced contract experts (52 responses) with construction/contract experience; (4) importance ranking analysis using mean Likert scores; (5) Kruskal-Wallis H-test and Mann-Whitney U-test (with Bonferroni correction) to compare favorability across contracts; (6) two illustrative case studies (metro tunnel projects in Hong Kong and Singapore) applying the importance/favorability framework to real contracts, validated through interviews with project variation management personnel.
key_background_studies: El-adaway et al. (2016) - compared variation-related provisions in traditional standard contracts (FIDIC 1999 edition) with descriptive explanations, categorizing into power/authority, execution/procedure, and price/time changes; this study builds on and updates this to the 2017 FIDIC edition
Syal and Bora (2016) - comparative review of Change Order clauses in US and Canadian standard contracts, focusing on procedures and costs; identified as lacking risk evaluation dimension
Abotaleb and El-adaway (2017) - analyzed payment contract conditions across FIDIC, AIA, and NEC
Assaad et al. (2020) - explored differences in back-to-back provisions across US-based standard contracts (AIA, ConsensusDocs, EJCDC)
McConnell and Clevenger (2018) - analyzed frequently disputed sections of AIA A201, highlighting Change Order clauses as a recurring dispute source
Thompson et al. (2000) - found NEC improved contractual relationships and management practices in UK construction, emphasizing fairness
Ibbs (2012) - quantitative literature review data on impact, possibility and intensity of variations on productivity
Wambeke et al. (2011) - investigated causes of variations related to schedule variances via literature review
Ko et al. (2021) - used natural language processing on historical variation order data to determine causes of variations
findings: Contract conditions on valuation of variations and change in law were rated most critical by contractors, while procedure and daywork clauses were less significant. The valuation method (C17) was ranked most important but showed no significant favorability difference across contracts since all allow negotiation. Absence of change-in-law clauses (as in AIA and NEC) resulted in lower contractor favorability than contracts explicitly addressing such changes (FIDIC, PSSCOC). Value engineering clauses were generally favorable to contractors but favorability depended on how benefit-sharing was structured (NEC's contractor-favorable sharing outperformed FIDIC's employer-favorable sharing). Limitation on variations was highly important, with contracts restricting variations to a reasonable scope rated more favorable. The two case studies validated the risk evaluation tool, showing that high-risk-scored contract items (e.g., absence of change-in-law and value engineering clauses) corresponded to actual project management challenges experienced by contractors.

ideas.idea: Standard contract formats are frequently modified by employers during tendering in ways that shift risk onto contractors by removing or replacing contractor-favorable clauses.
ideas.quote: these modifications tend to align with the employers’ interests and bring potential risks to contractors, often resulting in the removal or replacement of contractor-favorable clauses to unfavorable clauses

ideas.idea: Clearly defined valuation/payment methods for variations are viewed as the single most critical contractual condition for managing contractor risk and ensuring fairness.
ideas.quote: This condition determines how contract prices are adjusted with the priority in response to variations under different circumstances, directly impacting the contractor’s interest. A clearly defined valuation method ensures fairness in cost compensation and contributes to minimizing unnecessary disputes.

ideas.idea: The absence of contractual provisions addressing changes in law creates significant unassessed risk for contractors, forcing reliance on claims rather than structured variation mechanisms.
ideas.quote: the absence of a clause to manage changes in law through variations complicated project management for the contractor, who was forced to rely solely on claim procedures to address these issues

ideas.idea: Benefit-sharing arrangements in value engineering/proposal clauses strongly affect contractor motivation to propose efficiency improvements; unbalanced sharing discourages participation.
ideas.quote: If the clauses governing the sharing of benefits from value engineering result in a disproportionate allocation of profit to the employer, contractors may be reluctant to initiate value engineering, potentially missing opportunities for improved project outcomes.

ideas.idea: Clear limitations on the scope of variations protect contractors from unbounded or unreasonable instructions and reduce uncertainty in resource and schedule planning.
ideas.quote: if this clause is not stipulated, contractors will face uncertainty when they prepare the additional work and resource plan. In practice, excessive variations beyond the general scope frequently result in claims and disputes between contractors and employers.

ideas.idea: The absence of a contractor's right to decline variations is a recurring, significant risk factor observed across projects, exposing contractors to compulsory unplanned work.
ideas.quote: The absence of the right to decline variations by contractor [C5] was also identified as a notable risk, ranking as the fifth and sixth most significant variation-related contract risk in Projects A and B, respectively.

ideas.idea: Standard contracts vary in whether disputes over variation valuation are resolved unilaterally by the employer/engineer or through mutual agreement, affecting fairness perceptions.
ideas.quote: when the contractor disagreed with the valuation assessment, the method for determining the final value was left to the employer’s sole discretion, which typically favored the employer’s interests.

ideas.idea: A systematic risk evaluation tool combining importance weighting and favorability scoring can help contractors identify and prioritize high-risk contract clauses before and during project execution.
ideas.quote: This study applied the importance as a weighting value to highlight critical risks and the favorability as a reference to evaluate risks in actual projects.

ideas.idea: Despite being rooted in common law, different standard contracts diverge significantly in how they define and procedurally manage variations, reflecting differing contract philosophies (descriptive/civil-law-influenced FIDIC vs. collaborative NEC vs. flexible AIA).
ideas.quote: despite these formats being rooted in the same common law system, the definition of variation differs significantly across each format

objectives: To explore the critical cost influencing factors (CIFs) and critical stakeholders of prefabricated construction (PC) in China based on stakeholder theory and social network analysis, and to propose stakeholder-specific strategies to reduce PC capital cost.
problem_statement: High capital cost is one of the biggest obstacles to PC adoption in China, but few studies have examined the complex interactions between cost influencing factors or clarified the roles and management focus of different stakeholders in controlling PC cost.
methodology: A hybrid qualitative-quantitative approach: literature review to establish a preliminary list of CIFs; two rounds of expert interviews (17 experts from government, developer, designer, contractor and manufacturer stakeholder groups, selected via chain referral sampling) to determine stakeholder-associated CIFs and rate mutual influence on a 5-point Likert scale; consistency checked via within-group agreement index (Rwg); resulting adjacency matrix (18 nodes, 140 links) analyzed using social network analysis (whole-network and ego-network analysis) in NetMiner4.0 to identify critical factors, links, stakeholders and influence conduction paths; validation of proposed strategies by simulating removal of key nodes/links and recalculating network density and centrality.
key_background_studies: Mao et al. (2016) - analyzed nine PC cases finding lack of experience, skills and market demand increase cost
Hong et al. (2018) - compared eight projects across three regions to discuss PC cost composition and BIM inflation model
Qi et al. (2018) - found incremental cost stems from interior wall component production and hoisting/grouting
Xue et al. (2017) - used mean analysis to identify CIFs and found 85% of developers reject PC due to high cost
Wu et al. (2019b) - constructed transaction costs framework for PC supply chain tested via SNA
Xia et al. (2017, 2018) - integrated risk management and stakeholder management frameworks informing this study's stakeholder approach
Luo et al. (2019) - developed a risk network for PC supply chain in Hong Kong using SNA from stakeholder perspective, providing methodological precedent
Teng et al. (2017) - defined PC stakeholders and their roles used as basis for stakeholder classification in this study
findings: The government, developer and contractor are the most critical stakeholders in PC cost control; developer's cognition/attitude and transaction costs are the most critical cost influencing factors; relevant standards/codes and government cognition are foundational/root factors with wide-reaching influence; contractor's application of information technology and design accuracy/standardization are also highly influential; close interactions exist between designer, contractor and manufacturer; strategies including improved government standards, developer transaction cost reduction, contractor IT adoption, and designer-manufacturer collaboration were validated via network simulation to significantly reduce network density and centrality, indicating effective cost control.

ideas.idea: Developers' cognition and attitude toward PC is a central barrier that determines whether prefabrication technology is adopted, often leading to reliance on cheaper traditional cast-in-place methods.
ideas.quote: Developers have low enthusiasm to adopt PC due to their own reasons, such as insufficient cognition of PC, lack of PC cost control experience and other stakeholders' reasons

ideas.idea: Transaction costs borne by developers—for estimating, partner identification, approvals, monitoring and negotiation—are a major and often overlooked component of PC cost.
ideas.quote: the developer to pay additional transaction costs for estimating, partner identification, approval and license acquisition, monitoring and negotiation activities (Wu et al., 2019b)

ideas.idea: Lack of comprehensive government standards and codes for PC design, production, construction and inspection hampers effective regulation and drives up cost.
ideas.quote: Lack comprehensive policies and specific standardized implementation measures (Jiang et al., 2018) make the government unable to effectively supervise and regulate the construction activities of various stakeholders

ideas.idea: Mandatory minimum assembly/prefabrication rates set by government can create market barriers by increasing costs for developers, discouraging PC adoption.
ideas.quote: a high mandatory minimum assembly rate will hinder some developers from entering the PC market and form market barriers

ideas.idea: Design changes are a major source of hidden transaction costs and reputational damage for developers, reducing other stakeholders' willingness to collaborate.
ideas.quote: the hidden cost loss caused by design changes are mainly reflected in the decline in the reputation of developers and the reduced willingness of other stakeholders to cooperate with them subsequently

ideas.idea: Standardization and accuracy of design reduce production and construction costs by enabling economies of scale and reducing rework.
ideas.quote: High design accuracy and standardization can ensure the quality and schedule of the project, promote the scale of production, and reduce the capital cost of prefabrication

ideas.idea: Contractors' effective use of integrated information technologies (BIM, RFID, GPS) improves construction site management efficiency and reduces incremental on-site costs.
ideas.quote: The integrated use of BIM, GPS, RFID and other information technology can monitor the construction process and improve management efficiency

ideas.idea: Collaboration between designer and manufacturer during the design stage can improve component standardization and enable scale production, avoiding unnecessary cost.
ideas.quote: the manufacturer can participate in the work of the designer in advance and propose optimization suggestions to facilitate the standardization of component design

ideas.idea: Contracts and coordination mechanisms could be used by developers to encourage and restrict designers toward improved accuracy and standardization.
ideas.quote: in the process of entrusting design tasks, detailed contract terms can be formulated to encourage and restrict the designer to improve the accuracy and standardization of the design

ideas.idea: The complex interdependence between stakeholders means that cost overruns in PC arise from multi-party interactions rather than isolated causes, requiring integrated stakeholder-based contractual and management strategies.
ideas.quote: cost and CIFs mean differently for different stakeholders and there are currently few studies on the cost analysis of PC from the perspective of stakeholders

objectives: To develop a literature-based analysis framework of contract sources of ambiguity; to evaluate causes of disputes by analyzing selected Canadian Superior court cases; and to analyze relevant terms from Canadian standard contracts (CCDC) that can address the significant causes of dispute identified from the case analysis, comparing modular/offsite construction (MOC) with conventional on-site construction (COC).
problem_statement: There are no standard contracts for MOC in Canada, so MOC projects adopt and modify COC standard contracts, increasing the potential for contractual disputes. Prior research on contractual disputes has focused mainly on COC and taken niche or subjective qualitative approaches, leaving a gap in systematically understanding causes of disputes and litigation specific to MOC projects.
methodology: A two-phase mixed methodology: Phase 1 used qualitative literature review of 105 articles (57 COC, 48 MOC) to extract 396 sources of contractual ambiguity, clustered into a four-level hierarchical 'fishbone' framework (categories, subcategories, classes, subclasses) and quantified by weighted frequency. Phase 2 involved collecting Canadian Superior Court construction cases (2000-2019) from CanLII across four provinces (BC, ON, AB, QC), filtering 4708 cases down to 178 contractual dispute cases (20 MOC, 158 COC), analyzing project characteristics, party typology, contract types, and applying the Phase 1 framework to classify and quantify causes of dispute, then comparing literature-based versus case-based findings and mapping to CCDC 2 and CCDC 14 general conditions.
key_background_studies: Arcadis [2] - reported rising trend in dispute resolution time and project delays across regions, motivating the study of disputes.

Odeh and Battaineh [17] and other survey-based studies (e.g., [5,14,16,19]) - conducted questionnaire surveys to identify common causes of disputes, representing prior methodological approach used for comparison.
Cakmak and Cakmak [8] - defined causes of conflicts/disputes from responsible parties' perspective via literature analysis, an alternative qualitative approach referenced as background.
[1,12] - identified causes of construction litigation through literature analysis, cited as niche/subjective prior approaches that the current study seeks to improve upon.
[3] - provided the previously developed four-level hierarchical conceptual framework (categories, subcategories, classes, subclasses) that this study adopted as its starting structural model.
[18] - noted that MOC has different features from COC despite same construction codes/materials, and identified CCDC 14 as suitable for MOC.
[10] - identified CCDC 2 stipulated price contract as the most popular standard contract in the Canadian construction industry.
[13] - noted that in MOC, up to 85-90% of construction work is completed in the factory, with remaining work done on-site, relevant to payment structuring issues.
[6] Build Force Canada - forecasted significant construction industry growth in BC, ON, and AB, used to justify province selection.
findings: MOC has risen globally but lacks standard contracts in Canada, leading to modified COC contracts being used, increasing dispute potential. Literature review found 'ambiguity in contract terms' most critical for COC (31%) while 'lack of local industry readiness' was major for MOC (25%) literature-wise. Court case analysis of 178 cases (20 MOC, 158 COC) found General Contractors were the primary litigation initiators; stipulated price and non-standard written contracts were most litigious; no MOC case used a standard contract while 25 COC cases did. Case-based analysis showed 'ambiguity in contract terms' was dominant for both MOC and COC (over 70% of frequency), with 'unclear payment terms' as the top MOC-specific class and 'unclear terms for changes in work' top for COC. Discrepancies existed between literature-predicted MOC issues (e.g., transportation/lifting limitations, industry readiness) and actual court case findings, which did not surface these issues. Payment terms, especially progress and final payment definitions in CCDC 2/14 (e.g., 'Products' definition, clause 5.2.3, 5.2.8), were identified as poorly suited to MOC's off-site fabrication process, creating financial burden for modular contractors regarding claiming costs for modules not yet delivered/incorporated. Study recommends revising CCDC payment terms and insurance coverage clauses to better address MOC-specific delivery and fabrication timelines.

ideas.idea: No standard contract currently exists for MOC in Canada, forcing MOC projects to modify COC-based standard contracts, which raises dispute risk.
ideas.quote: there are yet no standard contracts for MOC (at least in Canada), so MOC projects usually adopt the standard contracts structured for conventional and on-site construction (COC) and modify them to suit project requirements.

ideas.idea: None of the analyzed MOC litigation cases used a standard contract, unlike COC cases where some did use standard contracts.
ideas.quote: There is no MOC project with a standard contract, while 25 COC cases with standard contracts seek judgment at the court.

ideas.idea: Payment issues, especially unclear progress and final payment terms, are the primary cause of litigation in MOC projects.
ideas.quote: In accordance with the number of Canadian court cases in MOC projects, ‘payment issues’ (i.e., progress payment, final payment, withhold) are the primary concerns.

ideas.idea: CCDC 14's payment clause (5.2.3) is designed for on-site completion inspection and does not adequately address MOC's off-site fabrication model, where most work occurs in a factory before delivery.
ideas.quote: This payment definition is only suitable for the COC method. The completed works are measured and certified based on the on-site completion inspection but not applicable for the MOC method.

ideas.idea: The contractual definition of 'Products' in CCDC standard contracts may not be interpreted to include prefabricated modules, creating ambiguity and financial burden for modular contractors seeking payment before installation.
ideas.quote: the definition of ‘Products’ might not be interpreted as modules among the contractual parties since the standard contracts express it as material, machinery, equipment, and fixtures incorporated into the work.

ideas.idea: MOC contracts may need new clauses allowing claims for modules/components not yet delivered or delivered but not incorporated, along with extended insurance coverage during transport/storage.
ideas.quote: a contract for the MOC project may need to add contract terms that allow claiming for modules or components yet to deliver to the place of the work and delivered but not yet incorporated into the work. Simultaneously, extend the insurance coverage for the modules or components during transportation or stored elsewhere.

ideas.idea: CCDC 14 (design-build stipulated price) is considered the most suitable standard contract for MOC projects among existing Canadian standard forms.
ideas.quote: CCDC 14 design-built stipulated price contract, on the other hand, is the most suitable one for MOC [4, 18].

ideas.idea: Literature-identified MOC-specific ambiguity sources such as transportation/lifting limitations and lack of local industry readiness did not appear as actual causes of litigation in court cases, indicating a gap between perceived and litigated issues.
ideas.quote: Unlike the MOC literature, ambiguities related to external factors such as ‘lack of local industry readiness’, ‘transportation and lifting limitation’ could not be spotted in MOC court cases in Canada.

ideas.idea: Ambiguity in contract terms is the dominant cause of litigation for both MOC and COC projects in Canadian court cases, suggesting a shared underlying contractual drafting problem regardless of construction method.
ideas.quote: Based on the case analysis, ‘ambiguity in contract terms’ is a major concern for the Canadian construction industry, with more than 70% of the total frequency. This, interestingly, applies to both MOC and COC projects.

ideas.idea: Modular builders and clients frequently dispute completed project quality and defects, which leads to withholding of final payment balances.
ideas.quote: modular builders and clients often dispute the completed project quality and defect issues that caused final payment rejection or withheld the contract balance amount.
